A Wildfire Cuts the Rail Line to Machu Picchu

A wildfire that broke out on 4 August 2026 near the railway between Ollantaytambo and Machu Picchu forced Peru to suspend train service to the Inca citadel, one of South America’s most visited sites. Authorities said the blaze reached the area around kilometre 107 of the route and caused rocks to fall onto the tracks.

With the fire still active and a risk of landslides on the narrow gorge, operators halted circulation on the affected section. Mitigation work began early the next morning, and rail service resumed on 5 August once crews cleared the tracks.

The disruption left hundreds of Peruvian and foreign travellers waiting at stations in Cusco and the Sacred Valley, many of whom said they had received little clear information from rail operators about when service might resume.

Ten Train Frequencies Suspended

Reports from Cusco said at least ten scheduled train frequencies were cancelled on the Ollantaytambo–Machu Picchu line, the main way visitors reach the citadel. PeruRail confirmed the cancellation of several departures from both Ollantaytambo and Machu Picchu Pueblo (Aguas Calientes).

The route is a single-track mountain railway shared by operators including PeruRail and Inca Rail. Because there is no road directly to Machu Picchu Pueblo, a rail closure effectively seals off the town and the trailheads used by day visitors.

Tour groups reported missed entry times, and some travellers said pre-paid tickets for early-morning slots were lost when the trains did not run.

Government Offers Rescheduling and Refunds

Peru’s Ministry of Culture said it was coordinating with public and private bodies through its regional cultural directorate in Cusco to respond to the emergency, and activated a special protocol for unforeseen and force-majeure situations.

Under that protocol, the ministry said affected visitors would be able to reschedule or obtain a refund for their Machu Picchu entrance tickets, which are sold through the official Tuboleto platform. The measure is aimed at travellers who could not reach the citadel because of the rail suspension.

Separately, the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Tourism (Mincetur) said it was carrying out permanent monitoring of the situation and confirmed that trains had been suspended for safety reasons, adding that service would resume only once conditions allowed.

Why the Railway Is the Lifeline

Machu Picchu sits high in the Andes above the Urubamba River, and the train is the practical gateway for the vast majority of visitors. From Cusco, tourists typically travel to Ollantaytambo and board a train down the valley to Machu Picchu Pueblo, then take a shuttle up to the ruins.

There is no conventional road to the town, so weather, fires and landslides on the rail corridor can strand travellers with few alternatives beyond a long trek. Similar disruptions have occurred in past years, including flooding that has repeatedly damaged the tracks.

For that reason, Peruvian authorities treat any incident on the line as both a safety issue and a tourism-management challenge, since thousands of people can be affected within hours.

What It Means for Travellers and Cusco’s Economy

Tourism is a mainstay of the Cusco region, and Machu Picchu is its anchor. Extended or repeated disruptions can ripple through hotels, guides, restaurants and transport operators that depend on a steady flow of visitors.

For travellers already in Peru, the immediate advice is to confirm train status with operators before heading to the valley and to keep proof of purchase for tickets and tours in case rescheduling or refunds are needed. Visitors planning trips should build in buffer days during the dry-season fire risk.

Officials said they would keep coordinating with rail operators and emergency services to protect visitors and residents, and to restore access as soon as the corridor is judged safe.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why were trains to Machu Picchu suspended in August 2026?

A wildfire near kilometre 107 of the Ollantaytambo–Machu Picchu railway on 4 August 2026 sent rocks onto the tracks and made circulation unsafe, forcing operators to suspend service on that section.

Can affected tourists get a refund for Machu Picchu tickets?

Yes. Peru’s Ministry of Culture activated a force-majeure protocol allowing affected visitors to reschedule or obtain refunds for citadel entrance tickets bought through the official Tuboleto platform.

Is there another way to reach Machu Picchu without the train?

There is no direct road to Machu Picchu Pueblo, so the railway is the main access. When it closes, the alternatives are limited to long treks, which is why rail suspensions strand many visitors.

World.title: Pampa Energía Posts Record Q2, Eyes US$11 Billion Plan
World.content:
Energy: Buenos Aires

Key Facts —Results. Pampa Energía reported Q2 2026 sales of US$746 million (up 53% year-on-year) and adjusted EBITDA of US$415 million (up 75%). —Profit. Net income attributable to shareholders reached US$172 million, about 4.3 times the same quarter of 2025. —Oil ramp-up. Crude oil output jumped 194% to 23,400 barrels per day as the Rincón de Aranda field in Vaca Muerta scaled up. —Investment. Pampa and affiliate Transportadora de Gas del Sur (TGS) are advancing four main projects worth close to US$11 billion. —Context. Pampa is an Argentine energy group active in oil, gas, power generation and petrochemicals, and reports its accounts in US dollars.

Pampa Energía posted record-strong second-quarter results on higher Vaca Muerta oil output, while pressing ahead with a portfolio of oil, gas and power projects worth close to US$11 billion.

Pampa Energía is ramping up shale oil output at Rincón de Aranda in Vaca Muerta, Neuquén. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A Record-Strong Second Quarter

Pampa Energía (NYSE: PAM; Buenos Aires: PAMP) reported sales of US$746 million in the second quarter of 2026, up 53% from a year earlier. Adjusted EBITDA rose 75% to US$415 million, and net income attributable to shareholders reached US$172 million, roughly 4.3 times the figure booked in the same quarter of 2025.

The company said the gains were driven by Argentina’s new wholesale-power framework, which supported higher spot prices and business-to-business supply contracts, together with higher crude oil output and stronger gas sales to power plants. Because Pampa reports in US dollars as its functional currency, its figures do not require peso conversion.

The results extend a run of expansion tied to Vaca Muerta, the vast shale formation in Argentina’s Neuquén province that has turned the country into a growing oil and gas exporter.

Shale Oil Output Nearly Triples

Total oil and gas production rose 28% to 107.5 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day. Within that, crude oil output surged 194% to 23,400 barrels per day, while gas production grew 10% to 84,100 barrels of oil equivalent per day.

The jump reflects the ramp-up of Rincón de Aranda, a field in the “black oil” window of Vaca Muerta. Pampa has made the block the centrepiece of an upstream push aimed largely at export markets.

Power generation, still a core business, rose 14% to 5,363 gigawatt-hours, and the gross margin per megawatt-hour climbed 30% to US$33.6, helped by seasonal spot prices and tighter integration between Pampa’s gas and power operations.

The company operates through Oil and Gas; Generation; Petrochemicals; and Holding, Transportation and Others segments. It generates electricity through thermal plants, hydroelectric plants, and wind farms with a 5,472 megawatt (MW) installed capacity. The company also explores for and produces oil…

A Near US$11 Billion Investment Push

Beyond the quarter, Pampa is advancing a set of large projects that, together with its affiliate Transportadora de Gas del Sur (TGS), add up to close to US$11 billion in planned investment across oil, gas and midstream infrastructure.

The largest single piece is the full development of Rincón de Aranda, an upstream plan of about US$4.5 billion approved under Argentina’s large-investment incentive regime; the company has said it envisions drilling 259 wells and running the field through 2041. Pampa is also backing a granulated-urea plant near Bahía Blanca estimated at about US$2.7 billion.

The remaining projects sit in transport and liquefied natural gas, including stakes in a new Vaca Muerta oil pipeline and a floating LNG venture designed to ship Argentine gas abroad. Taken together, they mark a strategic tilt toward exports.

Why the Incentive Regime Matters

Several of Pampa’s projects have been admitted to Argentina’s Régimen de Incentivo para Grandes Inversiones (RIGI), a framework that offers tax and foreign-exchange benefits to very large, long-horizon investments. For international investors, the regime is meant to provide legal stability in a country with a long record of policy swings.

Rincón de Aranda has been classified as a strategic long-term export project, a status that supports the company’s plan to sell most of its output abroad. Pampa estimates exports from the field could total roughly US$17 billion over its useful life.

Attribution matters here: these are company and government projections, not guaranteed outcomes, and they depend on oil prices, execution and Argentina’s macroeconomic path.

Balance Sheet and What Comes Next

The build-out is capital-intensive. Net debt rose to US$1.3 billion as of 30 June 2026, from US$801 million at the end of 2025, which the company attributed to higher spending at Rincón de Aranda and increased collateral tied to oil hedging. Cash and equivalents stood at US$979 million.

For the first half of 2026, sales reached US$1,319 million, up from US$900 million a year earlier, with foreign-market sales more than doubling to US$313 million.

Pampa scheduled a results videoconference for 5 August 2026, led by chief executive Gustavo Mariani. The near-term questions for investors are how quickly Rincón de Aranda can lift output and whether export infrastructure is delivered on schedule.

Frequently Asked Questions

How did Pampa Energía perform in the second quarter of 2026?

Pampa Energía reported Q2 2026 sales of US$746 million (up 53%), adjusted EBITDA of US$415 million (up 75%) and net income attributable to shareholders of US$172 million, about 4.3 times the same quarter of 2025.

What is Pampa Energía’s US$11 billion investment plan?

It refers to four main projects that Pampa and affiliate TGS are advancing across oil, gas and infrastructure, worth close to US$11 billion in total, led by the roughly US$4.5 billion Rincón de Aranda development and a roughly US$2.7 billion urea plant.

Where is Pampa Energía’s oil growth coming from?

Mainly from Rincón de Aranda, a field in the black-oil window of the Vaca Muerta shale in Neuquén, where crude output rose 194% year-on-year to 23,400 barrels per day in Q2 2026.

World.title: Argentina’s BCRA Reform Bill Would Ban State Financing
World.content:
Economy: Buenos Aires

Key Facts —Bill. President Javier Milei announced a bill to overhaul the charter of the Central Bank (BCRA) in a 30 July 2026 national address and sent it to Congress. —Single mandate. The reform would make preserving the value of the currency the BCRA’s sole mission, reversing a 2012 change that had broadened its objectives. —No state financing. It would bar the BCRA from financing the national Treasury, provinces and municipalities, including buying government debt in the primary market. —Profits and independence. The bill repeals transfers of the BCRA’s accounting profits to the Treasury and would require a two-thirds congressional vote to remove the bank’s leadership. —Next step. The measure entered the Chamber of Deputies and was referred to committee; the IMF has pressed for the charter reform.

President Javier Milei has sent a BCRA reform bill to Argentina’s Congress that would ban the Central Bank from financing the state and restore a single mandate to protect the value of the currency.

The Banco Central in Buenos Aires, focus of Milei’s BCRA reform bill. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

What Milei Proposed

In a national television address on 30 July 2026, President Javier Milei unveiled a bill to rewrite the organic charter of the Banco Central de la República Argentina, the law that defines the bank’s mission and powers, and said it would go to Congress.

The government casts the reform as a way to lock in monetary discipline after years of high inflation. Milei, a self-described libertarian economist, blamed past money-printing for financing what he called a political ‘robbery,’ framing the bill as protection against a return to those practices.

Banning Monetary Financing of the State

The core provision would prohibit the BCRA from financing the state at any level. According to Infobae and Bloomberg, the ban covers the national Treasury, provincial and municipal governments, and would also block purchases of government debt in the primary market.

For a country where deficits were long covered by printing pesos — a practice widely blamed for recurrent currency crises and triple-digit inflation — the change is meant to remove the central bank as a lender to the government.

A Single Mandate and Stronger Independence

The bill would restore a single mandate: preserving the value of the currency. That reverses a 2012 reform that had added several objectives, such as employment and development, to the bank’s remit.

It also aims to shield the institution from political pressure. The draft would require a two-thirds majority in Congress to remove the bank’s leadership and repeal the transfer of the BCRA’s accounting profits to the Treasury, according to Argentine media.

From Closing the Bank to Reforming It

The move marks a notable shift for Milei, who campaigned on shutting the central bank altogether and dollarising the economy. Reforming rather than abolishing it, commentators noted, is a more pragmatic route to the same goal of constraining monetary financing.

Analysts cited by the Buenos Aires Herald and MercoPress compared the design to models that prize price stability and independence, with some drawing parallels to Peru’s long-standing framework.

The IMF and the Political Road Through Congress

The reform aligns with the International Monetary Fund, which has pressed Argentina to strengthen the central bank’s independence as part of its program. That external backing gives the government additional leverage to argue for passage.

Approval is not guaranteed. The bill entered the Chamber of Deputies and was referred to committee, and Milei’s bloc lacks a majority, meaning he must negotiate with other parties. The opposition has historically resisted ceding fiscal room, and debate is expected to be contentious.

What Comes Next

The immediate step is committee review in the lower house, where lawmakers can amend the text before any floor vote. Timing will depend on the government’s ability to build alliances.

For investors, the bill is a signal of intent on inflation and fiscal restraint; its ultimate weight will depend on what survives Congress. Until then, the BCRA reform bill is a proposal, not yet law.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does Milei’s BCRA reform bill do?

It would bar the Central Bank from financing the national Treasury, provinces and municipalities, restore a single mandate to preserve the currency’s value, repeal profit transfers to the Treasury and require a two-thirds vote to remove bank leadership.

Has Argentina’s Congress approved the reform?

No. Milei sent the bill to Congress after a 30 July 2026 address; it entered the Chamber of Deputies and was referred to committee. His bloc lacks a majority, so passage is uncertain.

Why does the reform matter?

Argentina long financed deficits by printing pesos, fuelling high inflation. The bill aims to end monetary financing and strengthen central-bank independence, a change the IMF has encouraged.

World.title: CJNG Leaders Face US Charges, US$100 Million Bounty
World.content:
Security: Michoacán

Key Facts —Charges. On 5 August 2026, the US Justice Department unsealed criminal charges against five senior leaders of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG). —Accused. Prosecutors named Julio César Montero Pinzón, Carlos Andrés Rivera Varela, Hugo Gonzalo Mendoza Gaytán, Ricardo Ruiz Velasco and Julio Alberto Castillo Rodríguez, all described as fugitives; the charges are allegations yet to be tested in court. —Allegations. The indictments allege decade-long conspiracies to traffic cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin and fentanyl to the United States, plus firearms offences carrying up to two consecutive life terms. —Rewards. The State Department raised total reward offers to more than US$100 million for information on eight CJNG fugitives, with individual bounties of up to US$25 million. —Backdrop. The move follows the February 2026 killing of CJNG founder Nemesio Oseguera, ‘El Mencho,’ in a Mexican military operation; Mexico’s government has ruled out a US troop presence on its soil.

US prosecutors have charged five CJNG leaders and offered more than US$100 million in rewards, escalating Washington’s pressure campaign against the Mexican cartel months after its founder was killed.

Security in Michoacán, Mexico, the backdrop to US charges against five CJNG leaders. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

What US Prosecutors Announced

On 5 August 2026, the US Department of Justice said it had unsealed criminal charges against five senior leaders of the Cártel de Jalisco Nueva Generación, one of Mexico’s most powerful drug-trafficking organisations, in an announcement coordinated with the DEA, FBI, Homeland Security Investigations and other agencies.

‘Today’s unsealing of criminal charges against five high-ranking CJNG leaders marks another decisive step in our campaign to dismantle the cartels,’ acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said in the department’s statement. The defendants have not entered pleas and are presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

Who the Five Accused Are

According to court filings summarised by the department, prosecutors identify the five as Julio César Montero Pinzón, Carlos Andrés Rivera Varela, Hugo Gonzalo Mendoza Gaytán, Ricardo Ruiz Velasco and Julio Alberto Castillo Rodríguez. All remain at large.

The filings allege that Montero Pinzón and Rivera Varela founded and led an armed enforcement unit known as the ‘Grupo Elite,’ while Mendoza Gaytán — described as El Mencho’s godson — is accused of procuring weapons. Castillo Rodríguez is described as El Mencho’s former son-in-law. These remain unproven allegations.

The Charges and Potential Penalties

The unsealed indictments, filed in the District of Columbia, allege that the five took part in decade-long conspiracies to manufacture and distribute cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin and fentanyl destined for the United States, the department said.

The filings also allege the use of firearms, including machineguns and destructive devices, in furtherance of the trafficking. If convicted, each defendant would face up to two consecutive life sentences, according to the Justice Department.

Rewards and the Wider Crackdown

Alongside the charges, the State Department’s narcotics bureau announced it was raising total reward offers to more than US$100 million for information leading to the arrest or conviction of eight CJNG fugitives, with individual bounties ranging up to US$25 million.

The department framed the actions as part of a Homeland Security Task Force established under a Trump administration executive order, and noted that Washington designated the CJNG a foreign terrorist organisation in February 2025.

Michoacán and the Security Backdrop

Michoacán frames this story for a reason: the western state is one of the most violently contested corners of Mexico, where the CJNG has fought rivals such as Cárteles Unidos and La Familia Michoacana. Mexican security forces have surged into the state at various points in 2026.

The US role, however, is being exercised through indictments, rewards and intelligence and law-enforcement cooperation rather than boots on the ground. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has publicly ruled out a US military deployment on Mexican territory, and no US combat presence in Michoacán has been confirmed.

The wider backdrop is the February 2026 killing of CJNG founder Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as ‘El Mencho,’ in a Mexican military operation that US authorities said they supported with intelligence. His death set off a violent scramble for control.

What Comes Next

Because the five accused are fugitives, the charges are for now a pressure tactic: they globalise the manhunt, expose assets and raise the cost of sheltering the men. Any trial would depend on capture or extradition.

For Mexico, the sequence keeps security cooperation with Washington in the spotlight ahead of the 2026 World Cup, while testing how far the two governments will coordinate without crossing Mexico’s red line on sovereignty.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who did the US charge in the CJNG case?

The Justice Department unsealed charges against five senior CJNG leaders: Julio César Montero Pinzón, Carlos Andrés Rivera Varela, Hugo Gonzalo Mendoza Gaytán, Ricardo Ruiz Velasco and Julio Alberto Castillo Rodríguez. The charges are allegations that must be proven in court.

How much reward money is on offer?

The State Department raised total reward offers to more than US$100 million for information on eight CJNG fugitives, with individual bounties of up to US$25 million, announced on 5 August 2026.

Are US troops deployed in Michoacán?

No US combat deployment in Michoacán has been confirmed. Mexico’s government has ruled out a US military presence on its soil; Washington’s role runs through indictments, rewards and intelligence and law-enforcement cooperation.

World.title: Bolivia’s US$1.9 Billion IMF Loan Deal Awaits Congress Approval
World.content:
Economy: La Paz

Key Facts —Deal. IMF staff and the Bolivian authorities reached a staff-level agreement on 29 July 2026 for a 36-month Extended Fund Facility (EFF) of about US$1.9 billion. —Status. The arrangement still requires approval from the IMF’s Executive Board and, the Fund and Reuters note, from Bolivia’s Congress; no money has been disbursed yet. —Purpose. The program aims to restore macroeconomic stability, rebuild international reserves, reduce fiscal and external imbalances and strengthen social safety nets, the IMF said. —Catalyst. The Fund says the program could help unlock more than US$5 billion in additional financing from the World Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank and other partners. —Context. Bolivia, under President Rodrigo Paz, is battling its worst economic crisis in four decades, with fuel and US dollar shortages and inflation above 20%.

The IMF and Bolivia have reached a staff-level deal on a Bolivia IMF loan of about US$1.9 billion, a 36-month program that still needs board and congressional approval before any funds are released.

La Paz, Bolivia, where the government reached a US$1.9 billion staff-level deal with the IMF. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

What the IMF and Bolivia Agreed

On 29 July 2026, the International Monetary Fund announced that its staff and Bolivian officials had reached a staff-level agreement on a new 36-month arrangement under the Extended Fund Facility worth about US$1.9 billion, according to the Fund’s own statement.

The talks were led on the IMF side by a team headed by Joana Pereira, with discussions held between May and July in Bolivia and in Washington. If it proceeds, it would be Bolivia’s first multi-year IMF arrangement since 2006.

A Staff-Level Deal, Not Yet Approved

A staff-level agreement is a preliminary step, not a signed loan. The IMF said the arrangement will go to its Executive Board only after Bolivia implements agreed prior actions, and as of early August no board decision or disbursement had taken place.

There is a second gate at home. Reuters reported that IMF borrowing is politically sensitive in Bolivia and that the program will also need to pass a fragmented Congress, one of President Paz’s toughest challenges.

The headline figure also fell short of expectations. Reporting by Bloomberg and Reuters noted the government had hoped for something closer to US$2.5 billion to US$2.8 billion.

What the Program Would Fund

The IMF says the program is designed to restore macroeconomic stability, rebuild depleted international reserves, cut fiscal and external vulnerabilities and protect the most vulnerable through stronger social safety nets.

Crucially for a cash-strapped state, the Fund argues its seal of approval could catalyse a wider package worth more than US$5 billion over the program, drawing in the World Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank and other lenders.

That framing matters because the loan alone is modest relative to Bolivia’s needs; its value lies partly in reopening access to other financing.

The Crisis Behind the Request

Bolivia is grappling with what analysts call its worst economic crisis in four decades. Years of falling natural-gas output have drained the export earnings that once funded fuel subsidies and a fixed exchange rate.

The result is acute shortages of US dollars and fuel, inflation running above 20% and a fiscal deficit that outside estimates put in double digits as a share of GDP. Long queues at service stations have become a symbol of the strain.

Political Hurdles at Home

President Rodrigo Paz, who took office in late 2025, has pursued austerity, including cuts to costly fuel subsidies, and declared a state of emergency in June after weeks of road blockades by opponents.

His government has separately lined up billions in multilateral commitments from the IDB, the CAF development bank and Japan’s JICA, alongside a World Bank loan approved earlier in 2026. The IMF deal is meant to anchor that broader effort.

Even so, ratifying an IMF program in a divided legislature is far from assured, and opponents may frame conditions such as subsidy cuts as politically costly.

What Comes Next

The sequence now is procedural but decisive: Bolivia must complete prior actions, the IMF board must sign off, and Congress must give its backing before funds flow. Each step carries its own risk of delay.

For markets and ordinary Bolivians alike, the test is whether the agreement can be converted into disbursements and reforms fast enough to ease the dollar and fuel shortages squeezing daily life.

Frequently Asked Questions

How big is the Bolivia IMF loan?

The IMF and Bolivia reached a staff-level agreement on a 36-month Extended Fund Facility of about US$1.9 billion, announced on 29 July 2026. It is smaller than the roughly US$2.5 billion to US$2.8 billion the government had sought.

Has the IMF loan been approved?

Not yet. The deal is at staff level and still requires approval from the IMF’s Executive Board and, according to the Fund and Reuters, from Bolivia’s Congress. No funds have been disbursed.

What is the money for?

The IMF says the program aims to restore macroeconomic stability, rebuild international reserves, reduce fiscal and external imbalances and strengthen social safety nets, and could unlock more than US$5 billion in additional financing.

World.title: Dollar Stuck Near ₡450 as Costa Rica Keeps Policy Rate
World.content:
The Banco Central de Costa Rica set its reference exchange rate on Wednesday at ₡449.80 for the purchase of United States dollars and ₡455.01 for their sale, holding the colon at a level of strength that has persisted through much of the year and that continues to shape the purchasing power of every household whose income arrives in a foreign currency.

The reference rate is not the rate most people encounter at a bank counter. The Central Bank calculates it from transactions carried out on Monex, the wholesale foreign exchange market where financial institutions trade currency among themselves, and publishes it each business day as the country’s official benchmark.

Commercial banks set their own window rates independently, and those figures routinely sit several colones on either side of the reference. A traveler exchanging cash at an airport counter or a resident converting a pension deposit will almost always receive less favorable terms than the published benchmark suggests, which is why the reference rate functions as a measure of the currency’s value rather than as a quotation any individual can transact at.

The exchange rate sits within a monetary policy framework that the Central Bank has kept deliberately still. The Monetary Policy Rate stands at 3.00 percent, with the deposit facility at 2.25 percent and the credit facility at 3.75 percent. The basic passive rate, the reference figure that governs a large share of colon-denominated lending and savings products in Costa Rica, was reported at 3.64 percent. The effective rate on dollar deposits stood at 3.04 percent, meaning savings held in colones currently earn a higher nominal return than equivalent balances held in dollars, one of several conditions that has supported demand for the local currency.

Inflation remains the anomaly in the picture. The Central Bank reported year-on-year inflation at negative 0.318 percent through June, against an official target of 3 percent with a tolerance band of one percentage point in either direction. That places the country in mild deflation and well beneath the range the Central Bank aims for.

Falling consumer prices have accompanied the currency’s appreciation, since a stronger colon reduces the cost of imported goods, fuel among them, and those reductions filter through the price index. The combination has produced an unusual situation in which the cost of living measured in colones has edged downward while the cost of living measured in dollars has risen.

Economic activity has continued to expand through the period. The Central Bank’s monthly index of economic activity, measured on a trend-cycle basis, recorded year-on-year growth of 3.541 percent through May.

For anyone converting foreign currency into colones, the arithmetic is direct. At Wednesday’s reference purchase rate, a monthly income of $2,000 converts to roughly ₡899,600, and $5,000 to approximately ₡2,249,000. Those same amounts would have yielded substantially more colones during the period of weaker currency that preceded the appreciation, and the difference is absorbed entirely by rent, groceries, utilities, school fees and every other obligation denominated in local currency. Fixed incomes arriving from abroad have not adjusted, while the colon amounts those incomes must cover have not fallen in proportion.

The reverse applies to exporters and to businesses that earn in colones while carrying dollar-denominated debt, for whom the stronger currency reduces the local-currency burden of repayment but compresses margins on goods sold abroad. Tourism operators who price in dollars and pay wages, rent and suppliers in colones sit on the difficult side of that equation, absorbing the gap between a stable dollar price and rising colon costs.

The Central Bank publishes the reference rate each business day, along with window rates reported by commercial banks and a summary of Monex trading. The rate does not update on weekends or public holidays, when Friday’s figure carries forward until the next business day.

World.title: San José’s Parque Central Closes for Six Months of Renovation
World.content:
If your route through downtown San José cuts across Parque Central, you need a new one. The park closed Monday and will stay closed for about six months while crews rebuild it from the ground up. The Municipality of San José shut the whole park rather than fencing off sections, because the work touches every part of it.

Expect the barriers to stay up until February 2027. Plan around Avenida 2 or Avenida 4 rather than through the middle, and give yourself an extra few minutes if you normally cross here on the way to the Cathedral or the Melico Salazar theater. Both remain open, as do Plaza de la Cultura, Parque Morazán and Parque España a few blocks east and north.

The contract went to Montedes S.A. and is worth ₡619,149,088, or roughly $1.36 million at the Central Bank reference rate of ₡454.18 for August 4. The municipality has said it wants the park to work again as the city’s main meeting point, and the design leans that way. Crews will lay new paving stones in varying colors, expand the green areas and put them on an irrigation system, and replace the benches and other street furniture. Pergolas will go in to create shade, and a new lighting system is meant to make the park usable after dark rather than something you walk quickly past.

Two additions stand out. One is a sensory park, designed so that people with different disabilities can actually use the space. The other sits underneath the park’s best-known feature: the historic kiosk will get a café built into its basement level. That café will not open with the park. The municipality plans to put it out to public tender once construction finishes, which pushes its likely opening into the first half of 2027. So when the barriers come down in February, expect a finished park and an empty basement.

The scale of the closure reflects how heavily the park gets used. Municipal figures put annual foot traffic above 2.3 million people, and the site has anchored the capital since 1885, when what was then the Plaza Principal was first planted with trees and laid out with paths and a fountain.

Six-month construction timelines in downtown San José have a history of slipping, and the municipality has not said what happens if the schedule does. For now, February 2027 is the date on the contract.

World.title: Costa Rica Approves Wildlife Crossings Law to Protect Animals
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Legislative Assembly unanimously approved a bill today requiring wildlife protection measures in new and existing public infrastructure projects, a major legal step aimed at reducing animal deaths on roads and reconnecting fragmented habitats. The Wildlife Crossings Bill passed its second and final debate with 56 votes in favor. One lawmaker was absent.

The proposal now moves to the Executive Branch for the president’s signature and publication in La Gaceta, Costa Rica’s official government newspaper. It will take effect once published. The legislation adds to Costa Rica’s Organic Environmental Law that requires appropriate wildlife crossings wherever scientific studies show that a national or municipal road disrupts natural movement or divides aquatic or land habitats.

The requirement applies everywhere, with particular attention paid to protected areas, national parks, forest reserves, state-owned natural areas and locations identified as natural wildlife crossing points. Crossings may include tunnels, culverts, dry underpasses, fencing and elevated bridges or ropes used by monkeys, sloths, squirrels and other tree-dwelling animals. The design will depend on the species, terrain and risks identified at each location.

The bill does not establish a fixed nationwide number of crossings. Instead, technical and scientific studies will determine where structures are necessary, what kind should be installed and how they should be maintained. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport, municipal governments and other state agencies must coordinate with the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC), when planning new projects. That process may determine that a wildlife crossing is required or that the project does not need one.

Existing roads are also covered. Wildlife protection measures must be considered when authorities replace road components or carry out rehabilitation, improvements, widening or maintenance in areas where roads have disrupted ecological connections. The law requires wildlife measures to be included during the earliest planning and budgeting stages of public infrastructure projects. The costs of building and maintaining the crossings must be calculated before construction begins rather than added after a project is underway.

Costa Rica’s National Environmental Technical Secretaria (SETENA), will be responsible for verifying that projects include the required wildlife commitments before receiving environmental approval. Developers must conduct technical studies to identify high-risk areas, including places with documented wildlife collisions. SINAC must approve those studies, while the company responsible for the project must install the crossings according to its environmental management plan.

Within 24 months after regulations for the law take effect, SINAC has to begin identifying natural wildlife crossings and other vulnerable points along existing roads and infrastructure. Agencies will then coordinate the measures needed to protect animals at those locations. The regulations must also establish standards for design, maintenance and monitoring so authorities can determine whether the crossings are being used and working as intended.

Wildlife issues have been documented across Costa Rica for decades. More than 19,000 roadkill records were compiled between 1996 and 2025. On a 20-kilometer (12-mile) section of Route 253 between Comunidad and Papagayo, researchers estimated approximately 7,000 wildlife collisions during 2019 alone.

Road construction can also isolate animal populations even when collisions do not occur. By dividing forests and natural migration routes, highways can restrict access to food, breeding areas and other habitat. The new legislation specifically calls for crossings that support animal movement, genetic exchange and healthier ecosystems.

Former Frente Amplio lawmaker Ariel Robles introduced the proposal in June 2022. Lawmakers approved it in its first debate on April 21, 2026, before extending its four-year legislative deadline in June to prevent the bill from being archived. Once signed and published, the legislation will make wildlife connectivity a required part of Costa Rica’s public infrastructure planning instead of an optional environmental measure.

World.title: Guatemala’s Fuego Volcano Eruption Forces 1,700 Evacuations
World.content:
A powerful eruption of Guatemala’s Fuego Volcano has forced authorities to evacuate at least 1,700 residents from areas near the crater and declare the highest alert level Tuesday in zones exposed to falling ash. Fuego, considered the most active volcano in Central America and located near the capital, entered an eruptive phase Monday morning.

Its activity intensified overnight into Tuesday, with streams of lava flowing down its slopes and enormous columns of gas and ash rising into the sky. “The volcano is going through one of its most critical explosive phases,” producing mudflows, incandescent rocks, gases and ash, said Edwin Rojas, director of the Institute of Volcanology, known as Insivumeh.

Guatemala’s National Coordinator for Disaster Reduction, Conred, began evacuating communities near the volcano Monday evening and declared an orange danger alert nationwide. On Tuesday, the agency raised the alert to red in the departments of Sacatepéquez, Chimaltenango and Escuintla, which are home to 1.6 million people.

According to Conred Executive Secretary Claudinne Ogaldes, about 29,000 people are directly exposed to ashfall, making evacuations from the area essential. Ogaldes urged residents of nearby communities to wear masks and cover their water and food supplies. Conred said more than 1,700 people had been evacuated.

“We have become accustomed to living with a volcano that is always active, but this time it was simply too much,” said Sonia Vasquez, a 50-year-old resident of El Porvenir who spent the night in a shelter. Alejandro Garcia, another resident, also evacuated Monday evening after the alert was issued.

“We ran out, terrified,” he said, after seeing lava flowing down the volcano’s slopes. Despite the higher alert level, authorities reopened a road leading to the colonial city of Antigua, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Guatemala’s main tourist destinations. Operations at Guatemala City’s international airport have not been affected so far.

Lava Fountain

The Ministry of Education suspended in-person classes at schools in three communities near the volcano. “It would be better if we could move somewhere else because we live with this fear, since the volcano gives no warning,” said Lidia Ortiz, another evacuee. According to Insivumeh experts, a lava fountain reaching between 200 and 300 meters above the crater formed Monday, while the ash column rose to more than 7,000 meters.

As the ash dispersed at altitudes between 5,000 and 6,000 meters, it traveled as far as 130 kilometers westward. The institute said 34 earthquakes were recorded in Guatemala during the previous 24 hours, most with epicenters in the Pacific Ocean. Guatemala is located along the Pacific Ring of Fire and experiences significant seismic and volcanic activity.

Several mass evacuations have taken place in recent years because of eruptions at Fuego, which rises 3,763 meters above sea level and is located about 35 kilometers from Guatemala City in a straight line. In June 2025, around 800 people were evacuated because of eruptions at Fuego.

In 2018, 215 people were killed and about 200 others were reported missing after volcanic flows devastated a village on the slopes of the volcano.

World.title: Sanitation worker killed after falling into path of school bus on Lord’s Bank Road
World.content:
Sanitation worker killed after falling into path of school bus on Lord’s Bank Road

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have detained a school bus driver following a fatal traffic accident that claimed the life of a sanitation worker on Lord’s Bank Road in the Belize District.

The accident occurred at approximately 1:15 p.m. on Wednesday, August 5, 2026. Police say Andrew Smith was standing near the left rear of a garbage truck that had been parked along the roadside when he allegedly fell into the traffic lane.

Smith was subsequently struck by an approaching school bus and died from his injuries. Public reports have identified the victim as 39-year-old Andrew Alexander Smith. (Facebook)

The bus driver was detained, and urine samples were obtained as part of the standard investigative process. Police have not indicated whether impairment is suspected.

Investigations into the circumstances surrounding the fatal accident are continuing.

The cause remains framed as preliminary, since police are still investigating how Smith fell into the roadway.

World.title: F**k Around & Find Out: Delivery truck man shoots two robbers who held him up
World.content:
F**k Around & Find Out: Delivery truck man shoots two robbers who held him up

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two men are receiving medical treatment under police guard after they were shot during an armed robbery on Mahogany Street in Belize City on Wednesday afternoon.

According to police, the incident occurred at approximately 1:00 p.m. while a salesperson was seated inside a parked delivery truck. Two armed men reportedly approached the vehicle and demanded the sales proceeds in the salesperson’s possession.

The salesperson complied with the demand initially then subsequently fired upon the alleged robbers, shooting and injuring both men. Earlier reports confirmed that police had responded to a robbery and shooting involving a delivery truck in the area.

The injured men were transported for treatment and remain under police guard. Their identities, medical conditions and the amount of money stolen have not yet been disclosed.

Police investigations into the incident are continuing.

World.title: Jimmy Rojas remanded after allegedly climbing lamp post and damaging nearly $49,000 in police camera equipment
World.content:
Jimmy Rojas remanded after allegedly climbing lamp post and damaging nearly $49,000 in police camera equipment

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Jimmy Rojas was remanded to the Belize Central Prison on Wednesday after being arraigned on two counts of damage to property involving government-owned surveillance cameras in the Saint Martin de Porres area.

Police allege that cameras and related equipment valued at approximately $49,000 were damaged at the corners of Tibruce Street and Croton Lane, and Flamboyant and Lavender streets, during the early morning hours of August 1.

Investigators said surveillance footage showed a slim-built man climbing the camera posts and repeatedly striking the equipment with an object resembling a knife. Police reportedly identified the man as Rojas.

Rojas appeared unrepresented before a Senior Magistrate and pleaded not guilty to both charges. Although he was offered bail on the new allegations, the court revoked his bail in a separate burglary case after finding that he had allegedly breached his curfew and failed to attend a scheduled court appearance.

He was consequently remanded to prison until September 14, 2026, when both the damage-to-property and burglary cases are scheduled to return to court.

Rojas was previously charged with burglarizing the security booth at Saint Luke Methodist Primary School in March. He had also been charged in connection with the 2024 murder of Jose Matus, also known as “El Whapo,” but that charge was later withdrawn on the instructions of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

World.title: Lennox Gentle remanded for murder of Kiffer McKenzie
World.content:
Lennox Gentle remanded for murder of Kiffer McKenzie

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Twenty-four-year-old Lennox Linsford Gentle was arraigned on Wednesday for the murder of Kiffer Alexander McKenzie, who was fatally shot in downtown Belize City on June 13.

Gentle, a resident of Vernon Street, was escorted to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court under heavy police security. He appeared unrepresented before a Senior Magistrate, who explained that no plea would be taken because the charge is an indictable offence. Bail could not be granted at the Magistrate’s Court level, and Gentle was remanded to the Belize Central Prison until October 1, 2026.

McKenzie was seated inside his blue Jeep near the corner of Albert and Orange streets with his two children when a gunman approached the driver’s side and fired several shots. The shooter reportedly escaped on a motorcycle.

Despite being injured, McKenzie drove along Albert Street before colliding with a parked vehicle near Tropicana. He was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he was pronounced dead shortly after 10:20 a.m.

Police recovered several expended 9mm shells and bullet fragments from the primary scene. Investigators also collected a blood sample from McKenzie’s vehicle.

According to police, information obtained through the department’s Fusion Center and a statement from a female Special Constable helped investigators identify the alleged shooter and eventually led to Gentle’s arrest.

McKenzie was the son of the late George “Junie Balls” McKenzie.
