On 3 August, Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that he did not rule out adopting such legislation. However, he said the authorities had not yet discussed any specific proposals.

“There is indeed a need to respond to the coordinated attack against our identity,” Kobakhidze said.

He also identified possible subjects of future regulation, including saints, kings and prominent public figures.

According to Kobakhidze, insults directed at Georgian saints and kings are part of “a chain of coordinated, commissioned actions.”

“These are not simply untalented people. These are people carrying out a specific assignment. The purpose of that assignment is simple: they are trying to weaken our national identity. That is why they are doing all this,” he said.

Kobakhidze did not specify who had allegedly commissioned the campaign. He also provided no evidence to support the claim.

“We must take every possible measure to counter such processes. If that requires adopting a law, we can discuss that as well.”

Kobakhidze’s remarks do not necessarily mean such a law will be adopted. However, they indicate that the initiative has already received political backing from the prime minister.

Meanwhile, MPs aligned with the ruling party have outlined possible restrictions in greater detail.

Georgian Dream MP Irakli Kadagishvili linked the issue to public swearing, abusive language and hooliganism.

“When people use obscene language against a specific individual or institution at a rally, is that freedom of expression or simply abusive language and hooliganism? We cannot just leave it like this.”

Kadagishvili said he did not know what the legislation might ultimately contain. At the same time, he suggested that the media could also fall within its scope.

The MP claimed that certain television channels — referring to opposition broadcasters — had aired 3,500 “anti-church” reports over the past year and a half. He did not explain how he arrived at that figure or what criteria he used to classify the reports as “anti-church”.

Kadagishvili also suggested that “offensive” media content could become subject to legal regulation.

Guram Macharashvili, a member of the People’s Power party, openly called for penalties for public insults. He said the law should protect faith, the church, the patriarch and national traditions.

“When you publicly insult values such as faith, the church, the patriarch or our traditions, that should, of course, be punishable.”

Macharashvili argued that Georgia had offered excessive protection to dissenting views.

“Dissent has always enjoyed a certain degree of protection in Georgia. But recently, I would say it has been protected in an ultra-liberal, excessive way, and that needs to change.”

What counts as an “insult” — and who decides?

Article 17 of Georgia’s Constitution guarantees freedom of thought and expression. It also prohibits persecution for expressing an opinion.

The constitution also guarantees media freedom and prohibits censorship.

The state may restrict freedom of expression only by law and only when necessary in a democratic society. Such restrictions may serve aims including public safety and the protection of other people’s rights. The constitution does not list “insulting national values” as a separate ground for limiting freedom of expression.

At the same time, freedom of expression is not absolute. The law may restrict incitement to violence, threats, harassment or defamation. However, such restrictions must be clearly defined and predictable.

By contrast, “insulting national values” is a far more ambiguous concept. It remains unclear whether the proposed law would protect the reputation of specific individuals or instead safeguard abstract values or historical figures.

It is also unclear who would decide which saints, kings and public figures deserve legal protection. Would the law apply only to historical figures? Where would the line be drawn between legitimate historical criticism and an “insult”?

For example, pro-government television channels also launched a campaign against literary scholar Levan Berdzenishvili after he criticised the policies of Georgian King Erekle II. Berdzenishvili neither joked about the king nor used obscene language. Nevertheless, Georgian Dream MPs and pro-government media sharply attacked him.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed restrictions would apply to satire, works of art or academic research. Another unanswered question is whether critical media coverage of members of the clergy could be treated as an “insult to sacred values”.

Protecting patriotism or deepening political divisions?

Opposition politicians see the initiative as an attempt to mobilise political support.

Giorgi Sharashidze of the For Georgia party argues that the government is trying to claim a monopoly on patriotism.

“They have a very calculated strategy — to gain exclusive ownership of patriotic issues. Everything serves that goal. They want everyone else to appear as opponents of Georgia’s identity, traditions and church, while presenting themselves as the sole defenders of those values.”

Giorgi Shalamberidze of the First Georgia party believes the proposed law could serve another political purpose.

“It could be a political manoeuvre. It may help mobilise a particular segment of voters, or it could mark the beginning of a much broader tightening of legislation in the long term.”

Shalamberidze acknowledged that freedom of expression can be restricted in certain circumstances. However, he pointed to Georgia’s current political environment.

“If this becomes law and is used as a tool, the question is how it will affect political actors, political parties and their freedom of expression, and to what extent it will become a mechanism for restricting their rights.”

Historians’ concerns

It remains unclear where the proposed law would draw the line between insulting a historical figure and offering a critical assessment. That uncertainty raises concerns for historians, researchers and authors.

Assessing historical figures often requires revisiting disputed facts, competing interpretations and long-established narratives.

If the state decides which interpretations are acceptable, the law could become a tool for restricting academic research and scholarly debate.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed rules would apply to academic publications, public lectures, textbooks or documentary films.

Another unanswered question is who would decide where legitimate historical criticism ends and an “insult” begins.

Historian Irakli Khvadagiani argues that placing faith and artistic expression into legal categories contradicts their very nature.

“Faith and creativity do not recognise prohibitions, nor do they accept categories imposed unilaterally. The idea of banning them through legislation is absurd. Humanity went through this centuries ago. It is simply the obsession of a dictator trying to bend society to his will.”

Risk of creating artificial divisions?

Conflict analyst Paata Zakareishvili believes the proposed legislation could fuel ethnic and religious tensions. In his view, the vague concept of “protecting national identity” risks creating new fault lines within society.

“There are not enough supporters of this ideology in Georgia for Georgian Dream to sustain permanent tensions between Christians and Muslims, between Georgians and non-Georgians, or between Georgian speakers and those who do not speak the language.”

Zakareishvili sees elements of far-right ideology in the government’s approach. He argues that it runs counter to the principles of equality and justice.

“This is a classic example of pure far-right ideology. Humanity has gone through this countless times, and it has repeatedly led to catastrophe and world wars, bringing nothing but destruction.”

The conflict analyst also links the initiative to the electoral cycle. Georgia’s next parliamentary elections are not due until October 2028. However, Zakareishvili believes the ruling party has already begun preparing its campaign.

“Georgian Dream is getting ready for the elections. Before the vote, it needs to create exactly these kinds of flashpoints.”

Cases of violence carried out in the name of “protecting traditions” Invoking the need to protect national and religious values is not a new phenomenon in Georgian politics. In 2023, a man attacked Zurab Japaridze, leader of the Girchi – More Freedom party, in the city of Gori. The attacker said he acted because Japaridze had insulted the church and was “corrupting children”.

Later that year, protesters disrupted a lecture by Levan Berdzenishvili in Kvareli. They accused him of insulting King Erekle II and Christian values. In Tbilisi, demonstrators also threw eggs at Berdzenishvili.

On 5 July 2021, opponents of Tbilisi Pride attacked journalists and activists. They justified the violence by saying they were defending the family, the church and traditional values. More than 50 journalists were injured.

In November 2019, far-right and anti-LGBT groups tried to disrupt the premiere of the film And Then We Danced. The Georgian Orthodox Church described the film as “an insult to Georgia’s traditional values”. Protesters attempted to storm cinemas. One of them threw a stone at civil activist Anna Subeliani, causing a serious head injury. Police arrested 12 people that evening.

In January 2024, activist Nata Peradze splashed paint on an icon in Tbilisi’s Holy Trinity Cathedral depicting Saint Matrona of Moscow alongside Joseph Stalin. Far-right groups later gathered outside Peradze’s home, demanding that she be punished.

On 17 May 2013, thousands of people, including members of the clergy, attacked participants in an anti-homophobia rally. At least 17 people were injured. In 2021, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the violence had taken place in circumstances of the state’s effective acquiescence.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is particularly relevant in this context because the substance and rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia years earlier.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially justified their version as a tool to ensure transparency over foreign funding. They later expanded it into a mechanism used against independent media outlets and civil society organisations.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is relevant here because both the substance and the rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia in recent years.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially presented their version as a transparency measure for foreign funding. They later expanded it into a tool used against independent media and civil society organisations.

It is therefore worth looking at how Russia gradually developed legislation under the banner of protecting “traditional values”, religious feelings and historical memory.

Russia did not build its legal framework for protecting religion, historical memory and “traditional values” overnight. The system evolved step by step.

Offending religious feelings

In 2012, members of the punk group Pussy Riot staged an anti-Vladimir Putin performance inside Moscow’s Cathedral of Christ the Saviour. A court convicted them of hooliganism motivated by religious hatred.

A year later, Russia toughened Article 148 of its Criminal Code by criminalising public acts that show clear disrespect for society and are committed with the intention of offending the religious feelings of believers.

One of the best-known cases under the law involved blogger Ruslan Sokolovsky, who filmed himself playing Pokémon Go inside a church and posted the video online. In other videos, he also criticised religion and the Russian Orthodox Church.

In 2017, a court gave Sokolovsky a three-and-a-half-year suspended prison sentence. The case involved several criminal charges, including offending believers’ religious feelings and inciting hatred.

In 2024, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Sokolovsky’s conviction had violated his right to freedom of expression. The court found that offensive or vulgar speech does not automatically amount to hate speech.

“Traditional values” as state policy

In November 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on protecting “traditional Russian spiritual and moral values”.

The document lists patriotism, dignity, life and the traditional family among those values. It also includes service to the fatherland, historical memory and continuity between generations.

According to the decree, external forces threaten these values by acting inside Russia through extremist and terrorist organisations.

The decree also identifies the United States and other “unfriendly states” as sources of those threats.

Russian authorities have explicitly linked cultural and values policy to national security.

A similar narrative has emerged in Georgian Dream’s campaign. Both initiative groups have spoken of a coordinated attack on Georgia’s “national identity”. Prime Minister Kobakhidze has used the same wording.

Legal protection of history

Article 354.1 of Russia’s Criminal Code is titled “Rehabilitation of Nazism”. Lawmakers originally introduced it to prohibit the denial of crimes established by the Nuremberg Tribunal.

However, the law goes much further. It also bans the dissemination of what authorities consider to be “knowingly false information” about the Soviet Union’s actions during the Second World War. The article also protects the honour and dignity of war veterans.

In 2021, lawmakers added a new offence covering the “insulting of the memory of the defenders of the Fatherland”. The law also criminalises offensive use of military glory symbols.

As a result, the legislation does more than prohibit denial of historical facts. It also protects the state’s official interpretation of the Soviet Union’s role in history.

According to a 2025 study by the human rights project OVD-Info, Russian courts handed down 25 convictions under Article 354.1 between 2015 and 2019. Many of the cases concerned interpretations of the Soviet Union’s actions and historical comparisons.

Between 2022 and May 2025, OVD-Info recorded 212 prosecutions under the same article.

A court gave Kazan resident Zulfiya Sitdikova a two-year suspended sentence over posters reading “No to war” and “9 Way”. She replaced the “M” in “May” with a “W”, and investigators interpreted this as desecration of Victory Day symbols.

Authorities also opened a criminal case against historian Mikhail Belousov. Investigators accused him of denying facts established by the Nuremberg Tribunal and spreading false information about the Soviet Union.

Prosecutors also opened two cases against historian Tamara Eidelman. They argued that her video lectures showed disrespect for Russia’s military remembrance days.

Russia has therefore created a system in which historians and society no longer have the final say in historical debates. Instead, investigators, expert witnesses and the courts have become the ultimate arbiters.

Where will Georgia draw the line?

Georgia has not yet introduced such a bill, so it is impossible to say whether it will follow the Russian path.

However, statements by members of the ruling party already suggest a broad range of protected subjects, including the church, the patriarch, saints, kings, public figures, traditions and even media content.

Russia’s experience also suggests that broadly defined protected values can gradually expand over time.

Protecting national values in Georgia

World.title: Georgian scam call centres: old fraudsters, new address? An investigation
World.content:
Georgian scam call centres that came under the spotlight during an international investigative project in 2025 have reportedly resumed operations from a new location. According to the investigative outlet Monitor, people linked to AK Group have relocated to an office at 68 Mirian Mepe Street in Tbilisi.

The outlet says its journalists conducted covert surveillance at the address for six months. They say they identified several of the same individuals who had been seen near AK Group’s previous office last year. According to Monitor, the footage also shows some of the same vehicles that regularly appeared at the company’s former location.

Journalists say they repeatedly spotted vehicles used by Akaki Kevkhishvili, who is widely believed to be the real operator of AK Group. The cars carried the registration numbers AK100KK and AK200KK. Investigators seized one of them in 2025 as part of the ongoing criminal investigation.

According to Monitor, AK Group’s registered owner and director, Meri Shotadze, also regularly visited the same address. She used two different vehicles, one of which investigators have also seized, while the other is registered to another person.

The investigation also claims that several agents who previously worked at AK Group’s former office have reappeared at the new location. They include Anzhelika Chkhapelia, who allegedly used the alias Marina Novikova; Misha Bayramov; Valerian Gigauri; Giorgi Gotman; and Ketevan Malashkhia, who allegedly used the alias Ashley Moriarty. According to Monitor, Malashkhia is a cousin of Akaki Kevkhishvili’s wife. The outlet also identified a Belarusian citizen, Lita, who had previously denied working at the call centre.

The journalists also say they identified security staff at the new office who had previously been seen outside AK Group’s former premises. They named former law enforcement officer Manuchar Gegia and former Zugdidi traffic police chief Levan Gogia.

According to the outlet, the office on Mirian Mepe Street closed after it announced the publication of its latest investigation. Both floors of the building are now being offered for rent.

Monitor says the premises had been leased since 2022 by RTM Imports, a company owned by Irakli Kvlividze, the brother of Akaki Kevkhishvili’s wife.

The journalists say they informed the Prosecutor’s Office on 1 July 2026 that AK Group’s managers and employees had been regularly operating from the office at 68 Mirian Mepe Street. According to Monitor, prosecutors have not clarified whether they investigated the information or whether the inquiry into the alleged fraud is still ongoing.

Background

In 2025, Monitor and more than 32 international media organisations published an investigation into AK Group’s activities. According to the report, the group employed 85 people and defrauded more than 6,100 people across Europe and Canada between 2022 and 2025. The journalists estimated that the operation generated more than $35 million in revenue over that period.

After the investigation was published, law enforcement authorities opened a criminal inquiry into organised fraud and the laundering of proceeds from crime on an especially large scale. Prosecutors have charged 11 people in the case.

In a separate bribery case, authorities also arrested former Georgian State Security Service chief Grigol Liluashvili. Prosecutors accuse him, in one of the counts, of providing protection to the call centres. A court has also frozen the assets and company shares of the alleged organisers and employees of the call centre network.

Investigation continues

According to Monitor, the Prosecutor’s Office told the outlet that it had requested legal assistance from Germany to help identify potential victims. Prosecutors also said they had sought additional information from journalists involved in the investigation, but claimed they had declined to cooperate.

In a written response, the Prosecutor’s Office said that “the final decision in the case largely depends on information and materials to be obtained from abroad through legal assistance.”

A separate Monitor investigation found that Akaki Kevkhishvili and Meri Shotadze had previously worked at another call centre, 100 Marketing Solutions. Authorities began investigating the company in 2023 and froze its shares as part of the inquiry. However, a court lifted the freeze in 2026.

Are Georgian scam call centres still operating?

World.title: Armenia approves new government as Pashinyan promises appointments based on merit
World.content:
Armenia approves new government

Alongside the opening of Armenia‘s 9th parliamentary term, the country formed a new government. In line with the constitution, Nikol Pashinyan took office as prime minister. He headed the electoral list of the Civil Contract party, which won a parliamentary majority.

The party submitted the required nomination documents for its leader to President Vahagn Khachaturyan, who then signed a decree appointing Pashinyan as prime minister.

On the previous day, at the proposal of Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and by decree of President Vahagn Khachaturyan, Deputy Prime Ministers Mher Grigoryan and Tigran Khachatryan were reappointed to their posts.

Most cabinet ministers were also reappointed.

Changes were made in the prime minister’s office. Former chief adviser to the prime minister and former Armenian ambassador to the United States, Lilit Makunts, has been appointed chief of staff. Her predecessor, Araik Harutyunyan, became an MP with the ruling Civil Contract faction on August 2.

At the same time, Pashinyan announced that he plans to appoint graduates of leading universities from around the world, selected through the government’s talent pool, to senior positions in the government.

“You will soon see these decisions implemented in practice,” the prime minister said.

Almost all ministers kept their portfolios

At Prime Minister Pashinyan’s recommendation, the following ministers retained their posts:

Defence – Suren Papikyan,

Internal Affairs – Arpine Sargsyan,

Foreign Affairs – Ararat Mirzoyan,

Territorial Administration and Infrastructure – David Khudatyan,

Environment – Hambardzum Matevosyan,

Health – Anahit Avanesyan,

Education, Science, Culture and Sport – Zhanna Andreasyan,

Justice – Srbuhi Galyan,

Labour and Social Affairs – Arsen Torosyan,

Economy – Gevorg Papoyan,

Finance – Vahe Hovhannisyan.

Only High-Tech Industry Minister Mkhitar Hayrapetyan did not keep his post. Pashinyan had previously said that Hayrapetyan himself had decided to step down.

David Tadevosyan replaced him. The prime minister introduced the new minister to ministry staff today. Mkhitar Hayrapetyan also attended the meeting. He said he would remain available around the clock if the new minister or his team needed advice.

“I am ready to contribute my modest knowledge and experience whenever you feel the need,” the former minister said.

David Tadevosyan graduated from the National Polytechnic University of Armenia. Between 2012 and 2014, he studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he earned a Master of Science in Engineering and Management.

Before taking up the ministerial post, Tadevosyan served as acting director of International Radio Network CJSC. Between 2024 and 2025, he headed Afeyan Initiatives for Armenia, an organisation founded by Armenian-American businessman, scientist and philanthropist Noubar Afeyan. Earlier in his career, Tadevosyan worked for the mining company Vallex Group, the Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Chemical Technologies, and SberSpinoff.

More than 1,000 applications for the government’s talent pool

On 15 June, shortly after his Civil Contract party won the 2026 parliamentary elections, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan invited graduates of the world’s leading universities to join the government. He encouraged them to put their knowledge and professional experience to work in public administration.

Today, the prime minister said the initiative had attracted strong interest, with the government receiving 1,141 applications.

“Following the initial screening, 459 candidates – around 40% of all applicants – advanced to the second stage. The average age of the candidates is 34,” Pashinyan said.

The prime minister announced that the government would create a talent pool based on interview results and professional assessments. Officials will match the selected candidates’ education, work experience and professional skills with the specific needs of the public administration system.

He added that candidates included in the talent pool could receive offers for positions in the public sector or other forms of cooperation during the course of this year.

Armenia approves new government

World.title: Opinion from Tbilisi: ‘It’s important to understand what kind of hell government is leading us into’
World.content:
Lasha Tugushi, head of the Liberal Academy, has commented on Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s claim that Georgian politicians have never used harsher rhetoric towards Russia than they do today, either before or after the 2008 war. Tugushi argues that the prime minister is repeating a familiar narrative promoted by the ruling Georgian Dream party.

According to Tugushi, the government is trying to present itself as the only force capable of “saving” the country, while linking the events of 2008 and 2022 forms part of that political strategy.

According to Tugushi, the suggestion that Georgia was ever pro-Russian is “nonsense”, as portraying Russia in a positive light has always been regarded as shameful in Georgian society.

Earlier, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze published a lengthy social media statement linking the war in Ukraine to Georgia’s domestic politics and the country’s opposition. According to Kobakhidze, the “Global War Party” needed the war in Ukraine in order to “fuel Russophobia among its agents around the world, including in Georgia, at the highest level.”

Lasha Tugushi said: “Anti-Russian sentiment existed in Georgia long before this. I remember the 1990s, when hostility towards Russia was very strong. The same was true after the war in Abkhazia. I cannot agree with the prime minister’s view that the key turning points were 2008 and 2022.

“I do not remember Georgia ever being pro-Russian. That is nonsense. What’s more, in respectable society it has always been considered shameful to say that Russia is a good country or to speak positively about Russian symbols.

“As for the focus on 2008 and 2022, that is part of a political game in which the leaders of Georgian Dream repeat a familiar narrative: that there is only one benevolent political force capable of saving Georgia – Georgian Dream. Everyone else, they claim, is either an enemy or a traitor seeking to drag the country into a devastating war.”

“But let’s remember who suspended Georgia’s EU integration, who is pursuing an anti-European policy today, who is confronting the ambassadors of Western countries, the European Parliament and the OSCE, who is picking fights with Sweden and France. Who came up with the scare story about the ‘deep state’? Georgian Dream did all of that.

“That does not mean the previous government made no mistakes or that everything was perfect. We need to understand that politics cannot be viewed in black-and-white terms. Things should be called by their proper names. The previous government has plenty of its own sins, and it paid the price for them. But today we see countries that were once on a par with Georgia moving closer to EU membership, while we, instead of advancing towards integration, are drifting further away from the West.”

“There are two main pillars on which the current government relies.

The first is fear – the claim that enemies want to open a second front in Georgia.

The second is the argument that our Georgian identity is under threat.

These are the two narratives they use to frighten people and rely on a fearful public in order to remain in power indefinitely.

But the fact is that they are not succeeding in their campaign against democracy to the extent they would like. It is crucial to see clearly what kind of hell this government is leading us into and what it actually looks like.

Over the past few years, Georgian Dream has taken many steps backwards and not a single step forward. This is an anti-national path. It is building authoritarianism and working against the Georgian people. I have many questions. For example, can Georgian Dream correct the grave mistakes it has made? I would like to believe it can find that path and that at least something will change.”

On Georgian Dream’s policies

World.title: Three charged for 'threats' amid probe into Black US teens' shady death
World.content:
Three people have been charged for allegedly threatening a US judge, authorities and witnesses connected to the investigation of a black teenager's mysterious death now shrouded in rampant speculation and an air of racial division.

Nolan Wells, 18, travelled on July 4 by boat with friends who, in photographs, all appeared to be white, to an unserviced island off the Mississippi coast for a party that one of the group described as a "final hurrah" before returning to college and work.

His friends later made it home, while Mr Wells did not. His body was found washed up on the island two days later.

Mysterious death ignites racial division in US Black teen Nolan Wells went to a party with white friends and didn't come home alive. His death is now shrouded in rampant speculation.

His family's search for answers has attracted the attention of notable US civil rights figures, celebrities and politicians demanding transparency in a police investigation into what caused his death.

The results of a state-commissioned autopsy have not yet been released but a second, independent post-mortem last month produced "inconclusive" preliminary results.

Mississippi authorities have not made any arrests or named suspects in relation to Mr Wells's death, and toxicology reports have not yet been released amid speculation the teenager may have been drinking heavily during the Independence Day party.

The alleged threats came amid an historic distrust of law enforcement and authorities in a state notorious for its fraught racial history.

Unsealed court documents show the individuals charged with allegedly making the threats were located in three separate states outside Mississippi and did not know Mr Wells, his family, friends or those involved in the investigation.

On July 14, a criminal complaint was lodged in a federal court in Mississippi against Joseph Dumarce, who was found to live in the Californian city of Sacramento — about 3,700 kilometres away from Mr Wells's hometown of Ocean Springs.

Federal Bureau of Investigation Special Agent Brodey Gibson alleged Mr Dumarce sent a threatening Facebook message on July 11 to the Jackson County Mississippi Chancery Court Judge's office.

The court documents show Mr Dumarce allegedly threatened to send a package that could explode to the office, which would result in "so much blood everywhere".

FBI investigators tracked the message to a Facebook account named "yaeyae962", which they then used to find other mobile apps using the account's email, and then later Mr Dumarce's home address, date of birth and mobile number.

Judge Ashlee Cole later posted an online screenshot of Mr Dumarce's message.

Loading...

She wrote in an earlier Facebook post that her son last saw Mr Wells on July 4 around 3pm and decided to "stay on the island and return inland later with another group of friends".

Ms Cole wrote that she deactivated her Facebook and that she feared for the safety of her children.

"No one in our family is trying in any way to impede with the investigation by law enforcement or to otherwise hamper the family and law enforcement's quest for answers," Ms Cole wrote, adding that her son "cooperated fully" with the sheriff's investigation.

Images widely shared online showed Nolan Wells was with white friends during a trip believed to have taken place on July 4. (Supplied: Christine Wonsley/Facebook)

More than a fortnight later, a second criminal complaint was filed with the same Mississippi court against Ohio citizen Michelle Edwards, who allegedly sent bomb threats to authorities.

Jackson County Sheriff's Office investigator Jonathan Rayner claimed Ms Edwards used a blocked phone number on July 23 to call the George County Chancery Clerk's office 21 times in an eight-minute window.

Ms Edwards allegedly said the words "do not go outside," "the clock is ticking" and "die" during those calls.

Nolan Wells's death has attracted the attention of notable US civil rights figures and politicians who have suggested his race may have been a factor in his death. (Reuters: David 'Dee' Delgado)

Half an hour later, she allegedly called the Jackson County Sheriff's Office eight times in 18 minutes, and said: "Y'all got a bomb outside, don't come outside b----h".

On July 30, a third criminal complaint was issued against Edward Porter from Illinois, who allegedly called a witness in the Nolan Wells investigation, claiming to be outside their home and threatening to kill them.

Mr Porter also later allegedly called a second witness and threatened to dismember them, FBI officer Christopher Cloc said in the court documents.

Mr Porter's threats were made against two members of the family of Bart Edminston Jr, a 21-year-old who knew Mr Wells and provided aid to a group aboard the boat he and his friends used on July 4, according to Russell Latino, a lawyer representing them.

Anonymous 'misconduct' complaint against Nolan's mum

On Wednesday, the civil rights lawyer acting for Mr Wells's family, Ben Crump, revealed the teen's mother Christine Wonsley had been notified of a "professional misconduct investigation" against her by the Mississippi Board of Nursing.

Mr Crump said the investigation was opened after the board received an anonymous complaint about her proficiency as a nurse, but the board has not detailed what that complaint was.

Christine Wonsley encouraged her son's friends, family and community members to "be like Nolan" and to spread kindness. (AP: Yuki Iwamura)

"Christine Wells Wonsley was robbed of her son one month ago, almost to the day. She has spent every moment since asking one question: what happened to Nolan?" Mr Crump said in a statement.

"Now, someone is going after her nursing license, anonymously, without the courage to put a name on it.

" This is a warning shot at a grieving mother, meant to pressure and scare her into staying quiet. It is a distraction, it is intimidation, and we will not let it stand. "

Mr Crump said Ms Wonsley had cared for patients over multiple years "without a single complaint against her".

"Then her son was found dead. She did what any grieving mother would do: she took a leave of absence to bury her child and search for answers," he said.

"And only now, after all of that, does an anonymous person want the Board of Nursing to believe she is a bad nurse. Nothing about her practice changed."

Nolan Wells's parents were supported by civil rights advocates, including Reverend Al Sharpton (far right), at a funeral service held for him in Ocean Springs. (AP: Gerald Herbert)

In the days after Mr Wells's death, the local sheriff's office said foul play was not suspected and that he may have drowned.

Across social media, users have parsed timelines, circulated videos and shared rampant speculation about what may have happened, which authorities say remain unverified.

As calls have grown for a transparent investigation, some people have cautioned against drawing conclusions before authorities release their full findings.

On Friday, Ms Wonsley said her family was simply pleading for answers.

"We just want to know what happened and why our baby didn't come home," she said at a press conference.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Man charged with manslaughter over fatal crash in Cairns
World.content:
Queensland police have charged a 36-year-old man with multiple offences, including manslaughter, after a crash that killed a 25-year-old woman in northern Cairns.

Jake Edward Warn, from Warrami, 125 kilometres south of Cairns, has been refused police bail and his case has been listed in the Cairns Magistrates Court today.

Mr Warn allegedly stole a Toyota LandCruiser ute from Palm Cove shortly before 1:30pm yesterday while he was allegedly affected by an intoxicating substance.

Police cordoned off the crash site as investigations were underway. (ABC Far North: Christopher Testa)

Police said he was driving south on the Smithfield Bypass when he crashed into a northbound Subaru Impreza and a Toyota Rav4, killing the sole occupant of the Rav4, a 25-year-old woman from nearby Kewarra Beach.

"Police allege shortly after the crash, the 36-year-old man entered a Toyota C-HR and forced the driver, a 71-year-old man, to drive him from the scene," a Queensland Police Service (QPS) statement said.

Less than an hour later, police arrested Mr Warn on Reservoir Rd in Manoora, on the western side of the city, and took him to Cairns Hospital.

A further four people were taken to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries following the Smithfield crash.

Police closed the Smithfield Bypass to traffic for hours yesterday following the crash. (ABC Far North: Sophie Johnson)

The 71-year-old man, who was allegedly forced to drive Mr Warn to Manoora, was not physically injured.

Cairns Criminal Investigation Branch detectives laid five charges against Mr Warn this morning.

Jake Edward Warn's case is expected to be heard in court in Cairns today. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

The charges are one count each of manslaughter; failing to remain at an incident and render assistance showing callous disregard for the needs of a person injured; dangerous operation of a vehicle and being adversely affected by an intoxicating substance; unlawful entry of a vehicle for committing an indictable offence; and stealing a vehicle.

"Investigations are ongoing, and police are urging anyone with relevant information or vision to come forward," the QPS statement said.

World.title: More alleged victims surface in child sex abuse case against paediatrician
World.content:
A Perth paediatrician who allegedly recorded himself abusing children in his clinic has been charged with another 15 child sex offences against seven more alleged victims.

Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.

Chia Liang Saw, 41, was first charged on May 30 this year, with the court hearing he came to the attention of police after allegedly communicating with a self-described "paedophile vigilante", whom Dr Saw's lawyer said had "taken on the persona of a child".

Dr Saw last appeared in court in early July accused of more than 50 offences.

He is now facing 72 charges relating to 18 alleged victims after an extensive investigation launched, according to police.

The new charges include six counts of indecent dealing with a child under 13 years old, three counts of sexual penetration of a child under 13 years old, and one count of producing child exploitation material.

The other five new charges relate to allegations Dr Saw indecently recorded children.

In June, the paediatrician was accused of recording himself abusing children using hidden cameras at his consulting rooms in Nedlands, in Perth's west, and Midland in Perth's east, where he treated children with behavioural issues.

Dr Saw is yet to enter any pleas, and has had his medical licence suspended.

Chia Liang Saw is accused of recording some of his alleged abuse using hidden cameras. (Supplied)

The ABC does not suggest the suspension means Dr Saw is guilty of the charges.

He is expected to face Perth Magistrates Court today.

Young females allegedly abused

Police prosecutors told the court in June Dr Saw's alleged victims, who then numbered 10, were mainly young female patients aged between 12 and 15.

The court also heard one victim was a 10-year-old girl who was allegedly abused in a home.

Chia Liang Saw is due to appear again in the Perth Magistrates Court on Thursday. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Police alleged Dr Saw stalked his victims on social media and had visited the Sugar Daddy dating website.

Sugar dating is typically a type of relationship where young women trade their time for the financial sponsorship of an older man.

It was also alleged Dr Saw admitted deleting incriminating material.

Prosecutors told the court Dr Saw had expressed feeling "shame and distress", with the defence counsel saying his client's name was now "mud".

But the defence lawyer said Dr Saw's explanation for the clinic recordings was that they were made in an effort to protect himself from allegations of "untoward behaviour".

World.title: Locals angered after vandals graffiti 100-year-old war memorial
World.content:
Victoria Police are investigating the vandalism of a 100-year-old war memorial in the Victorian town of Beaufort last month.

Beaufort RSL president Donald Carnes said the vandals painted offensive slogans including "death to Australia", "death to the ADF", "land back" and "blood on your hands".

Police said in a statement that Beaufort Memorial Park on Havelock Street was graffitied sometime between Saturday July 25 and Sunday July 26.

"The paint has since been removed and an investigation is underway," Victoria Police said.

The memorial was unveiled in the 1920s to honour local men and women who were involved in World War I.

Locals gather at the site for Anzac Day and Remembrance Day.

Police are investigating the incident. (Supplied)

Whole town 'hurt'

Mr Carnes said he was horrified and shocked by the vandalism.

"I feel really hurt somebody would compromise something like that," he said.

"A lot of the people whose names [are on the memorial] unfortunately didn't come home.

"The memorial is there for their memories.

"The whole town is really hurt. The memorial has sat there for over 100 years and has never been compromised in any way."

The memorial has names of soldiers who fought in both world wars. (Supplied)

'Strongly condemn'

The Pyrenees Shire Council said in a statement it was deeply saddened and disappointed by the vandalism.

A spokesperson said council staff quickly removed the graffiti on Monday and are actively monitoring the site.

Mayor Damien Ferrari said the memorial was sacred to the town.

"The graffiti on the war memorial at Beaufort Memorial Park has deeply upset our community," Cr Ferrari said.

"This site stands as place of remembrance, respect and reflection, and the damage caused does not reflect the values of the shire.

"We strongly condemn this act and will work to restore the memorial as quickly as possible."

Pyrenees shire Mayor Damien Ferrari says the memorial is sacred. (Supplied)

'Shameful'

Member for Ripon Martha Haylett said the incident was "shameful".

"So many from Beaufort gave everything for the freedoms we enjoy today," Ms Haylett said in a statement.

"Defacing the place we honour them is a disgrace.

"Acts like this have no place in our community. I want to thank the council for their quick response in getting the graffiti cleaned up."

World.title: Inquest into mother's death examines Albury Hospital transfer delays
World.content:
Kate Manley's family remember her as a strong, independent mother who was full of energy and brought laughter into the lives of everyone who knew her before she died at Albury Wodonga Health's Albury hospital.

Ms Manley died on November 16, 2022 of a suspected pulmonary embolism, a blood clot emergency closely related to deep vein thrombosis.

A five-day inquest into her death has concluded at Albury Local Court.

On Tuesday, counsel assisting the coroner Patrick Rooney read a family statement issued by her twin brother Alex to the court.

"[Kate] was compassionate, creative and had drive … [and] brought fun, warmth and laughter into the lives of those who knew her," the family statement said.

The 46-year-old qualified chef was described as being the glue that held the family together, with her daughter Ruby "the centre of her world".

Kate Manley was remembered by family as someone who was "independent, strong, beautiful and full of energy". (Supplied: Manley family)

Evidence from several Albury Wodonga Health (AWH) staff, executives and medical experts was provided to the inquest.

Ms Manley was diagnosed with catatonia not long after presenting at the hospital on November 11, after medical staff said she had minimal responses when they attempted to speak to her.

She died in the hospital's medical ward five days later, having been admitted to Nolan House, the mental acute psychiatric ward located at Albury Hospital.

Five-hour wait for patient transfer

The court heard Ms Manley had waited five hours to be transferred from Nolan House to the medical ward, where her blood-clot risk could be assessed.

"Obviously and tragically, further examination and treatment would have occurred at the medical ward if there had been more time," Mr Rooney told Coroner Rebecca Hosking.

The inquest has heard communication issues between wards at the hospital may have led to Kate Manley's death. (Supplied: Albury Wodonga Health)

Mr Rooney said there were communication issues between Nolan House and medical ward staff as to the severity of Ms Manley's deteriorating condition.

Issues over patient tracking systems

The inquest also examined how the location of Nolan House may have impacted the events leading up to Ms Manley's death.

The unit is located at Albury in NSW, but is administered under Victorian laws.

Kate Manley, 46, died of a pulmonary embolism at Albury Hospital on November 16, 2022. (ABC News: Annie Brown)

During hearings on Tuesday, acting director of mental health and wellbeing Dannielle McLeish said the hospital had several combined systems in place to track patient movements.

She told the court that the inclusion of paper-based systems, which were required under Victorian laws, in addition to electronic tracking systems, was challenging to manage and confusing for staff.

"It's important to have a single source for the location of a patient," Ms McLeish said.

Former AWH interim CEO Andrew Way had given a statement prior to the inquest saying that from information provided to him, communication between Nolan House and the medical ward was "ineffective".

On Tuesday, Professor Way told the court that during his short three-month tenure as interim CEO, he made efforts to go to Nolan House to talk with frontline staff to discuss those issues.

"Whilst I would admit that they're not perfect, they struck me as being consistent with what I would have expected of a unit of this scale and size," he told the court.

Steps already taken to improve transfers

In his submission, Mr Rooney referred to a previous coronial inquest into the death of Roger Schnelle at Nolan House.

A recommendation from that coronial investigation called for both NSW Health and Victoria's Department of Health to implement a sole electronic medical record across Albury Wodonga Health medical and mental health services.

He said AWH also encouraged that recommendation and such a record should be compatible with both NSW and Victorian systems.

Counsel acting for AWH, Lorna McFee, said the health service had already taken steps to improve patient transfers and other systems since Ms Manley's death.

She also submitted a statement from AWH's board members sharing their condolences to Ms Manley's family.

Coroner Hosking said that she expected to hand down findings and recommendations within a month.

World.title: Farmers fined for blocking VNI West transmission work
World.content:
Farmers in Victoria's west have been fined for refusing to let authorised officers onto their properties to progress transmission line planning works.

On Tuesday, 12 farmers received $814 fines in the mail from the Victorian government for not allowing workers access to their land to prepare to build the controversial VNI West project.

Another six formal warnings were also sent to property owners for denying access.

Stud sheep farmer from Marnoo, Trent Carter said he was refusing to pay the fine and would fight it in court.

"It's a wake-up call to every property owner around the country whether rural or residential," he said.

" What we think is ours, isn't necessarily ours and it's open slather for governments to come in and do what they'd like to do if they want. "

"I'll be seeking legal advice going forward, we've got to represent everybody else who's a property owner and set a precedent, not get bullied."

Twelve farmers have been fined for denying authorities access to their properties. (Supplied: Farmers Fightback)

Ongoing battle

Farmers have been threatening to deny access to their land for transmission planning work, despite warnings of large fines and clashes with police.

For VNI West to continue, authorised officers need to access private land within the planned route, to assess the potential agricultural, environmental, cultural and heritage impacts.

The fines received yesterday from the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Change (DEECA) state farmers prevented officers entering their land "without reasonable excuse hindering, obstructing or delaying authorised activity".

A spokesperson for DEECA said under the Electricity Industry Act 2000, authorised officers may issue an infringement where they are satisfied a person has denied property access without a reasonable excuse.

"VicGrid worked hard to keep landholders informed, providing more than 30 business days' notice of planned visits and multiple reminders before property access," the spokesperson said.

"Authorised Officers made the decision to issue fines after property access was denied without a reasonable excuse."

"Anyone who believes they have received an infringement notice in error can seek an internal review."

The organisation responsible for planning the transmission works, VicGrid said it "does not issue infringement notices and cannot determine the outcome of any review or court process".

In a statement, a VicGrid spokesperson said it had "made every effort to reach voluntary agreements with landholders over many years".

"We’ve increased access and early benefit payments, agreed on-site inductions and seasonal timing requirements and offered landholders the opportunity to choose their own survey specialists," the spokesperson said.

VicGrid reiterated that transmission companies have "long held powers under the Electricity Industry Act 2000 to access land to carry out activities required to maintain and plan for transmission infrastructure, including conducting surveys".

But Mr Carter said the process has been difficult, with poor correspondence and requests made by authorities at inconvenient times.

"They were trying to gain access in mid April in the middle of sowing. Last time it was the middle of harvest," he said.

"I said to [government] we were at the beginning of our lambing season which runs from April to mid August.

"During lambing minimal disturbance is required to ensure animal welfare standards are met."

World.title: Pineapple growers raise biosecurity concerns as Asian imports considered
World.content:
Australian pineapple growers fear a proposal to allow imports of the fruit from India and Indonesia could expose them to foreign pests and diseases.

The federal Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF) has released a draft assessment report on the risks of importing decrowned pineapples after both countries requested market access under existing trade obligations.

The report found the fruit could be safely imported if strict biosecurity requirements were met to manage eight identified pests, most of which are species of mealy bugs.

Australia's annual pineapple production rose 16 per cent in the 2024-2025 financial year. (ABC Rural: Tayla Larsen)

But farmers believe imports are an unnecessary risk, as local fruit is meeting domestic demand.

While the assessment does not automatically mean trade will occur, farmers want risk management procedures to be closely scrutinised.

'Minimal uptake'

Second-generation grower Colin Hawken is worried the trade could open his farm at Mungar, south-west of Maryborough, to new threats.

"There are certain pests and diseases in India and Indonesia that we don't have here," he said.

"If we do get those diseases here, we've got nothing to fight them with."

Colin Hawken believes the Australian industry can meet domestic demand without imported fruit. (ABC Rural: Tayla Larsen)

As a member of the World Trade Organization, the department said Australia has international obligations it must meet, including assessing import proposals and developing conditions that are scientifically backed and don't unnecessarily restrict trade.

Under those obligations, the department cannot assess the potential economic impact of additional market competition, but it can rate the risks of identified pests and diseases.

Decrowning pineapples helps to remove potential pests hiding in the leaves. (ABC News: Meg Bolton )

Australia currently allows fresh decrowned pineapples to be imported from the Philippines, Solomon Islands, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Taiwan, while import conditions are being finalised for Malaysia.

Australia received approximately 18 tonnes of pineapple from Taiwan in 2025, and there were no imports from any other country in the past five years.

Chief executive of Queensland Fruit and Vegetable Growers Scott Kompo-Harms said the imports were not needed.

Scott Kompo-Harms, chief executive of Queensland Fruit and Vegetable Growers. (Supplied: QFVG)

"Australia's biosecurity is one of our greatest natural assets, and we need to protect that," he said.

" If there are control measures that are put in place, we want to see that they are being abided by over the long term with regular monitoring. "

To reduce the risk of pests, the DAFF report suggested treatments such as fumigation and irradiation and recommended unit inspections and traceability to the farm and packing houses.

Year-round supply

While Indonesia's and India's pineapple production surpasses Australia's, growers here believed there was enough supply to satisfy domestic demand.

In the 2024/25 financial year, Australian farms produced 68,373 tonnes of pineapples … more than two-thirds were sold as fresh fruit.

"We can provide pineapples 365 days a year, and we can look after our own market," Mr Hawken said.

"At the moment pineapples are a bit short, and we're receiving a premium price, but other times of the year we're certainly at or below cost of production."

The national farmgate value was estimated to be $78.6 million.

In recent years growers have invested in new varieties and marketing campaigns to make fresh pineapples more appealing as they competed with canned products.

Scott Maxwell says the draft risk analysis was a key topic at the industry's annual field day. (ABC Rural: Tayla Larsen)

Scott Maxwell, chairman of Australian Pineapples, said the momentum the industry has experienced could be at risk.

"Every imported pineapple that's bought is an Australian pineapple that's not bought from an Australian farmer, which affects Australian jobs," he said.

" Growers are very concerned because it affects their livelihoods, they're the ones left to clean up the mess if there is an incursion. "

Consultation open

The pineapple industry is making a formal submission in response to the draft report.

The consultation period runs until September 14.

Stakeholders' comments will inform the final report, which will include responses to technical issues.

That report is expected to be released in the second half of 2027, and even if importation is recommended, both India and Indonesia will need to demonstrate they can implement all required controls before trade can begin.

World.title: Netball's uniform debacle hints at bigger problem for women in sport
World.content:
The Diamonds' 2026 Commonwealth Games campaign may well go down in history for all the wrong reasons, remembered not only for a shock semi-final loss to Jamaica but also for the dress controversy that preceded it.

After the Diamonds' 99-38 demolition of Tonga, media coverage focused not on the lopsided result but on the ill-fitting dresses players tugged at throughout matches.

Players like Sophie Garbin may have insisted the outfits were fine, but as ABC journalist Britt Carter put it, "if a shooter has to pull it down more than 10 times in a quarter, how much of that energy could be re-directed?"

Loading Instagram content

For elite women athletes, the problem is not just the impact poor-fitting uniforms have on performance.

Research shows that many adolescent girls drop out of sport citing body image issues, while concerns about uniforms have also been identified as a barrier to participation.

These are not just problems for younger people or community sport.

The ABC and Deakin University's recent survey of elite Australian athletes in women's sport found that 25 per cent have negative feelings about their body image, while 44 per cent have experienced an eating disorder and/or disordered eating.

The latter figure is much higher than what the Butterfly Foundation, a national charity for anyone affected by eating disorders and body image issues, estimates at 17 per cent for the general population.

Teigan O'Shannassy wants to see women and girls feel more comfortable in their bodies on the netball court. (Getty: Sanka Vidanagama)

Sydney-based netballer Teigan O'Shannassy is one of those who lives with a history of eating disorders and disordered eating.

She argues more awareness about the struggles elite female athletes face is key.

Dresses an issue during Super Netball season

O'Shannassy, who the ABC interviewed before the Commonwealth Games, admitted having issues with the Swifts' dress in the most recent Super Netball season, with teammates seen adjusting them during some matches.

"When you're playing in a dress in front of thousands of people, you want to be able to perform, and don't want to have to think about how you look or how you feel in the dress," she told the ABC.

" If you're struggling with your body image, having to do that and put on something that you don't want to wear, or you don't feel comfortable in, is really hard. "

Teigan O'Shannassy (left) has played for the Canberra Giants and the Sydney Swifts in her netball career. (Getty: Jason McCawley)

O'Shannassy, 27, has previously been diagnosed with anorexia nervosa and remembers vividly the moment her career came to a crossroads.

If you or someone you know needs help: The Butterfly Foundation: National helpline 1800 ED HOPE (1800 33 4673)

She was playing for the Giants at the time, in the middle of COVID-19 lockdowns, and was about to leave with the team for a Queensland hub.

O'Shannassy was called into a meeting with her head coach, assistant coach, dietitian, doctor and physio and told she would be staying behind so she could see a dietitian and therapist weekly.

"Looking back, I think that was probably the best decision they could have made," she said.

"I think it was one of the best things that could have happened to me. But obviously I was absolutely gutted. I thought my career was over."

Those feelings intensified when the Giants told her they would not offer her another contract, but invited her to stay on as a training partner.

The Swifts called with the same offer before O'Shannassy decided to leave.

Netballer Teigan O'Shannassy has struggled with body image throughout her career in the national league. (Getty: James Worsfold)

"Something needed to change," she said.

"I just felt like I was stuck in this constant cycle of injuries and under-fuelling because I felt like I wasn't training [enough] and I didn't deserve to eat."

'The more we can talk about it, the better'

Given her personal experience, O'Shannassy says she was "unfortunately not surprised" by the results of the ABC and Deakin survey.

"When I was really struggling, I honestly thought I was the only person that was struggling with my body and food and having all these negative thoughts around it," she said.

"But since I've spoken up about it, people have come to me and said 'oh, I struggle with this too', which in a way I think is helpful, that we're so open about it.

"I think the more we can talk about it, the better. Even for me, talking about my body in a positive way is still something that I need to work on, and I think everyone can do that every day."

Teigan O'Shannassy now teaches other women about nutrition and health. (Getty: Brett Hemmings)

O'Shannassy, who has since trained as an associate nutritionist and runs a business called Tossed Together, is passionate about building community understanding of the unique challenges athletes face.

These include, in a team sport like netball, the pressure to be more like your teammates or competitors.

She remembers first coming through competitive pathways at 17 and having her body compared unfavourably to others by her coaches.

"We got told, 'you should be lifting this amount of weight, you should all look like this player, you should be able to do what certain players can do,'" she said.

"That stuck so much in my head. I'd have niggle after niggle and just felt like my body was never good enough.

"I just wanted to be like the other netballers who were so strong and looked like athletes."

By contrast, O'Shannassy described her younger self as "tall, lanky and uncoordinated", and says she "never felt like I looked like an athlete".

Teigan O'Shannassy began playing for the Canberra Giants in her late teens. (Getty: Mark Nolan)

The requirement to undertake body composition testing, including skin folds and DEXA scans, also bred unhealthy comparisons.

"I remember being 19, 20, and hearing some girls saying what body fat [percentage] they were, and thinking 'oh god, I'm a bit higher than them' and just freaking out about it," O'Shannassy said.

Social media exposes further body scrutiny

Danni Rowlands, the Butterfly Foundation's director of education initiatives, is a former state netballer herself and shares a similar story to O'Shannassy.

She was diagnosed with an eating disorder at age 21 and remembers skin fold testing significantly influencing how she felt about her body as a junior athlete.

A former netballer herself, Danni Rowlands now advocates for a shift in sporting cultures through the Butterfly Foundation. (Supplied.)

"I was identified as being too high in body composition, so I was supported through a dietitian to reduce body fat," she said.

"I went on to make the state team and play nationals, which was amazing, but unfortunately played the entire tournament with a stress fracture in my ankle, which was later identified as being caused by under-nourishment and over-training.

" That just kicked off this whole cycle at a very vulnerable age where I connected my weight to my worth and success as an athlete. "

Since retiring from sport, she has worked to shift sporting cultures, heading Butterfly Foundation's BodyKindSports initiative, which recognises adolescence as a vulnerable time for athletes' relationship with their body, particularly young girls.

"We want to protect and support athletes in those early pathways so that they can thrive, and that the consequence of participating in sport isn't a lifelong struggle with eating, training and poor body image," Rowlands said.

The Diamonds claimed the bronze medal at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. (Getty: Lintao Zhang)

She holds particular concerns for contemporary women athletes who are more accessible to the public than ever on social media.

"This idea that athlete bodies are commodities and we can all have a piece of them, and critique as we want [online], absolutely adds a layer of pressure for athletes that makes it more intense than ever before," Rowlands said.

" There are intense appearance pressures on women athletes to look pretty, and feminine, but not too muscular, or too thin. They just can't win, which is tough. "

She added that when players do have issues with their uniforms, as in the Commonwealth Games example, this can generate further unwanted attention on their bodies.

"Looking at women across a lot of sports, there's much more exposure of body parts compared to men," she said.

"I think we have to ask: why is this the case? Is it because it's going to help them perform better, or is it because we're treating female bodies differently in sport?"

Uniforms a factor in girls dropping out of sport Studies show a large percentage of girls drop out of sport when they become teenagers. One of the contributing factors is the clothes they have to wear.

O'Shannassy admitted being under the spotlight, and being photographed or filmed constantly, added a layer of discomfort for those with body image issues.

"For a female, that can be really triggering. You're always being watched, and I think that's something that can be kind of daunting," she said.

"As an athlete, obviously it's such a cool job, and there's so many positive things that come out of it, but the highs are high, and the lows are low.

"If you've never done it, you just really don't know what it can be like."

Athletes 'not immune' to body image issues

Moving forward, both O'Shannassy and Rowlands shared messages of support for women in sport.

Rowlands encouraged athletes who might be struggling to "seek support sooner rather than later".

"Being an athlete doesn't make you immune to any of those pressures. If anything, it intensifies them further. So be kind to yourself, and if you are struggling, reach out," she said.

All Teigan O'Shannassy ever wanted to do in her life was play netball. (Getty: Jason McCawley)

O'Shannassy, meanwhile, hopes sharing her story will continue to inspire others who may be experiencing something similar.

Although her worst days are well behind her, she says it can help to acknowledge that an eating disorder is not "something you can just turn off, or wake up and you're fine".

"You might have that voice in your head forever," she said.

"For me, it's just, I hear that voice and I acknowledge it, but I don't let it control me anymore."

She says it is important to find the thing that motivates you to keep fighting, which for her has always been her chosen sport.

"For me it was netball, all I ever wanted to do was play netball," she said.

"And I knew that if I didn't eat or didn't fuel myself I was never going to get there."

World.title: ‘We’re hog-tying’: Gippsland police accused of repeat misconduct after one victim suffers brain damage
World.content:
Police officers across Gippsland have been repeatedly accused of using excessive force and unlawfully deploying tasers or capsicum spray, resulting in legal claims against the force and the recent conviction of an officer. Brodie Holt sustained permanent brain damage after an arrest outside a Traralgon hotel in 2022, with his lawyer saying the case raises broader concerns about alleged police misconduct in rural and regional towns across south-eastern Victoria. Then 23-year-old Brodie Holt was placed in an induced coma after an alleged violent assault by police outside a Traralgon hotel. An investigation by The Age has uncovered five incidents – including two on the same night involving the same officer – through costly civil actions being pursued by victims in court. Only two of the incidents were subject to investigation by the force’s professional standards unit – officers were cleared in one case, and the other remains ongoing.



Related Article Courts ‘Hunting women’: Policeman who preyed on domestic violence victims jailed Victoria Police said they had not investigated three further incidents because they had not received any complaints, despite the civil claims providing details of the excessive force allegations in two of the cases. “We do not shy away from taking action as necessary to uphold community trust and confidence in our organisation,” the spokesperson said. Revelations of the mounting civil claims also come a month after a Gippsland police officer was convicted on assault charges after tasering a man nine times in under 46 seconds while on duty in Warragul. The scale of the alleged misconduct has fuelled doubts about the capacity of the state’s corruption watchdog to properly investigate hundreds of complaints from the region each year.



Between July 2018 and December 2024, the Independent Broad-based Anti-Corruption Commission received 2365 allegations of misconduct and corruption against police in the Morwell and Bairnsdale regions, but just 0.2 per cent were investigated. Out of the 300 misuse-of-force complaints, three were investigated. Each complaint can contain multiple allegations. Kellie said her son’s wrist was also injured by the handcuffs. In the same time, the substantially larger Wangaratta and Goulburn Valley regions recorded 2157 complaints – 229 of which were force complaints. None were investigated by IBAC, which has a higher threshold for investigating than Victoria Police. Holt, 27, last month received a massive legal settlement from the state government, after his lawyers estimated that his medical expenses, loss of earnings and future care would cost almost $14 million. The young tradie was verbally abused and repeatedly assaulted by several officers trying to find who had thrown a beer can at them. The Supreme Court statement of claim alleges an officer smashed Holt’s head against a brick wall before he was tackled to the ground while handcuffed, leading to his head smacking the concrete pavement.



The arresting officers were also accused of lying to paramedics when they claimed Holt had “fallen to the ground and knocked himself out”. Holt’s mother and litigation guardian, Kellie, finds it difficult to put into words the life-altering impact her son’s injuries have had. “For me, that’s the night I lost my son,” she told The Age. “He’s just not him any more.” Kellie said Brodie’s traumatic brain injury has stripped away his independence, leaving him unable to work, drive, or navigate daily life without assistance. “He hates that he’s different. He just can’t explain how, but he knows he’s different,” Kellie said.



The police officer who arrived at her doorstep hours after Brodie was rushed to hospital said her son had suffered an “intoxicated fall”. It took months of fighting for Kellie to learn what really happened to her son that night. The alleged violent police assaults Brodie Holt, Traralgon, May 7, 2022: Holt suffered permanent brain damage after an alleged violent assault by police.

Holt suffered permanent brain damage after an alleged violent assault by police. Darryl Ivory, Traralgon, January 26, 2023: Ivory has accused three officers of unlawfully arresting him and dousing him with capsicum spray despite complying with police.

Ivory has accused three officers of unlawfully arresting him and dousing him with capsicum spray despite complying with police. Jy Smith-Goode, Traralgon, January 26, 2023 : Just hours later, Smith-Goode was allegedly “hog-tied” during an alleged violent arrest by the same officers.

: Just hours later, Smith-Goode was allegedly “hog-tied” during an alleged violent arrest by the same officers. Warragul man, Warragul, May 19, 2024: Senior Constable Aaron Bowen doused a man with capsicum spray and tasered him nine times in less than a minute soon after entering the victim’s home.

Senior Constable Aaron Bowen doused a man with capsicum spray and tasered him nine times in less than a minute soon after entering the victim’s home. Peter Walker, Moe, March 2025: Walker alleges he was unlawfully arrested by officers who pointed a Taser at him despite his compliance. “I was like, ‘Nah, that doesn’t seem right’,” she said. Despite Brodie’s injuries, an internal investigation completed in March 2023 found no evidence that police assaulted him and “no grounds for the complaints whatsoever”.



“What Brodie wants, and what I want too, is justice. I want someone held accountable. But I know that’s not going to happen,” Kellie said. Jy Smith-Goode claims he was tasered on the bare-buttocks, doused with capsicum spray and “hog-tied” with three pairs of handcuffs The cases of Traralgon men Jy Smith-Goode and Darryl Ivory occurred within hours of each other and with the same police officer on Australia Day in 2023. Indigenous man Smith-Goode was Tasered on his bare bottom, doused in the face with capsicum spray and “hog-tied” with three sets of handcuffs, despite initially complying with police, according to court documents. The then-23-year-old was suffering a mental health episode while walking down a highway and wearing only a towel around his waist, when he was confronted by two officers and told he was breaching his bail conditions.



According to an amended statement of claim filed with the Supreme Court, one officer allegedly placed Smith-Goode in a “chokehold headlock”, before he was OC-sprayed by another. The 23-year-old urinated involuntarily and cried out for help as officers struggled to handcuff him, before “one of the police officers tasered the plaintiff into the left side of the plaintiff’s bare buttocks.” Senior Constable Steven Pope is then accused of saying: “Yep, we’re hog-tying”. “One or more of the police officers used a third set of handcuffs to bind the plaintiff’s wrists to his ankles behind his back in a ‘hog-tie’ position, while the plaintiff yelled and pleaded for help,” the statement of claim alleges. Pope has been named in three statements of claim alleging excessive force – Holt, Smith-Goode and Ivory.



Smith-Goode’s lawyers will pursue exemplary damages, alleging that Pope and another officer were “dishonest and deliberately misleading” when they completed a Use of Force form following the incident. It is alleged the two officers exaggerated the conduct of Smith-Goode, while failing to mention that he had been hog-tied or placed in a chokehold. “What Brodie wants, and what I want too, is justice. I want someone held accountable.” Brodie’s mother, Kellie Holt Victoria Police are yet to file a defence in the matter, and a spokesperson declined to answer questions about the case. Ivory recently settled a civil claim against the force, after a breath test allegedly turned violent – hours before Smith-Goode’s arrest.



The 49-year-old was argumentative and refused to get off his scooter to attend the police station when “Pope said words to the effect of ‘I will quite happily taser you because I’m not f---ing around mate’,” County Court documents claim. Related Article Graphic content

Victoria Police conduct Tasered nine times in 46 seconds: The arrest that saw a cop convicted of assault Pope is accused of then deploying OC spray against Ivory. The financial settlement was agreed to by Victoria Police without admission of liability and was conditional on Ivory agreeing to a non-disclosure agreement. Lawyer Jeremy King, from Robinson Gill, said the state’s corruption taskforce was unable to cope with a surge in police misconduct across regional Victoria, particularly Gippsland.



“There are clear and undeniable issues with police in the Gippsland region. We have seen a significant number of serious cases and complaints of police brutality from this region over the last few years,” King told The Age. He said it was an example of the system failing regional communities. “IBAC should have stepped up for our regional community and given them a way to call out misconduct without fear of local reprisals. The sad fact is that they haven’t. They take less than one per cent of complaints made to them and bounce the rest back to Vic Pol,” he said. In the most recent civil case, Peter Walker alleges he was assaulted by two officers in Moe following a dispute with a relative over the storage of a car in March 2025.



The officers pointed a Taser at Walker during the arrest, despite him being compliant and repeatedly stating he suffered from a permanent impairment. Walker was detained and charged with assaulting police and resisting arrest, but a magistrate dismissed the case after ruling officers had no power to arrest or detain him. Loading Last month, this masthead revealed senior constable Aaron Bowen had become the first Victorian police officer to be charged over deployment of a Taser, found guilty of 10 assault charges while arresting a man at his Warragul home in May 2024. Body camera footage captured Bowen dousing the man in the face with capsicum spray and using a Taser nine times in 46 seconds.



Bowen was convicted and fined $11,000 by the court and has been suspended without pay as Victoria Police lead an internal investigation into his conduct. The victim’s lawyer, Meliza Ludowkye, said the incident left her client suffering a “deep distrust” of police after the violent arrest, which he was now pursuing as a civil claim in the Supreme Court. “He is seeking formal acknowledgement of what occurred and fair compensation for the harm he has suffered.” In 2010, Gippsland became one of the first regions in the state to equip some of its officers with stun guns. Until then, Tasers were only issued to police within the force’s elite units. By 2014, the weapons had been rolled out to almost all frontline officers in regional Victoria – a decision criticised at the time by civil liberties groups and legal advocates.



Research from 2024 by Dr Tamar Hopkins found that Aboriginal people represented 15.4 per cent of the cases where police reported using a taser in East Gippsland, but only accounted for 3.5 per cent of the population.
