World.title: These Sydney schools teach 1500 students. A $9b data centre is moving next door
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life These Sydney schools teach 1500 students. A $9b data centre is moving next door David Barwell August 6, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The race to power Australia’s artificial intelligence boom has reached a vacant paddock in western Sydney, where plans for the nation’s largest data centre development have sparked a battle over potential impacts on nearby schools, homes and critical freight infrastructure. The NSW government is in the final stages of deciding whether to approve a $9 billion data centre campus that would see US technology company AirTrunk develop six four-storey data hall buildings across 52 hectares of vacant land at Kemps Creek. If approved, the project would be built over a decade and operate 24 hours a day, supported by 852 diesel backup generators, 936 cooling units, 14.4 million litres of diesel fuel storage, electrical substations and 2.65 million kilograms of lithium-ion battery storage. At completion, the facility would have a power capacity of 1.2 gigawatts – roughly equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of about one million Australian homes – making it the first Australian data centre to exceed the one-gigawatt threshold.



Planning documents stated the development is vital for Australia’s digital sovereignty, ensuring the nation keeps pace with the rapid growth of artificial intelligence, cloud computing and data storage. But the scale of the proposal has intensified concerns among schools, residents, freight operators and government agencies about the cumulative impact of data centre developments across western Sydney, where a growing cluster of facilities has earned the region the nickname “data centre alley”. A concept image of the data centre campus at Kemps Creek. NSW Department of Planning The AirTrunk proposal would join a concentration of nearby facilities, including Stack Infrastructure’s planned 450-megawatt campus at Erskine Park, NEXTDC’s approved 250-megawatt facility at Horsley Park, Microsoft’s 190-megawatt development at Kemps Creek and the Echidna data centre at Eastern Creek. In a submission to the Department of Planning, Sydney Water warned existing wastewater networks were “not designed to handle the significant discharge anticipated from data centres”.



In a statement to the Herald, project manager Plan PM said the proposal had been modified following weeks of consultation with Sydney Water, resulting in an agreement to incorporate dry-cooling technology at the site to eliminate the operational water use required for cooling systems. Planning documents show the precinct would draw power through underground transmission lines connected to Transgrid’s Sydney West substation and aims to achieve net zero operational emissions by 2030 using carbon offset mechanisms. The planned development joins a growing list of Western Sydney data centres, including this approved facility which will be operated by Microsoft at Kemps Creek. “We will continue to work constructively with stakeholders and community to assess long-term servicing options as the application progresses,” Plan PM said in statement. The impending decision comes as governments grapple with how to accommodate the rapidly increasing electricity and water demands of the AI boom. Last month, the federal government released a proposed national framework for data centres that would require facilities to fund additional renewable energy generation and electricity grid infrastructure.



NSW already hosts almost 90 operational data centres, according to state government figures, with another 15 major projects worth a combined $52 billion progressing through the planning system. The AirTrunk proposal has also exposed tensions between industrial development and surrounding communities. The site sits near three schools educating more than 1500 students, including Mamre Anglican School, about 60 metres from the site, Emmaus Catholic College, about 170 metres away, and Trinity Catholic Primary School, approximately 320 metres away. In submissions to the Department of Planning, Catholic Schools Parramatta Diocese and The Anglican Schools Corporation warned that around-the-clock operations could expose students to continuous noise from industrial cooling units, diesel exhaust from routine generator testing and increased traffic during school pick-up and drop-off periods. Concerns were also raised about the visual impact of the 40-metre height of buildings. Mamre Anglican School principal Ross Whelan questioned whether a development of such industrial scale belonged next to a school.



“Members of our school community ... will have concerns regarding the potential health impacts and risk from both the operation and site infrastructure requirements,” he wrote. Related Article Commercial real estate Microsoft, Macquarie pump billions into power hungry data centres The project faces further headwinds from the freight and logistics sectors. NSW Ports and the Australasian Railway Association have urged the government to reject the application, arguing the site is strategically important industrial land adjoining the planned Western Sydney Intermodal Terminal, Western Sydney Freight Line and near the new Western Sydney International Airport. NSW Ports warned that converting the land into a data centre would “permanently lock out” nationally significant freight land needed to move shipping containers efficiently between Port Botany and Western Sydney by rail. Planning documents estimate the development would generate $13.7 billion in economic output during construction, support 2775 operational jobs and include measures to mitigate noise and vibration impacts on nearby properties.



For local residents like Ted Pochodyla, whose home is adjacent to the development site, the plans have prompted fears his home could be exposed to further noise, traffic and vibrations in the increasingly industrialised area. Ted Pochodyla, pictured at his home in Kemps Creek. Wolter Peeters “I am slowly being surrounded by industry on all sides, and it worries me greatly the negative impact this construction may have on my health and everyday life,” Pochodyla said. The NSW Department of Planning is expected to hand down its determination on the project in the coming weeks. AirTrunk was contacted for additional comment but did not respond to questions. World.title: Australia news LIVE: Labor MP Ed Husic to take break from duties after ‘serious’ car crash; Coalition will force Albanese to cede ground on gambling reforms
World.content:
Communications Minister Anika Wells says she wants to see the government’s gambling legislation get through the Parliament.

The Albanese government was given an ultimatum on its gambling package yesterday: work with the Coalition or the Greens on amendments, or the legislation won’t pass. Both parties have raised issue with the laws, which they think are insufficient to protect Australians from harm.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told question time in the last session of Parliament: “This is good reform … and the parliament should vote for it... If they don’t, then they do have the option of the status quo.”

But Wells said it was not yet her intention to drop the package -- a move that would upset many members of the Labor caucus who want a strong crackdown.

“That was some weeks ago now,” Wells said, referring to the prime minister’s comments last month.

“I’d say we’re some ways off that yet. I’m having constructive discussions with both the shadow communications minister for the Coalition and the shadow communications spokesperson for the Greens. We’ll keep those discussions going. We’d love to see this passed.”

World.title: Perth paediatrician now faces 72 child sex abuse charges
World.content:
A Perth paediatrician on bail over dozens of child sex abuse allegations will return to court on Thursday after being hit with another 15 charges.

Dr Chia Liang Saw, 41, was initially arrested and charged in May, with police alleging he engaged in persistent sexual conduct with a child and possessed child exploitation material.

Perth paediatrician Dr Chia Liang Saw. LinkedIn

Saw’s request for bail was repeatedly delayed, with prosecutors adding further charges as more alleged victims were identified, before he was eventually released under strict conditions last month.

Now, the paediatrician faces a total of 72 charges relating to 18 victims, with the new allegations including six counts of indecent dealing with a child under 13 years old, three counts of indecently recording a child under 13 years old, and three counts of sexual penetration of a child under 13 years old.

World.title: The astounding moment when this Fiddler on the Roof soars
World.content:
Theatre Royal, August 5. Until October 3

Tevye’s is such an indomitable heart as makes him larger than life: a force of nature who wears all that 1905 Imperial Russia can throw at a poor Jewish dairy farmer. Beyond coping, this champion of tradition even learns to adapt to a changing world. He can find joy in the face of adversity, and consoling humour in his unanswered querying of his God.

Few musicals are so dependent on one actor.

Troy Sussman follows Australian predecessors such as Hayes Gordon and Max Gillies. Gillies milked every drop of comedy from Tevye’s homespun philosophies and idle fancies. Gordon added voice and presence. When either sang If I Were a Rich Man, you were drawn deep into their hearts and humble aspirations; were warmed by their good cheer.

Troy Sussman as Tevye with Ben Adler as The Fiddler. Daniel Boud

Sussman can’t quite get there – yet. He seemed nervous to begin on opening night, and therefore initially lacked presence. His singing voice, too, missed something of that barrel-chested rotundity, and not all the comedy was maximised. Yet, he slowly became more convincing, suggesting he may well come to fill out this great role, and the production will grow accordingly.

When composer Jerry Bock, lyricist Sheldon Harnick and book writer Joseph Stein, director Jerome Robbins and performer Zero Mostel first unleased the show in 1964, it became Broadway’s longest-running musical, finally knocked off that perch by the vastly inferior Grease in 1972. To put its success in perspective, it ran longer than likes of My Fair Lady, Oklahoma!, South Pacific and The Sound of Music, thanks to Tevye and such other songwriting triumphs as Matchmaker, Matchmaker, To Life and the almost transcendental Sunrise, Sunset.

This London production (with Australian cast), originally directed by Jordan Fein, contains in Tevye’s Dream a sequence to astound. Tevye must reconcile his wife, Golde (Alexis Fishman), to their oldest daughter (Freya Boltman) marrying a poor young tailor (Felix Star) for love (of all things!), rather than a rich, elderly butcher (an excellent John Waters).

Golde’s bed suddenly becomes almost stage-width, with dead Grandma Tzeitel occupying the other end, and a clutch of the two-dozen cast dressed in white night attire helping enact the faux dream of which Tevye tells her. Golde can be forgiven for being taken in. Anyone would succumb to such simultaneously unearthly and witty staging.

Fishman and the daughters seem rather undercooked, while Sigrid Thornton overacts as Yente, the matchmaker. The singing, dancing and music are uniformly good, however, and Tom Scutt’s set is a land of wheat fields, rather than the usual village of Chagall-like dwellings.

Even the roof atop which fiddler Ben Adler beautifully plays is made of wheat. And it flies! Just like Tevye’s big heart – including when the Russians expel the community, which so often happened to their forebears across the centuries with scant warning.

“Perhaps that’s why we always wear our hats,” quips Tevye.

World.title: Jason speaks Japanese, runs marathons and a business – but he couldn’t swim until Gary came along
World.content:
NationalGood Weekend Jason speaks Japanese, runs marathons and a business – but he couldn’t swim until Gary came along Erin O'Dwyer August 6, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Dr Gary Shiels, 80, discovered that his friend, Dr Jason Graham-Nye, 56, couldn’t swim – despite Jason having lived his entire life by the beach – Gary made it his mission to teach him.

Gary Shiels (left) and Jason Graham-Nye. “I’d never seen a fear like Jason’s,” Gary says. “He’s been the best of my prodigies.” Wolter Peeters Jason: We met at the gym in 2023. Gary gave me some tips and we had coffee afterwards. We really hit it off. He’d finished his PhD and I was about to submit mine. His was on healthy ageing. It was so cool to meet someone who was still learning in his 70s – it made me feel like a spring chicken. He’s a surf lifesaving legend, a former president of the North Bondi Surf Club and its patron. He started saying to me, “You should get your bronze medallion and join the surf club”, but I said nothing. It was too mortifying to admit that I was terrified of the water. I’ve done many difficult things in my life – worked as a Japanese interpreter, run 15 marathons, built a company – but I had to say to Gary, “I can’t put my head under the water.” I was ashamed.



When I was a kid, our neighbours had a pool and invited [the late, well-known Sydney swim teacher] Alf Vockler over to show us how to swim. Vockler literally threw me into the deep end. It was so traumatising and I said to myself, “I’m never doing that again.” And I didn’t. Related Article Good Weekend ‘A fundamental part of growing up’: Why Aussie kids can’t swim any more Last December, Gary ambushed me at coffee and suggested I make learning to swim my New Year’s resolution. My sons [Harper, 21, and Fynn, 23] thought this was hilarious. Gary told me he’d had a similar swimming experience to me as a kid, but his mother had refused to let him give up. I had this 50-year-old story in my head: “I can’t swim. Chapter closed.” Gary didn’t argue with the story; he just showed me a different ending. I thought, “What else in my life isn’t as fixed as I think?” We had our first day in the pool together a few days later. I turned up in board shorts; he instructed me to get jammers [stretchy knee-length swimwear], a cap and a snorkel. I felt like a five-year-old again. Meanwhile, everyone was ploughing up and down the pool, doing tumble turns. He had me swim half the length of the 25-metre pool freestyle. I was freaked out and it was slow; I got a lung-full and had to stand up. He was very calm. He said, “Take a break and go again.” Eventually, I managed one lap, then two. As soon as he helped me figure out how the body is meant to lie in the water – co-ordinating the neck turn with the stroke – something clicked. I was in the pool every second day.



Gary’s always right. He gives you one piece of advice, it works and so by the time you’ve thought of a counter-argument, you’ve already improved. He’s extremely knowledgeable about all things relating to physical activity, including the science. I’d like the occasional opportunity to disagree with him, but he doesn’t give it to me. When he’s not there, I make excuses for myself; he calls it “the almanac of excuses”. We play golf together now, too, and he’s built a relationship with my sons. I watch him interact with them and think, “Wow, that’s so cool”; he’s perpetually curious, asks great questions and is a wonderful conversationalist. Hopefully, what they’ve seen is their father being exceptionally incompetent at something and sticking with it anyway. Overcoming a really difficult obstacle is the essence of life. It certainly helps you feel more calm, which you carry into everything else you do. ‘I had to say to Gary, “I can’t put my head under the water.” I was ashamed.’ Jason Graham-Nye I can swim about 200 metres freestyle without the snorkel now. Gary even has plans for me to do an ocean swim. It’s like a second life – I’m addicted. I’m so grateful to him. Gary: Jason wasn’t a member of the surf club and he was very cagey about why. When he told me he was terrified of the water, it was incomprehensible to me. I said, “You can’t live in Bondi and not be able to swim!” From then on, I was on a mission.



As a lad, he got thrown in the water, panicked and nearly drowned. He didn’t go back in for 50 years. I had a similar experience at Bondi Baths, but my mother was very tenacious. She said, “Gary, you’re going to swim if it kills me.” She dragged me off to Alf Vockler, who taught swimming at Watsons Bay. Strangely, Alf was the perpetrator of Jason’s problems but the solution to mine. Related Article Good Weekend ‘Things aren’t as stretchy and flexible’: Shane Gould on the reality of sex in your 60s It took a bit of cajoling to get Jason on board with my plan to teach him to swim. I was worried it might mean the end of our friendship if I kept pressing him. Even up to our first lesson, I wasn’t sure he’d follow through. The longer you have a belief that you can’t do something, the harder it is to convince yourself that you can. Time had been Jason’s enemy. In 60 years of coaching and being coached, I’ve seen almost everything, but I’d never seen a fear like Jason’s. Frankly, it’s been a revelation: he improved so quickly. We train four times a week and he hasn’t missed a single session. He’s been the best of my prodigies. I didn’t tell anyone I was teaching Jason to swim: I felt protective of him. I knew the problem was in his head: he was worried he was going to swallow water and drown. I came up with the idea of swimming with a snorkel. All of a sudden, he could put his head under the water and breathe. A positive attitude is essential for success in anything: it’s a matter of getting rid of the demons between the ears.



Jason has a strong moral compass. I’ve watched him speak out on some very difficult issues. In 2024, he gave an interview to ABC’s Four Corners about bullying at his former school, Cranbrook. It put him and his family at considerable risk, but he did it anyway. He presents quite a jovial disposition to the world, but underneath it, there’s a very serious person. He’s honest and determined, two qualities I look for in any friend. Related Article Good Weekend Two uni besties had a falling-out. An unusual project came to their rescue I’ve connected with his sons, too, now. Both are strong young men but neither were strong swimmers. Harper’s a board rider who wasn’t a confident swimmer; Fynn’s based in London and never went in the water. Swimming is a potentially life-saving skill. Jason’s next challenge will be the North Bondi Classic; he can choose a one-kilometre or two-kilometre distance in this out-and-back ocean swim. He’s now comfortable in a pool with a black line on the bottom. In the ocean, there are no lines: just sharks and the uncertainty of the unknown. I’ll do a few ocean swims with him and then paddle my surf-ski beside him. Once you realise that what’s holding you back has no foundation, the obstacles just fall away.

World.title: ASX extends record run as gold miners rally; News Corp results, SpaceX tumbles
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX extends record run as gold miners rally; News Corp results, SpaceX tumbles Staff writers Updated August 6, 2026 — 10:57am ,first published August 6, 2026 — 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket extended its record run in early trade, boosted by gold miners after the bourse hit an all-time high on Wednesday amid hopes for a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The S&P/ASX 200 rose 47.80 points, or 0.5 per cent, to 9275.60 as of 10.45am AEST, with materials doing the heavy lifting. The local bourse had added 0.9 per cent on Wednesday to close at a record high. The Australian dollar was stronger at US70.59¢. Relief washed over global markets after Trump said the US and Iran held productive talks – but it was short-lived. Bloomberg Gold miners rallied in early trade after the price of the precious metal jumped the most since February as prospects for a deal to reopen the strait reduced expectations for Federal Reserve interest rate hikes, while a break above a key technical resistance level fuelled additional buying. Bullion advanced more than 4 per cent to around $US4250 an ounce overnight, after posting small gains in the first two sessions of the week. Silver also climbed. US President Donald Trump said a Hormuz deal is possible as early as today, as expectations build for an arrangement that allows for the reopening of the critical waterway. Oil prices softened on the prospect of a deal.



Goldminers Northern Star Resources jumped 5.3 per cent, Evolution Mining climbed 5.2 per cent and Newmont was up 4 per cent. The big iron ore and copper giants BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue Metals were also higher, rising 1.2 per cent, 0.6 per cent and 1.3 per cent, respectively. The financial sector, which accounts for a third of the ASX, was also higher, with all the big four banks advancing. Westpac added 0.9 per cent, CBA and ANZ each rose 0.8 per cent, while National Australia Bank climbed 0.5 per cent. Technology stocks took a breather after their rally of the past sessions. Software makers WiseTech Global, Xero and Technology One were down 2.4 per cent, 0.5 per cent and 1.4 per cent, respectively, while AI data centre operator NextDC dropped 1.6 per cent. Energy stocks retreated, with local oil and gas giants Woodside and Santos slipping 0.9 per cent and 0.4 per cent, respectively. The oil price held its recent losses overnight as Iran said it reached an agreement with Oman on a proposed shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, raising the prospect of more energy flows resuming through the critical waterway. Brent traded near $US79 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate was around $US75 after losing 11 per cent in the week’s first three sessions. A joint statement from the two countries is under review and the route would remain active for two to four months, although the agreement does not mean the full reopening, according to Iranian officials.



Trump said at a rally in Las Vegas on Wednesday evening that the US is talking to Tehran, and he will “see what happens” in ongoing negotiations. Oil prices have been swinging for months and were as high as $US102 per barrel at one point during the conflict, jolting already stubbornly high inflation. “US oil prices have already fallen below $US80 per barrel as the global oil market evaluates the potential of a deal with Iran,” said Rob Thummel, senior portfolio manager at Tortoise Capital. “If a deal is reached, then it is possible for oil to head toward $US70 per barrel.” News Corp’s local shares jumped 3.5 per cent after the Murdoch media empire released its results in New York after the closing bell, with the sprawling conglomerate - owner of Australian mastheads the Herald Sun, Daily Telegraph, Courier Mail and The Australian - reporting earnings were up 31 per cent in the year to June 30 to $US423 million ($600 million). Its fourth-quarter revenue of $US2.34 billion, up 11 per cent from a year ago, beat Wall Street forecasts. Information services behemoth Dow Jones remained the jewel in News Corp’s crown, but its real estate and book publishing divisions also posted strong growth. Underlying earnings in its news division slumped by 9 per cent as print advertising sagged, the FIFA World Cup drove up broadcasting costs and the company launched new masthead California Post. The company lashed out at artificial intelligence firms, calling some in the AI sector “pirates” and “crass kleptomaniacs”, promising to expose their “murky, illegal behaviour”.



News singled out AI answer engines Perplexity and Brave, with whom it is embroiled in ongoing legal battles, but also pledged to take the fight to “some of the world’s better-known companies” who deal with them in a chest-beating yearly earnings report. “Our claims against Brave focus on their data for AI products, which are legally gormlessly sourced and repurposed copyrighted material,” News Corp chief executive Robert Thomson said. Related Article Opinion

Aviation Jetstar really wants to charge you for everything but the seat Chris Zappone Senior reporter, aviation On Wall Street overnight, US stocks meandered to a mixed finish, but remained close to their records. The uncertain trading on Wall Street followed two days of big gains that gave the week and August a strong start. Several big technology companies slumped, though, ultimately weighing down the US market. The S&P 500 fell 0.2 per cent to close at 7,723.55. The index spent most of the day higher after surging to a record on Tuesday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.5 per cent to 54,349.12, reaching another record.



“The coiled spring investors have been waiting for has finally released, with the S&P 500 Index surging to record highs for the first time in two months,” said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist at Nationwide, in a report. The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 0.8 per cent to 26,363.44. It was weighed down by big technology companies losing ground, including a 4 per cent drop for Google’s parent company, Alphabet, and a 1.1 per cent drop for Microsoft. Wall Street has been generally rising as companies head into the closing stretch of their latest round of earnings reports with sharp overall gains. Three-quarters of the companies within the S&P 500 have reported results so far, and Wall Street expects profit growth of 50 per cent when they are all finished. The Walt Disney Co. rose 3.6 per cent after easily beating Wall Street’s profit forecasts, helped by a $US1 billion box office haul from Toy Story 5 and theme park revenue. Booking Holdings jumped 6.6 per cent after reporting that strong travel demand drove profit and revenue growth during its most recent quarter.



Elon Musk’s SpaceX plunged 13.6 per cent following the release late of its first quarterly report as a public company, which showed that its spending on artificial intelligence grew twice as much as its revenues. The company did help give semiconductor giant Nvidia a 3.4 per cent boost after announcing it would exclusively use that company’s chips for its AI technology. That announcement weighed on Advanced Micro Devices, which fell 7 per cent. Musk had previously said that SpaceX and his electric vehicle company, Tesla, would use chips from both Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia. Related Article Opinion

Sharemarket Burning billions: SpaceX’s sales are soaring, but its spending even more so Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Treasury yields slipped in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury slipped to 4.61 per cent from 4.63 per cent from late Tuesday. Strong corporate profits and expectations for more growth ahead have been steering stocks higher. Wall Street has also been worried about stock prices becoming unjustifiably high, especially within the technology sector and for companies focused on artificial intelligence. Profit growth, especially for some of the big chipmakers, like Nvidia, could help justify some of the big investments those companies are making in AI.



AI-focused companies, with their big market values, have been behind many of the big market swings and most of Wall Street’s gains. “The market appears to be moving from rewarding companies for AI spending to assessing the revenue and earnings that these investments can generate,” said Brian Therien, analyst, investment strategy, at Edward Jones, in a report. Inflation concerns have been hanging over markets and the Federal Reserve. The central bank has been holding its key benchmark rate steady as it monitors the costs and the impact on the economy. Wall Street expects the central bank to raise rates at least once before the end of 2026. Household spending remains resilient, despite the stress from higher costs on everything from gas to groceries. The jobs market has been one of the stronger areas of the US economy, though growth has been slowing. Wall Street will get another update on Friday with the monthly employment report for July. with AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: FIFA apologises but backlash against ‘cravenly self-interested’ Gianni Infantino grows
World.content:
SportSoccerFIFA FIFA apologises but backlash against ‘cravenly self-interested’ Gianni Infantino grows James Robson August 6, 2026 — 10:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

FIFA has apologised for errors made over Gianni Infantino’s failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup and says that senior staff in attendance at a crisis meeting in Morocco “reaffirmed their full support” for his presidency. World soccer’s governing body attempted to present a unified front amid the turbulence caused by Infantino’s controversial plans, with calls for him to step down. FIFA president Gianni Infantino is attempting to cling to power after his controversial plan to sell stakes in the World Cup. AP In a statement on Wednesday, FIFA said secretary general Mattias Grafstrom and members of the management board in attendance in Rabat had given their support to the embattled president. Referring to the plans to sell profits in the World Cup through a commercial subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), the statement said that “mistakes made were acknowledged” and that the “process should have been handled differently”.



Related Article Opinion

FIFA World Cup How the Trump factor finally turned the soccer world against Infantino FIFA said a letter had been sent to FIFA council and member associations apologising for errors and committed to “ensure they do not happen again”. Grafstrom’s stated support was notable after he distanced himself from Infantino’s now abandoned plans in an email to all FIFA staff calling the last week a “sad and reproachable series of events”. FIFA said Infantino had also reaffirmed his support for his secretary general, and that the FFE proposal was “now off the table”. “There are always lessons to be learnt, and FIFA will continue to improve its processes in light of this experience,” it said.



It added that, with the proposal withdrawn, FIFA would “no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process” and would take all necessary measures to protect its reputation. FIFA also denied a British media report suggesting Infantino, in seeking support for his presidency, had offered Morocco the hosting of the final at the 2030 World Cup. Spain, Portugal and Morocco are the main co-hosts for the 2030 edition. Morocco hope to host the final at the planned 115,000-seat King Hassan II Stadium near Casablanca; Spain have at least two contenders – the home stadiums of Real Madrid and Barcelona. Loading A FIFA spokesperson said it’s “false and misleading to claim the FIFA president has made any promise in relation to hosting the FIFA World Cup 2030 final. A decision will be made by FIFA in due course.” It remains to be seen if the meeting will ease the pressure on Infantino, who aims to win a fourth and final term in office at the March elections.



‘Serious questions’ Earlier Wednesday, the association of European soccer leagues – including the Premier League, La Liga and Serie A – called for governance reform of FIFA. It described the proposal as “dangerous” and said it pointed to deeper concerns about how the governing body operates. Gianni Infantino in Morocco, as he met with FIFA executives. AP It said it raised “serious questions about FIFA’s governance, internal culture and decision-making”. “Now more than ever, FIFA requires governance reform that ensures that all relevant stakeholders have a formal role in decisions that shape the future of our game.”



In the statement, European leagues hit out at the possibility of further expanding the World Cup to 64 teams and said that “FIFA must not be allowed to continue taking unilaterally disruptive decisions”. It said that until there was reform it would reject the “expansion or creation” of FIFA competitions. Portugal and Real Madrid great Luis Figo also called for Infantino to step down, saying he had “debased the office”. “I could write 10,000 words on the problems at FIFA. But the solution needs only three: Infantino must go,” Figo, who was a candidate for the presidency in 2015 before withdrawing, wrote in the Daily Mail. “I have loved football all my life. I was a professional player for 20 years. And believe me, I have met some rogues in my time in the game.



Related Article FIFA World Cup Resign or we’ll vote to oust you: Europe’s threat to Infantino “But what I have seen exposed in the last 10 days is the lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested behaviour I have ever witnessed. “The man who would do that – the man who would try to force through such major changes just to enrich himself and his friends – is a relic of the game’s past and should have no part in its future.” Canada’s Carney raises concerns Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney added to the global disenchantment, saying he no longer has confidence Infantino. He said the FIFA president committed a “fatal” governance failure by not consulting senior advisers.



“Certainly, I don’t have confidence in Mr Infantino,” said Carney, who had appeared alongside Infantino at several events during the 2026 World Cup co-hosted by Canada, Mexico and the United States. Related Article Updated

FIFA World Cup FIFA scraps World Cup sell-off plan after fierce backlash, pressure intensifies on Infantino The tumultuous week has raised questions about Infantino’s presidency of FIFA ahead of elections in March. UEFA, the governing body for European soccer, has applied the most intense pressure by voting to boycott the World Cup if Infantino pressed ahead with his proposal. Even after Infantino’s climbdown UEFA said it had lost confidence in FIFA’s leadership, possibly paving the way for a challenge to his presidency. The governing body for North and Central American and Caribbean soccer (CONCACAF) also said FIFA leadership had “stopped putting football first”, while the Asian confederation, of which Australia are members, also opposed the plan.



There have also been signs of division within the organisation, with chief of global soccer development Arsene Wenger distancing himself from the plans. Infantino’s senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro resigned last week and chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said staff were “deceived” by the president’s lack of openness. World.title: ‘We’re hog-tying’: Gippsland police accused of repeat misconduct after one victim suffers brain damage
World.content:
Police officers across Gippsland have been repeatedly accused of using excessive force and unlawfully deploying tasers or capsicum spray, resulting in legal claims against the force and the recent conviction of an officer. Brodie Holt sustained permanent brain damage after an arrest outside a Traralgon hotel in 2022, with his lawyer saying the case raises broader concerns about alleged police misconduct in rural and regional towns across south-eastern Victoria. Then 23-year-old Brodie Holt was placed in an induced coma after an alleged violent assault by police outside a Traralgon hotel. An investigation by The Age has uncovered five incidents – including two on the same night involving the same officer – through costly civil actions being pursued by victims in court. Only two of the incidents were subject to investigation by the force’s professional standards unit – officers were cleared in one case, and the other remains ongoing.



Related Article Courts ‘Hunting women’: Policeman who preyed on domestic violence victims jailed Victoria Police said they had not investigated three further incidents because they had not received any complaints, despite the civil claims providing details of the excessive force allegations in two of the cases. “We do not shy away from taking action as necessary to uphold community trust and confidence in our organisation,” the spokesperson said. Revelations of the mounting civil claims also come a month after a Gippsland police officer was convicted on assault charges after tasering a man nine times in under 46 seconds while on duty in Warragul. The scale of the alleged misconduct has fuelled doubts about the capacity of the state’s corruption watchdog to properly investigate hundreds of complaints from the region each year.



Between July 2018 and December 2024, the Independent Broad-based Anti-Corruption Commission received 2365 allegations of misconduct and corruption against police in the Morwell and Bairnsdale regions, but just 0.2 per cent were investigated. Out of the 300 misuse-of-force complaints, three were investigated. Each complaint can contain multiple allegations. Kellie said her son’s wrist was also injured by the handcuffs. In the same time, the substantially larger Wangaratta and Goulburn Valley regions recorded 2157 complaints – 229 of which were force complaints. None were investigated by IBAC, which has a higher threshold for investigating than Victoria Police. Holt, 27, last month received a massive legal settlement from the state government, after his lawyers estimated that his medical expenses, loss of earnings and future care would cost almost $14 million. The young tradie was verbally abused and repeatedly assaulted by several officers trying to find who had thrown a beer can at them. The Supreme Court statement of claim alleges an officer smashed Holt’s head against a brick wall before he was tackled to the ground while handcuffed, leading to his head smacking the concrete pavement.



The arresting officers were also accused of lying to paramedics when they claimed Holt had “fallen to the ground and knocked himself out”. Holt’s mother and litigation guardian, Kellie, finds it difficult to put into words the life-altering impact her son’s injuries have had. “For me, that’s the night I lost my son,” she told The Age. “He’s just not him any more.” Kellie said Brodie’s traumatic brain injury has stripped away his independence, leaving him unable to work, drive, or navigate daily life without assistance. “He hates that he’s different. He just can’t explain how, but he knows he’s different,” Kellie said.



The police officer who arrived at her doorstep hours after Brodie was rushed to hospital said her son had suffered an “intoxicated fall”. It took months of fighting for Kellie to learn what really happened to her son that night. The alleged violent police assaults Brodie Holt, Traralgon, May 7, 2022: Holt suffered permanent brain damage after an alleged violent assault by police.

Holt suffered permanent brain damage after an alleged violent assault by police. Darryl Ivory, Traralgon, January 26, 2023: Ivory has accused three officers of unlawfully arresting him and dousing him with capsicum spray despite complying with police.

Ivory has accused three officers of unlawfully arresting him and dousing him with capsicum spray despite complying with police. Jy Smith-Goode, Traralgon, January 26, 2023 : Just hours later, Smith-Goode was allegedly “hog-tied” during an alleged violent arrest by the same officers.

: Just hours later, Smith-Goode was allegedly “hog-tied” during an alleged violent arrest by the same officers. Warragul man, Warragul, May 19, 2024: Senior Constable Aaron Bowen doused a man with capsicum spray and tasered him nine times in less than a minute soon after entering the victim’s home.

Senior Constable Aaron Bowen doused a man with capsicum spray and tasered him nine times in less than a minute soon after entering the victim’s home. Peter Walker, Moe, March 2025: Walker alleges he was unlawfully arrested by officers who pointed a Taser at him despite his compliance. “I was like, ‘Nah, that doesn’t seem right’,” she said. Despite Brodie’s injuries, an internal investigation completed in March 2023 found no evidence that police assaulted him and “no grounds for the complaints whatsoever”.



“What Brodie wants, and what I want too, is justice. I want someone held accountable. But I know that’s not going to happen,” Kellie said. Jy Smith-Goode claims he was tasered on the bare-buttocks, doused with capsicum spray and “hog-tied” with three pairs of handcuffs The cases of Traralgon men Jy Smith-Goode and Darryl Ivory occurred within hours of each other and with the same police officer on Australia Day in 2023. Indigenous man Smith-Goode was Tasered on his bare bottom, doused in the face with capsicum spray and “hog-tied” with three sets of handcuffs, despite initially complying with police, according to court documents. The then-23-year-old was suffering a mental health episode while walking down a highway and wearing only a towel around his waist, when he was confronted by two officers and told he was breaching his bail conditions.



According to an amended statement of claim filed with the Supreme Court, one officer allegedly placed Smith-Goode in a “chokehold headlock”, before he was OC-sprayed by another. The 23-year-old urinated involuntarily and cried out for help as officers struggled to handcuff him, before “one of the police officers tasered the plaintiff into the left side of the plaintiff’s bare buttocks.” Senior Constable Steven Pope is then accused of saying: “Yep, we’re hog-tying”. “One or more of the police officers used a third set of handcuffs to bind the plaintiff’s wrists to his ankles behind his back in a ‘hog-tie’ position, while the plaintiff yelled and pleaded for help,” the statement of claim alleges. Pope has been named in three statements of claim alleging excessive force – Holt, Smith-Goode and Ivory.



Smith-Goode’s lawyers will pursue exemplary damages, alleging that Pope and another officer were “dishonest and deliberately misleading” when they completed a Use of Force form following the incident. It is alleged the two officers exaggerated the conduct of Smith-Goode, while failing to mention that he had been hog-tied or placed in a chokehold. “What Brodie wants, and what I want too, is justice. I want someone held accountable.” Brodie’s mother, Kellie Holt Victoria Police are yet to file a defence in the matter, and a spokesperson declined to answer questions about the case. Ivory recently settled a civil claim against the force, after a breath test allegedly turned violent – hours before Smith-Goode’s arrest.



The 49-year-old was argumentative and refused to get off his scooter to attend the police station when “Pope said words to the effect of ‘I will quite happily taser you because I’m not f---ing around mate’,” County Court documents claim. Related Article Graphic content

Victoria Police conduct Tasered nine times in 46 seconds: The arrest that saw a cop convicted of assault Pope is accused of then deploying OC spray against Ivory. The financial settlement was agreed to by Victoria Police without admission of liability and was conditional on Ivory agreeing to a non-disclosure agreement. Lawyer Jeremy King, from Robinson Gill, said the state’s corruption taskforce was unable to cope with a surge in police misconduct across regional Victoria, particularly Gippsland.



“There are clear and undeniable issues with police in the Gippsland region. We have seen a significant number of serious cases and complaints of police brutality from this region over the last few years,” King told The Age. He said it was an example of the system failing regional communities. “IBAC should have stepped up for our regional community and given them a way to call out misconduct without fear of local reprisals. The sad fact is that they haven’t. They take less than one per cent of complaints made to them and bounce the rest back to Vic Pol,” he said. In the most recent civil case, Peter Walker alleges he was assaulted by two officers in Moe following a dispute with a relative over the storage of a car in March 2025.



The officers pointed a Taser at Walker during the arrest, despite him being compliant and repeatedly stating he suffered from a permanent impairment. Walker was detained and charged with assaulting police and resisting arrest, but a magistrate dismissed the case after ruling officers had no power to arrest or detain him. Loading Last month, this masthead revealed senior constable Aaron Bowen had become the first Victorian police officer to be charged over deployment of a Taser, found guilty of 10 assault charges while arresting a man at his Warragul home in May 2024. Body camera footage captured Bowen dousing the man in the face with capsicum spray and using a Taser nine times in 46 seconds.



Bowen was convicted and fined $11,000 by the court and has been suspended without pay as Victoria Police lead an internal investigation into his conduct. The victim’s lawyer, Meliza Ludowkye, said the incident left her client suffering a “deep distrust” of police after the violent arrest, which he was now pursuing as a civil claim in the Supreme Court. “He is seeking formal acknowledgement of what occurred and fair compensation for the harm he has suffered.” In 2010, Gippsland became one of the first regions in the state to equip some of its officers with stun guns. Until then, Tasers were only issued to police within the force’s elite units. By 2014, the weapons had been rolled out to almost all frontline officers in regional Victoria – a decision criticised at the time by civil liberties groups and legal advocates.



Research from 2024 by Dr Tamar Hopkins found that Aboriginal people represented 15.4 per cent of the cases where police reported using a taser in East Gippsland, but only accounted for 3.5 per cent of the population. World.title: These Sydney schools teach 1500 students. A $9b data centre is moving next door
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life These Sydney schools teach 1500 students. A $9b data centre is moving next door David Barwell August 6, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The race to power Australia’s artificial intelligence boom has reached a vacant paddock in western Sydney, where plans for the nation’s largest data centre development have sparked a battle over potential impacts on nearby schools, homes and critical freight infrastructure. The NSW government is in the final stages of deciding whether to approve a $9 billion data centre campus that would see US technology company AirTrunk develop six four-storey data hall buildings across 52 hectares of vacant land at Kemps Creek. If approved, the project would be built over a decade and operate 24 hours a day, supported by 852 diesel backup generators, 936 cooling units, 14.4 million litres of diesel fuel storage, electrical substations and 2.65 million kilograms of lithium-ion battery storage. At completion, the facility would have a power capacity of 1.2 gigawatts – roughly equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of about one million Australian homes – making it the first Australian data centre to exceed the one-gigawatt threshold.



Planning documents stated the development is vital for Australia’s digital sovereignty, ensuring the nation keeps pace with the rapid growth of artificial intelligence, cloud computing and data storage. But the scale of the proposal has intensified concerns among schools, residents, freight operators and government agencies about the cumulative impact of data centre developments across western Sydney, where a growing cluster of facilities has earned the region the nickname “data centre alley”. A concept image of the data centre campus at Kemps Creek. NSW Department of Planning The AirTrunk proposal would join a concentration of nearby facilities, including Stack Infrastructure’s planned 450-megawatt campus at Erskine Park, NEXTDC’s approved 250-megawatt facility at Horsley Park, Microsoft’s 190-megawatt development at Kemps Creek and the Echidna data centre at Eastern Creek. In a submission to the Department of Planning, Sydney Water warned existing wastewater networks were “not designed to handle the significant discharge anticipated from data centres”.



In a statement to the Herald, project manager Plan PM said the proposal had been modified following weeks of consultation with Sydney Water, resulting in an agreement to incorporate dry-cooling technology at the site to eliminate the operational water use required for cooling systems. Planning documents show the precinct would draw power through underground transmission lines connected to Transgrid’s Sydney West substation and aims to achieve net zero operational emissions by 2030 using carbon offset mechanisms. The planned development joins a growing list of Western Sydney data centres, including this approved facility which will be operated by Microsoft at Kemps Creek. “We will continue to work constructively with stakeholders and community to assess long-term servicing options as the application progresses,” Plan PM said in statement. The impending decision comes as governments grapple with how to accommodate the rapidly increasing electricity and water demands of the AI boom. Last month, the federal government released a proposed national framework for data centres that would require facilities to fund additional renewable energy generation and electricity grid infrastructure.



NSW already hosts almost 90 operational data centres, according to state government figures, with another 15 major projects worth a combined $52 billion progressing through the planning system. The AirTrunk proposal has also exposed tensions between industrial development and surrounding communities. The site sits near three schools educating more than 1500 students, including Mamre Anglican School, about 60 metres from the site, Emmaus Catholic College, about 170 metres away, and Trinity Catholic Primary School, approximately 320 metres away. In submissions to the Department of Planning, Catholic Schools Parramatta Diocese and The Anglican Schools Corporation warned that around-the-clock operations could expose students to continuous noise from industrial cooling units, diesel exhaust from routine generator testing and increased traffic during school pick-up and drop-off periods. Concerns were also raised about the visual impact of the 40-metre height of buildings. Mamre Anglican School principal Ross Whelan questioned whether a development of such industrial scale belonged next to a school.



“Members of our school community ... will have concerns regarding the potential health impacts and risk from both the operation and site infrastructure requirements,” he wrote. Related Article Commercial real estate Microsoft, Macquarie pump billions into power hungry data centres The project faces further headwinds from the freight and logistics sectors. NSW Ports and the Australasian Railway Association have urged the government to reject the application, arguing the site is strategically important industrial land adjoining the planned Western Sydney Intermodal Terminal, Western Sydney Freight Line and near the new Western Sydney International Airport. NSW Ports warned that converting the land into a data centre would “permanently lock out” nationally significant freight land needed to move shipping containers efficiently between Port Botany and Western Sydney by rail. Planning documents estimate the development would generate $13.7 billion in economic output during construction, support 2775 operational jobs and include measures to mitigate noise and vibration impacts on nearby properties.



For local residents like Ted Pochodyla, whose home is adjacent to the development site, the plans have prompted fears his home could be exposed to further noise, traffic and vibrations in the increasingly industrialised area. Ted Pochodyla, pictured at his home in Kemps Creek. Wolter Peeters “I am slowly being surrounded by industry on all sides, and it worries me greatly the negative impact this construction may have on my health and everyday life,” Pochodyla said. The NSW Department of Planning is expected to hand down its determination on the project in the coming weeks. AirTrunk was contacted for additional comment but did not respond to questions. World.title: Australia news LIVE: Labor MP Ed Husic to take break from duties after ‘serious’ car crash; Coalition will force Albanese to cede ground on gambling reforms
World.content:
Communications Minister Anika Wells says she wants to see the government’s gambling legislation get through the Parliament.

The Albanese government was given an ultimatum on its gambling package yesterday: work with the Coalition or the Greens on amendments, or the legislation won’t pass. Both parties have raised issue with the laws, which they think are insufficient to protect Australians from harm.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told question time in the last session of parliament: “This is good reform … and the parliament should vote for it... If they don’t, then they do have the option of the status quo.”

But Wells said it was not yet her intention to drop the package - a move that would upset many members of the Labor caucus who want a strong crackdown.

“That was some weeks ago now,” Wells said, referring to the prime minister’s comments last month.

“I’d say we’re some ways off that yet. I’m having constructive discussions with both the shadow communications minister for the Coalition and the shadow communications spokesperson for the Greens. We’ll keep those discussions going. We’d love to see this passed.”

World.title: Perth paediatrician now faces 72 child sex abuse charges
World.content:
A Perth paediatrician on bail over dozens of child sex abuse allegations will return to court on Thursday after being hit with another 15 charges.

Dr Chia Liang Saw, 41, was initially arrested and charged in May, with police alleging he engaged in persistent sexual conduct with a child and possessed child exploitation material.

Perth paediatrician Dr Chia Liang Saw. LinkedIn

Saw’s request for bail was repeatedly delayed, with prosecutors adding further charges as more alleged victims were identified, before he was eventually released under strict conditions last month.

Now, the paediatrician faces a total of 72 charges relating to 18 victims, with the new allegations including six counts of indecent dealing with a child under 13 years old, three counts of indecently recording a child under 13 years old, and three counts of sexual penetration of a child under 13 years old.

World.title: The astounding moment when this Fiddler on the Roof soars
World.content:
Theatre Royal, August 5. Until October 3

Tevye’s is such an indomitable heart as makes him larger than life: a force of nature who wears all that 1905 Imperial Russia can throw at a poor Jewish dairy farmer. Beyond coping, this champion of tradition even learns to adapt to a changing world. He can find joy in the face of adversity, and consoling humour in his unanswered querying of his God.

Few musicals are so dependent on one actor.

Troy Sussman follows Australian predecessors such as Hayes Gordon and Max Gillies. Gillies milked every drop of comedy from Tevye’s homespun philosophies and idle fancies. Gordon added voice and presence. When either sang If I Were a Rich Man, you were drawn deep into their hearts and humble aspirations; were warmed by their good cheer.

Troy Sussman as Tevye with Ben Adler as The Fiddler. Daniel Boud

Sussman can’t quite get there – yet. He seemed nervous to begin on opening night, and therefore initially lacked presence. His singing voice, too, missed something of that barrel-chested rotundity, and not all the comedy was maximised. Yet, he slowly became more convincing, suggesting he may well come to fill out this great role, and the production will grow accordingly.

When composer Jerry Bock, lyricist Sheldon Harnick and book writer Joseph Stein, director Jerome Robbins and performer Zero Mostel first unleased the show in 1964, it became Broadway’s longest-running musical, finally knocked off that perch by the vastly inferior Grease in 1972. To put its success in perspective, it ran longer than likes of My Fair Lady, Oklahoma!, South Pacific and The Sound of Music, thanks to Tevye and such other songwriting triumphs as Matchmaker, Matchmaker, To Life and the almost transcendental Sunrise, Sunset.

This London production (with Australian cast), originally directed by Jordan Fein, contains in Tevye’s Dream a sequence to astound. Tevye must reconcile his wife, Golde (Alexis Fishman), to their oldest daughter (Freya Boltman) marrying a poor young tailor (Felix Star) for love (of all things!), rather than a rich, elderly butcher (an excellent John Waters).

Golde’s bed suddenly becomes almost stage-width, with dead Grandma Tzeitel occupying the other end, and a clutch of the two-dozen cast dressed in white night attire helping enact the faux dream of which Tevye tells her. Golde can be forgiven for being taken in. Anyone would succumb to such simultaneously unearthly and witty staging.

Fishman and the daughters seem rather undercooked, while Sigrid Thornton overacts as Yente, the matchmaker. The singing, dancing and music are uniformly good, however, and Tom Scutt’s set is a land of wheat fields, rather than the usual village of Chagall-like dwellings.

Even the roof atop which fiddler Ben Adler beautifully plays is made of wheat. And it flies! Just like Tevye’s big heart – including when the Russians expel the community, which so often happened to their forebears across the centuries with scant warning.

“Perhaps that’s why we always wear our hats,” quips Tevye.

World.title: Jason speaks Japanese, runs marathons and a business – but he couldn’t swim until Gary came along
World.content:
NationalGood Weekend Jason speaks Japanese, runs marathons and a business – but he couldn’t swim until Gary came along Erin O'Dwyer August 6, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Dr Gary Shiels, 80, discovered that his friend, Dr Jason Graham-Nye, 56, couldn’t swim – despite Jason having lived his entire life by the beach – Gary made it his mission to teach him.

Gary Shiels (left) and Jason Graham-Nye. “I’d never seen a fear like Jason’s,” Gary says. “He’s been the best of my prodigies.” Wolter Peeters Jason: We met at the gym in 2023. Gary gave me some tips and we had coffee afterwards. We really hit it off. He’d finished his PhD and I was about to submit mine. His was on healthy ageing. It was so cool to meet someone who was still learning in his 70s – it made me feel like a spring chicken. He’s a surf lifesaving legend, a former president of the North Bondi Surf Club and its patron. He started saying to me, “You should get your bronze medallion and join the surf club”, but I said nothing. It was too mortifying to admit that I was terrified of the water. I’ve done many difficult things in my life – worked as a Japanese interpreter, run 15 marathons, built a company – but I had to say to Gary, “I can’t put my head under the water.” I was ashamed.



When I was a kid, our neighbours had a pool and invited [the late, well-known Sydney swim teacher] Alf Vockler over to show us how to swim. Vockler literally threw me into the deep end. It was so traumatising and I said to myself, “I’m never doing that again.” And I didn’t. Related Article Good Weekend ‘A fundamental part of growing up’: Why Aussie kids can’t swim any more Last December, Gary ambushed me at coffee and suggested I make learning to swim my New Year’s resolution. My sons [Harper, 21, and Fynn, 23] thought this was hilarious. Gary told me he’d had a similar swimming experience to me as a kid, but his mother had refused to let him give up. I had this 50-year-old story in my head: “I can’t swim. Chapter closed.” Gary didn’t argue with the story; he just showed me a different ending. I thought, “What else in my life isn’t as fixed as I think?” We had our first day in the pool together a few days later. I turned up in board shorts; he instructed me to get jammers [stretchy knee-length swimwear], a cap and a snorkel. I felt like a five-year-old again. Meanwhile, everyone was ploughing up and down the pool, doing tumble turns. He had me swim half the length of the 25-metre pool freestyle. I was freaked out and it was slow; I got a lung-full and had to stand up. He was very calm. He said, “Take a break and go again.” Eventually, I managed one lap, then two. As soon as he helped me figure out how the body is meant to lie in the water – co-ordinating the neck turn with the stroke – something clicked. I was in the pool every second day.



Gary’s always right. He gives you one piece of advice, it works and so by the time you’ve thought of a counter-argument, you’ve already improved. He’s extremely knowledgeable about all things relating to physical activity, including the science. I’d like the occasional opportunity to disagree with him, but he doesn’t give it to me. When he’s not there, I make excuses for myself; he calls it “the almanac of excuses”. We play golf together now, too, and he’s built a relationship with my sons. I watch him interact with them and think, “Wow, that’s so cool”; he’s perpetually curious, asks great questions and is a wonderful conversationalist. Hopefully, what they’ve seen is their father being exceptionally incompetent at something and sticking with it anyway. Overcoming a really difficult obstacle is the essence of life. It certainly helps you feel more calm, which you carry into everything else you do. ‘I had to say to Gary, “I can’t put my head under the water.” I was ashamed.’ Jason Graham-Nye I can swim about 200 metres freestyle without the snorkel now. Gary even has plans for me to do an ocean swim. It’s like a second life – I’m addicted. I’m so grateful to him. Gary: Jason wasn’t a member of the surf club and he was very cagey about why. When he told me he was terrified of the water, it was incomprehensible to me. I said, “You can’t live in Bondi and not be able to swim!” From then on, I was on a mission.



As a lad, he got thrown in the water, panicked and nearly drowned. He didn’t go back in for 50 years. I had a similar experience at Bondi Baths, but my mother was very tenacious. She said, “Gary, you’re going to swim if it kills me.” She dragged me off to Alf Vockler, who taught swimming at Watsons Bay. Strangely, Alf was the perpetrator of Jason’s problems but the solution to mine. Related Article Good Weekend ‘Things aren’t as stretchy and flexible’: Shane Gould on the reality of sex in your 60s It took a bit of cajoling to get Jason on board with my plan to teach him to swim. I was worried it might mean the end of our friendship if I kept pressing him. Even up to our first lesson, I wasn’t sure he’d follow through. The longer you have a belief that you can’t do something, the harder it is to convince yourself that you can. Time had been Jason’s enemy. In 60 years of coaching and being coached, I’ve seen almost everything, but I’d never seen a fear like Jason’s. Frankly, it’s been a revelation: he improved so quickly. We train four times a week and he hasn’t missed a single session. He’s been the best of my prodigies. I didn’t tell anyone I was teaching Jason to swim: I felt protective of him. I knew the problem was in his head: he was worried he was going to swallow water and drown. I came up with the idea of swimming with a snorkel. All of a sudden, he could put his head under the water and breathe. A positive attitude is essential for success in anything: it’s a matter of getting rid of the demons between the ears.



Jason has a strong moral compass. I’ve watched him speak out on some very difficult issues. In 2024, he gave an interview to ABC’s Four Corners about bullying at his former school, Cranbrook. It put him and his family at considerable risk, but he did it anyway. He presents quite a jovial disposition to the world, but underneath it, there’s a very serious person. He’s honest and determined, two qualities I look for in any friend. Related Article Good Weekend Two uni besties had a falling-out. An unusual project came to their rescue I’ve connected with his sons, too, now. Both are strong young men but neither were strong swimmers. Harper’s a board rider who wasn’t a confident swimmer; Fynn’s based in London and never went in the water. Swimming is a potentially life-saving skill. Jason’s next challenge will be the North Bondi Classic; he can choose a one-kilometre or two-kilometre distance in this out-and-back ocean swim. He’s now comfortable in a pool with a black line on the bottom. In the ocean, there are no lines: just sharks and the uncertainty of the unknown. I’ll do a few ocean swims with him and then paddle my surf-ski beside him. Once you realise that what’s holding you back has no foundation, the obstacles just fall away.

World.title: ASX extends record run as gold miners rally; News Corp results, SpaceX tumbles
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX extends record run as gold miners rally; News Corp results, SpaceX tumbles Staff writers Updated August 6, 2026 — 10:57am ,first published August 6, 2026 — 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket extended its record run in early trade, boosted by gold miners after the bourse hit an all-time high on Wednesday amid hopes for a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The S&P/ASX 200 rose 47.80 points, or 0.5 per cent, to 9275.60 as of 10.45am AEST, with materials doing the heavy lifting. The local bourse had added 0.9 per cent on Wednesday to close at a record high. The Australian dollar was stronger at US70.59¢. Relief washed over global markets after Trump said the US and Iran held productive talks – but it was short-lived. Bloomberg Gold miners rallied in early trade after the price of the precious metal jumped the most since February as prospects for a deal to reopen the strait reduced expectations for Federal Reserve interest rate hikes, while a break above a key technical resistance level fuelled additional buying. Bullion advanced more than 4 per cent to around $US4250 an ounce overnight, after posting small gains in the first two sessions of the week. Silver also climbed. US President Donald Trump said a Hormuz deal is possible as early as today, as expectations build for an arrangement that allows for the reopening of the critical waterway. Oil prices softened on the prospect of a deal.



Goldminers Northern Star Resources jumped 5.3 per cent, Evolution Mining climbed 5.2 per cent and Newmont was up 4 per cent. The big iron ore and copper giants BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue Metals were also higher, rising 1.2 per cent, 0.6 per cent and 1.3 per cent, respectively. The financial sector, which accounts for a third of the ASX, was also higher, with all the big four banks advancing. Westpac added 0.9 per cent, CBA and ANZ each rose 0.8 per cent, while National Australia Bank climbed 0.5 per cent. Technology stocks took a breather after their rally of the past sessions. Software makers WiseTech Global, Xero and Technology One were down 2.4 per cent, 0.5 per cent and 1.4 per cent, respectively, while AI data centre operator NextDC dropped 1.6 per cent. Energy stocks retreated, with local oil and gas giants Woodside and Santos slipping 0.9 per cent and 0.4 per cent, respectively. The oil price held its recent losses overnight as Iran said it reached an agreement with Oman on a proposed shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, raising the prospect of more energy flows resuming through the critical waterway. Brent traded near $US79 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate was around $US75 after losing 11 per cent in the week’s first three sessions. A joint statement from the two countries is under review and the route would remain active for two to four months, although the agreement does not mean the full reopening, according to Iranian officials.



Trump said at a rally in Las Vegas on Wednesday evening that the US is talking to Tehran, and he will “see what happens” in ongoing negotiations. Oil prices have been swinging for months and were as high as $US102 per barrel at one point during the conflict, jolting already stubbornly high inflation. “US oil prices have already fallen below $US80 per barrel as the global oil market evaluates the potential of a deal with Iran,” said Rob Thummel, senior portfolio manager at Tortoise Capital. “If a deal is reached, then it is possible for oil to head toward $US70 per barrel.” News Corp’s local shares jumped 3.5 per cent after the Murdoch media empire released its results in New York after the closing bell, with the sprawling conglomerate - owner of Australian mastheads the Herald Sun, Daily Telegraph, Courier Mail and The Australian - reporting earnings were up 31 per cent in the year to June 30 to $US423 million ($600 million). Its fourth-quarter revenue of $US2.34 billion, up 11 per cent from a year ago, beat Wall Street forecasts. Information services behemoth Dow Jones remained the jewel in News Corp’s crown, but its real estate and book publishing divisions also posted strong growth. Underlying earnings in its news division slumped by 9 per cent as print advertising sagged, the FIFA World Cup drove up broadcasting costs and the company launched new masthead California Post. The company lashed out at artificial intelligence firms, calling some in the AI sector “pirates” and “crass kleptomaniacs”, promising to expose their “murky, illegal behaviour”.



News singled out AI answer engines Perplexity and Brave, with whom it is embroiled in ongoing legal battles, but also pledged to take the fight to “some of the world’s better-known companies” who deal with them in a chest-beating yearly earnings report. “Our claims against Brave focus on their data for AI products, which are legally gormlessly sourced and repurposed copyrighted material,” News Corp chief executive Robert Thomson said. Related Article Opinion

Aviation Jetstar really wants to charge you for everything but the seat Chris Zappone Senior reporter, aviation On Wall Street overnight, US stocks meandered to a mixed finish, but remained close to their records. The uncertain trading on Wall Street followed two days of big gains that gave the week and August a strong start. Several big technology companies slumped, though, ultimately weighing down the US market. The S&P 500 fell 0.2 per cent to close at 7,723.55. The index spent most of the day higher after surging to a record on Tuesday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.5 per cent to 54,349.12, reaching another record.



“The coiled spring investors have been waiting for has finally released, with the S&P 500 Index surging to record highs for the first time in two months,” said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist at Nationwide, in a report. The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 0.8 per cent to 26,363.44. It was weighed down by big technology companies losing ground, including a 4 per cent drop for Google’s parent company, Alphabet, and a 1.1 per cent drop for Microsoft. Wall Street has been generally rising as companies head into the closing stretch of their latest round of earnings reports with sharp overall gains. Three-quarters of the companies within the S&P 500 have reported results so far, and Wall Street expects profit growth of 50 per cent when they are all finished. The Walt Disney Co. rose 3.6 per cent after easily beating Wall Street’s profit forecasts, helped by a $US1 billion box office haul from Toy Story 5 and theme park revenue. Booking Holdings jumped 6.6 per cent after reporting that strong travel demand drove profit and revenue growth during its most recent quarter.



Elon Musk’s SpaceX plunged 13.6 per cent following the release late of its first quarterly report as a public company, which showed that its spending on artificial intelligence grew twice as much as its revenues. The company did help give semiconductor giant Nvidia a 3.4 per cent boost after announcing it would exclusively use that company’s chips for its AI technology. That announcement weighed on Advanced Micro Devices, which fell 7 per cent. Musk had previously said that SpaceX and his electric vehicle company, Tesla, would use chips from both Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia. Related Article Opinion

Sharemarket Burning billions: SpaceX’s sales are soaring, but its spending even more so Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Treasury yields slipped in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury slipped to 4.61 per cent from 4.63 per cent from late Tuesday. Strong corporate profits and expectations for more growth ahead have been steering stocks higher. Wall Street has also been worried about stock prices becoming unjustifiably high, especially within the technology sector and for companies focused on artificial intelligence. Profit growth, especially for some of the big chipmakers, like Nvidia, could help justify some of the big investments those companies are making in AI.



AI-focused companies, with their big market values, have been behind many of the big market swings and most of Wall Street’s gains. “The market appears to be moving from rewarding companies for AI spending to assessing the revenue and earnings that these investments can generate,” said Brian Therien, analyst, investment strategy, at Edward Jones, in a report. Inflation concerns have been hanging over markets and the Federal Reserve. The central bank has been holding its key benchmark rate steady as it monitors the costs and the impact on the economy. Wall Street expects the central bank to raise rates at least once before the end of 2026. Household spending remains resilient, despite the stress from higher costs on everything from gas to groceries. The jobs market has been one of the stronger areas of the US economy, though growth has been slowing. Wall Street will get another update on Friday with the monthly employment report for July. with AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading.
