World.title: FIFA apologises but backlash against ‘cravenly self-interested’ Gianni Infantino grows
World.content:
SportSoccerFIFA FIFA apologises but backlash against ‘cravenly self-interested’ Gianni Infantino grows James Robson August 6, 2026 — 10:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

FIFA has apologised for errors made over Gianni Infantino’s failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup and says that senior staff in attendance at a crisis meeting in Morocco “reaffirmed their full support” for his presidency. World soccer’s governing body attempted to present a unified front amid the turbulence caused by Infantino’s controversial plans, with calls for him to step down. FIFA president Gianni Infantino is attempting to cling to power after his controversial plan to sell stakes in the World Cup. AP In a statement on Wednesday, FIFA said secretary general Mattias Grafstrom and members of the management board in attendance in Rabat had given their support to the embattled president. Referring to the plans to sell profits in the World Cup through a commercial subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), the statement said that “mistakes made were acknowledged” and that the “process should have been handled differently”.



Related Article Opinion

FIFA World Cup How the Trump factor finally turned the soccer world against Infantino FIFA said a letter had been sent to FIFA council and member associations apologising for errors and committed to “ensure they do not happen again”. Grafstrom’s stated support was notable after he distanced himself from Infantino’s now abandoned plans in an email to all FIFA staff calling the last week a “sad and reproachable series of events”. FIFA said Infantino had also reaffirmed his support for his secretary general, and that the FFE proposal was “now off the table”. “There are always lessons to be learnt, and FIFA will continue to improve its processes in light of this experience,” it said.



It added that, with the proposal withdrawn, FIFA would “no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process” and would take all necessary measures to protect its reputation. FIFA also denied a British media report suggesting Infantino, in seeking support for his presidency, had offered Morocco the hosting of the final at the 2030 World Cup. Spain, Portugal and Morocco are the main co-hosts for the 2030 edition. Morocco hope to host the final at the planned 115,000-seat King Hassan II Stadium near Casablanca; Spain have at least two contenders – the home stadiums of Real Madrid and Barcelona. Loading A FIFA spokesperson said it’s “false and misleading to claim the FIFA president has made any promise in relation to hosting the FIFA World Cup 2030 final. A decision will be made by FIFA in due course.” It remains to be seen if the meeting will ease the pressure on Infantino, who aims to win a fourth and final term in office at the March elections.



‘Serious questions’ Earlier Wednesday, the association of European soccer leagues – including the Premier League, La Liga and Serie A – called for governance reform of FIFA. It described the proposal as “dangerous” and said it pointed to deeper concerns about how the governing body operates. Gianni Infantino in Morocco, as he met with FIFA executives. AP It said it raised “serious questions about FIFA’s governance, internal culture and decision-making”. “Now more than ever, FIFA requires governance reform that ensures that all relevant stakeholders have a formal role in decisions that shape the future of our game.”



In the statement, European leagues hit out at the possibility of further expanding the World Cup to 64 teams and said that “FIFA must not be allowed to continue taking unilaterally disruptive decisions”. It said that until there was reform it would reject the “expansion or creation” of FIFA competitions. Portugal and Real Madrid great Luis Figo also called for Infantino to step down, saying he had “debased the office”. “I could write 10,000 words on the problems at FIFA. But the solution needs only three: Infantino must go,” Figo, who was a candidate for the presidency in 2015 before withdrawing, wrote in the Daily Mail. “I have loved football all my life. I was a professional player for 20 years. And believe me, I have met some rogues in my time in the game.



Related Article FIFA World Cup Resign or we’ll vote to oust you: Europe’s threat to Infantino “But what I have seen exposed in the last 10 days is the lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested behaviour I have ever witnessed. “The man who would do that – the man who would try to force through such major changes just to enrich himself and his friends – is a relic of the game’s past and should have no part in its future.” Canada’s Carney raises concerns Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney added to the global disenchantment, saying he no longer has confidence Infantino. He said the FIFA president committed a “fatal” governance failure by not consulting senior advisers.



“Certainly, I don’t have confidence in Mr Infantino,” said Carney, who had appeared alongside Infantino at several events during the 2026 World Cup co-hosted by Canada, Mexico and the United States. Related Article Updated

FIFA World Cup FIFA scraps World Cup sell-off plan after fierce backlash, pressure intensifies on Infantino The tumultuous week has raised questions about Infantino’s presidency of FIFA ahead of elections in March. UEFA, the governing body for European soccer, has applied the most intense pressure by voting to boycott the World Cup if Infantino pressed ahead with his proposal. Even after Infantino’s climbdown UEFA said it had lost confidence in FIFA’s leadership, possibly paving the way for a challenge to his presidency. The governing body for North and Central American and Caribbean soccer (CONCACAF) also said FIFA leadership had “stopped putting football first”, while the Asian confederation, of which Australia are members, also opposed the plan.



There have also been signs of division within the organisation, with chief of global soccer development Arsene Wenger distancing himself from the plans. Infantino’s senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro resigned last week and chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said staff were “deceived” by the president’s lack of openness. World.title: ACT wants to expand pharmacists power and make it easier to open new pharmacies
World.content:
The ACT party wants to expand what pharmacists can do and make it easier to open new pharmacies.

If elected the party would let pharmacists treat more conditions, manage stable long-term conditions, cut red tape stopping new pharmacies from opening, and introduce 24-hour prescription collection through "secure electronic lockers."

ACT leader David Seymour announced the party's Pharmacy First policy in Auckland on Thursday.

Seymour said the current rules confined pharmacists to a small number of permitted services, and he wanted to give them permission to do more.

"Meanwhile, time that pharmacists used to spend 'counting and pouring' is being freed up by automation, at the same time that community pharmacies are under serious revenue pressure.

"Pharmacists have the capacity, the need, and the proximity. All that's missing is permission."

The policy expanded on changes already implemented in government, allowing Pharmacists to treat UTIs, conjunctivitis, chest infections, and ear infections.

The party said it would expand the Minor Ailments Scheme to include conditions pharmacists are trained to assess and treat:

Throat and ENT: acute sore throat

Skin and eyes: school sores (impetigo), stye

Ear, nose and throat: tonsillitis and acute sore throat

Musculoskeletal and pain: gout, osteoarthritis

Sexual and reproductive health: vaginal thrush; chlamydia and gonorrhoea testing (self-swab kits), period pain

Blood tests: pharmacists will be able to order appropriate blood tests directly, at a patient's request or where they identify a clinical need

Seymour also said "rules that prevent new pharmacies from opening will go."

"The five-pharmacy ownership cap - a restriction the Government's own October 2025 Regulatory Impact Statement admits is 'not being meaningfully followed' - will be explicitly removed.

"Proximity requirements that block new pharmacies from opening near existing ones will also go. Any pharmacy that meets safety and quality standards should be able to open."

He also said secure prescription e-lockers would allow New Zealanders managing stable long-term conditions to collect "pre-dispensed medicines at any time using a digital code, similar to click-and-collect at a supermarket."

The lockers would not be used to dispense controlled drugs, refrigerated medicines, or medications requiring monitoring.

World.title: Labour to slim down Investment Boost policy, targeting it to small businesses
World.content:
Labour has confirmed it would slim down the coalition's Investment Boost policy, if elected, targeting it to small businesses only.

It's just unveiled a series of policies focused on backing small businesses - in the same week Christopher Luxon delivered an apology to them.

If elected, Labour says it would require big businesses to pay small suppliers within 15 days for invoices worth up to $25,000, as well as publish how quickly they pay their suppliers.

It would also replace the government's Investment Boost and lift the tax write-off for small businesses buying equipment or tools, from $1000 to $10,000.

The party said small businesses would then be able to immediately deduct the cost of new equipment from their tax bill.

And Labour would raise the GST registration threshold, from $60,000 to $80,000, meaning about 35,000 businesses would no longer need to sign up.

The party said it was about giving small businesses a "fair go", and the policies were based directly on feedback from the sector.

Leader Chris Hipkins said under a Labour government "small business owners will get paid sooner, get more support to invest in the equipment they need, and keep more of what they earn."

He called small businesses the "heart of New Zealand's economy."

"Small business owners take the risks, put in the hours, employ locally and keep our communities running.

"But under National, they're being squeezed by rising costs and falling demand."

Hipkins said Labour's policy was more targeted than the government's Investment Boost, because small businesses need the most support.

"Giving a company chief executive a tax rebate when they go and buy a new BMW, isn't going to grow the economy. Supporting small businesses will," he said.

Finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds said the party had not projected how much the economy would grow as a result of the policies, but said close to up to 600,000 businesses would benefit from it.

The party did not reveal what it would do with the leftover Investment Boost money, saying it would lay that out in its fiscal plan.

Labour Small Business spokesperson Dan Rosewarne said running a small business should mean "building something of your own, not spending your evenings chasing overdue invoices and filling in forms."

World.title: 'Wrong people are getting the wrong housing in the wrong places' -Salvation Army
World.content:
New Zealand has been building enough houses in recent years, but not in the right places or for the right people, the Salvation Army says.

It has released a new housing report which notes that, over the five years to March this year, the housing stock grew 9.1 percent while the population only increased 5.5 percent.

"On the face of it, New Zealanders are becoming better housed but alongside this surfeit of new housing is another story of small increases in rates of overcrowding and housing-related stress," the report said.

"The central question for policy is not whether New Zealand has enough housing in total, but whether the right housing is in the right places at prices people on modest incomes can afford. Any credible housing policy will need to grapple with distribution, not just supply."

Report author Alan Johnson said building houses was not the same as housing people well.

Do I have to buy that extended warranty? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

"This report shows clearly that the wrong people are getting the wrong housing in the wrong places. No party has yet given a convincing answer about what they intend to do about it

"Some of the housing problems we have are still questions of affordability despite the fact that rents seem to be falling in many places. Incomes, particularly for people who are either on benefits or working precariously, aren't sufficient to secure adequate housing."

He said developers were focused on producing homes to be sold on the private market, which put them out of reach of lower-income people.

Housing stock had grown fastest over the 2023-2026 period in Marlborough and the West Coast. Marlborough's housing stock increased by an estimated 15.8 percent. At the same time, the report estimated its population growth was 0.7 percent.

West Coast added 10.5 percent to its housing stock but its population lifted 3. 2 percent. Nelson increased its housing stock by 4.7 percent while its population increased 0.7 percent.

Johnson said 18 percent of new housing provided between 2019 and 2023 was unoccupied and could be second or third homes for wealthier households. Thames-Coromandel had the highest proportion of unoccupied dwellings, at 50 percent. Upper Hutt was the bottom of the table, at 5.2 percent.

He said housing indicators were improving in Auckland, where housing stock was up more than 6 percent over the three years, but other parts of the country were faring more poorly.

Rents had risen sharply in Gisborne, Taranaki, Southland and the West Coast. Social housing waiting lists relative to available stock were most acute in Northland, Bay of Plenty, the West Coast and Southland.

Johnson said it was likely that people moving out of Auckland in search of cheaper housing in other areas were gentrifying those areas, purchasing homes previously available to rent and reducing the rental housing supply.

"People are leaving Auckland and going elsewhere and possibly buying up the housing that was previously rented. We're seeing in some areas, particularly places like Gisborne and Hawke's Bay, a shrinking of the rental housing pool.

"I think this is not a new phenomenon, it's been happening in the last 10 years and the evidence of people leaving Auckland is quite clear, they're going to the provincial cities where housing is cheaper. That sometimes comes at the cost of people who already live there. I think that's a reasonably important trend that we need to reflect in our housing policies and particularly where we choose to build social housing."

He said there needed to be more investment in public housing,

"The Government needs to be building more social housing than it is. There was a legacy from the last government of a significant build and purchase of additional social housing units and this has waned quite considerably in the last year or 15 months.

"It's really the case that there will be many households that just can't foot it in the market and some level of intervention is required for them whether that's by way of subsidies through the accommodation supplement or direct provision through social housing. It appears as though there is a gap not being met."

About 1500 to 1600 homes were being added to the social housing stock each year, while applications were running at about 5500 to 6000 a quarter.

Johnson said Government spending on housing subsidies would hit $4.8 billion in the 2026/27 year. The accommodation supplement had declined in real terms by 14 percent per recipient over the past five years.

He said about 90 percent of the country's housing wealth was held by the wealthiest 40 percent of households.

Cotality chief property economist Kelvin Davidson said it was correct that building more houses did not mean everything was okay. 'It might just have lessened a previously huge shortage rather than removing shortages altogether.

"A little thing that we always highlight in our affordability reports is that even though the rent measures as a percentage of income look better recently they are only averages using median rents and median income. The typical household that rents might be paying a standard rent but have a below-average income, making their burden much tougher."

World.title: Asian candidates eye larger representation in Parliament
World.content:
The country's growing Asian population could see more representation in Parliament following the general election in November.

Eleven politicians of Asian heritage currently sit in the Beehive.

However, this number is almost certainly set to grow if recent polling and expected party list rankings hold true.

The latest RNZ-Reid Research poll in July gives Labour top spot with 34 percent of the party vote, followed by National at 28.7 percent, New Zealand First at 11.5 percent, the Green Party at 10.3 percent, ACT at 7.8 percent and Te Pāti Māori at 2.3 percent.

This result would give the ruling coalition 61 seats in total, with National picking up 36, New Zealand First 15 and ACT 10.

Conversely, Labour would get 43 seats, the Greens 13 and Te Pāti Māori three.

The above distribution would change significantly if the Opportunity Party managed to cross the 5 percent party vote threshold.

The RNZ-Reid Research poll in July had the party tracking at 4.7 percent.

On current polling, some candidates of Asian descent look likely to secure a seat in Parliament.

Former Health Minister and Labour List MP Ayesha Verrall, whose family hails from the Maldives, leads the pack as the highest-ranked Asian candidate with a ranking of six.

Indeed, Labour could have as many as four MPs of Asian heritage next term based on current polling.

In addition to Verrall, Sri Lankan New Zealander Vanushi Walters (list ranking 8), who is also the party's foreign affairs spokesperson, is likely to make the cut alongside career policeman Rakesh Naidoo (list ranking 13) and list MP Priyanca Radhakrishnan (list ranking 18) - both of Indian ethnicity.

Although Kharag Singh is ranked 61st on Labour's party list, the small business owner could secure a seat if he manages to regain the Takanini electorate back from National's Rima Nakhle.

Nakhle defeated Neru Leavasa of Labour to win Takanini by more than 8000 votes in 2023.

In 2023, Singh lost the Botany electorate to Prime Minister Christopher Luxon by more than 16,000 votes.

But with just under 40 percent of Takanini now identifying as Indian, Singh may fancy his chances.

Luxon, meanwhile, appears to be struggling to find Indian-origin candidates in realistic winnable positions to represent National in the election based on current polling.

In 2023, National selected an unprecedented five electoral candidates of Indian heritage to run for office.

However, all five were listed at 30 or higher and, standing in stronghold Labour seats, they lost their electorate battles and left National without an Indian MP over its current term.

Three of those candidates return in 2026, including Karuna Muthu from Wellington Bays and Ankit Bansal from Palmerston North.

Mahesh Muralidhar, who lost to Green Party leader Chlöe Swarbrick in Auckland Central by less than 4000 votes in 2023, is standing for the Tāmaki electorate this year.

Muralidhar's chances of winning Tāmaki got a shot in the arm in March when sitting electorate MP and former ACT deputy leader Brooke van Velden announced her retirement from politics.

Tāmaki has been a National stronghold for decades before van Velden turned it pink in 2023.

Muralidhar is hoping the seat turns blue once more.

Three new Indian New Zealanders are standing for National in the 2026 elections: Lalit Arya in Ōtāhuhu, Sunil Kumar in Glendene, and Ghouse Majeed in Manurewa.

The electorates apart from Tāmaki are opposition strongholds, and the five National candidates of Indian origin contesting those seats can realistically only hope to enter Parliament by virtue of high party list rankings based on current polling.

The National Party, ACT, New Zealand First and Te Pāti Māori have yet to release its party lists.

Labour, the Greens and the Opportunity Party have made their respective party lists public.

National does much better in terms of other Asian ethnicities, with senior MP and former minister Melissa Lee and list MP Nancy Lu already declared as candidates this time.

Lee, who is of South Korean origin, has been in the Beehive since 2008 and narrowly lost to Labour's Helen White in Mt Albert by 18 votes last election.

However, she entered Parliament for the current term based on her party list ranking of 13.

Lu, who is of Chinese heritage, was the highest-ranking candidate of Chinese descent in National, with a ranking of 20 in 2023.

She is once again standing as a list-only candidate in this year's election.

Another Chinese candidate in the blue corner is Carlos Cheung, who defeated Labour's Michael Wood in Auckland's Mt Roskill electorate in 2023.

Cheung would want to replicate his victory from three years ago or secure a higher list ranking this time. He was ranked 48 in National's party list in 2023.

One of the two Labour candidates of Chinese heritage is former MP Naisi Chen (2020-23), who is taking on Swarbrick in Auckland Central this year.

Chen lost to Minister Erica Stanford in the East Coast Bays electorate by more than 20,000 votes in 2023.

She is ranked 35 on Labour's list this time and would be hoping for an increase in her party's vote to enable her to return to Parliament.

Another is three-time Rotorua Lakes councillor Fisher Wang, who is contesting the Rotorua electorate on a Labour ticket.

Considering Trade Minister Todd McClay has held the seat ever since he defeated Labour's Steve Chadwick in 2008, Wang needs to cause a major upset if he is to enter Parliament this time. He is ranked a lowly 68 on the Labour party list.

Two remaining Asian candidates standing for Labour - Naresh Perinpanayagam (list ranking 57) and Sunita Gautam (an electorate-only candidate in the National stronghold of Selwyn) - don't seem likely to secure a seat come November based on current polling.

Ruling coalition partner ACT has named six candidates of Asian origin to date.

Of these, incumbent MP Parmjeet Parmar is likely to return to Parliament if she secures a similar party list ranking as in 2023 based on current polling.

Parmar was ranked nine on ACT's party list three years ago.

Other Asian ACT candidates include Abu Dhabi-born Ali Dahche, who is standing against Luxon in Botany, Himanshu (Ash) Parmar in the Waikato electorate, Malkiat Singh in Papakura, Manu Singh in Māngere and Yang Qu in Mt Roskill.

Himanshu Parmar narrowly missed out last time due to his relatively low party list ranking of 13.

With Waikato historically voting National, Parmar's only realistic hope of making it this time is to secure a list ranking in the single digits based on current polling.

On the other side of the aisle, the Greens have five candidates of Asian heritage, of which at least three are likely to return to the Parliament based on current polling.

These are sitting MPs Lan Pham, who is of Vietnamese heritage (list ranking six), China-born Lawrence Xu-Nan (list ranking eight) and Philippines-born Francisco Hernandez (list ranking 10).

Yasmine Serhan, who is the Green Party's electorate candidate for Glendene and is ranked 18 on the party list, may have to wait another term before she hopes to become New Zealand's first Palestinian MP based on current polling.

The sole Green candidate of South Asian origin is Shreejan Pandey (list ranking 22), who has Nepali heritage.

New Zealand First has declared at least one candidate of Asian origin in Bernadette Soares, who is standing for the party in Upper Harbour.

Soares moved to New Zealand from India in 1989 and runs a beauty product business.

Not new to electoral politics, she was a New Conservative candidate in 2020.

In 2023, she was the Upper Harbour electorate candidate for Destiny Church-linked Hannah Tamaki's party, Vision NZ.

Last but not least is the Opportunity Party, which could upend some of the above scenarios if it hits that 5 percent threshold to get a share of seats in Parliament.

In doing so, Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong could potentially be the first person of Asian heritage to head a political party in Parliament

Wong could even secure Opportunity a place in Parliament if she wins the Mt Albert electorate race.

Five candidates of Asian origin have been named in Opportunity's party list, although none have a realistic chance of making the cut based on current polling, with the party securing six seats if it attains 5 percent of the vote.

World.title: Proposal to scrap RSE worker limits cancelled by Cabinet, documents reveal
World.content:
Immigration Minister Erica Stanford wanted to scrap annual limits on Pacific migrant workers under the Recognised Seasonal Employer (RSE) scheme, but apparently could not get the sign-off from Cabinet.

Stanford made her case in a meeting last month, according to papers released on Wednesday, proposing it would reduce administration costs for RSE employers, while increasing remittances sent back to the Pacific.

Stanford recently announced a swathe of technical changes to the RSE scheme, such as allowing workers to apply for migrant exploitation protection visas, and extending how long an employer could stay in the scheme if they treated their staff properly.

Her office told RNZ Pacific it was considered, but ultimately put aside ahead of the announcement. A decision on the proposal was absent from the decision minutes, suggesting it never got past the committee stage.

The Cabinet paper stated that a limitless scheme would foster a "manageable" increase in workers, though it noted it could further crowd out New Zealand workers - a common criticism of the seasonal worker schemes.

"On balance, I consider this risk low and able to be mitigated," the proposal read.

"Officials will monitor RSE volumes and proportions of the overall workforce and I expect regular reporting on volumes will help identify if there is a need to resume using the cap."

A disdain for the cap from the horticulture industry was flagged, in that the process of allocating how many workers an employer could hire was unfair and complex.

RNZ / Nick Monro

Mixed views

It was noted Pacific partners had mixed views on the proposal, but that no partners expressed "strong concerns" about removing it.

Meanwhile, employers regard the number of beds they can provide as their own effective cap, the paper argued.

It suggested employers were generally prioritising New Zealand workers - who still make up three-quarters of the horticulture workforce, thus explaining why the number of RSE workers coming to New Zealand is typically a few thousand fewer than the cap itself.

"Worker volumes have plateaued since 2022 despite cap increases," it noted.

"Since the cap was first met in 2013, it has consistently been increased in response to demand, suggesting it has rarely been an effective or enduring mechanism for limiting RSE volumes."

Increasing the cap from 19,500 to 20,750 workers for the 2024/25 season featured in the National-ACT coalition agreement when the current term of government began. That level remains today.

At the last general election in 2023, the ACT Party campaigned on scrapping limits, while Stanford's National party campaigned on a smaller increase.

ACT celebrated the RSE changes in a press release from its Agriculture spokesperson, Andrew Hoggard, last week.

"Fruit doesn't wait around for forms to be processed. When it's ready to pick, growers need workers in the orchard," he said.

World.title: Christopher Luxon wants a referendum on MMP - How does the current system work?
World.content:
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon says he will hold a referendum on the MMP voting system if he's elected back into power.

So how does the current MMP voting system work?

Here's what you need to know.

What is MMP?

MMP stands for Mixed Member Proportional representation, the electoral system used in New Zealand.

A majority of New Zealanders voted for it - twice, first in a non-binding referendum in 1992, and again in a binding referendum at the election the following year. It was introduced in the next election, in 1996.

Jim Bolger and Winston Peters at the head of the newly-minted first MMP coalition government in 1996. Supplied

MMP aims to ensure that people will be represented in Parliament both by a person in their local area (electorate), and by a group (a political party).

How does it work?

New Zealanders have two votes - one for a local representative, and one for a political party. You just pick the person in your electorate you think best advances your interests, and the political party that best represents your interests.

Simple, right?

The complexity comes in when trying to calculate how these votes translate into the seats available for members of Parliament (MPs).

There are (typically) 120 seats:

Currently 72 are electorate seats, which are won by candidates standing in specific areas. This will drop to 71 after this election

which are won by candidates standing in specific areas. This will drop to 71 after this election Currently 48 are list seats and are allocated depending on the proportion of party votes won, taking into account the number of electorate seats each party has won. This will rise to 49 after this year's election

Basically, it all means that the proportion of party votes should be about the same as the proportion of seats in the Parliament. Electorate MPs will belong to one party or another unless they're running as an independent, but voters do not need to vote for an electorate representative that matches their party vote.

Other things to consider

A party has to win at least 5 percent of votes or an electorate seat to win a seat in Parliament.

If they win an electorate seat, the party gets allocated a percentage of list seats based on their party vote - known as the "coat tail" rule.

If a party wins more electorates than its share of party votes allows for, extra seats can be added to the Parliament to make up for the "overhang" and ensure the proportions remain correct. For instance, this meant there were 121 MPs in 2005, 122 MPs in 2008 and 121 in 2011. Currenty there are 123 sitting MPs based on the results of the 2023 election.

New Zealanders get two votes under the MMP system. RNZ

So who wins the election?

In contrast to some countries overseas, the United States for example, the election in New Zealand is not voting for the country's leader. People vote only for the parties and electorates.

But someone has to be in charge. Someone has to make sure the organisations doing all the management of the country - funding hospitals and schools, repairing roads and infrastructure, managing prisons - all that administrative stuff, and more, is being done properly.

This responsibility - and the power it entails - belongs to the government.

Who gets to become the government is basically whichever party can get a majority - more than 50 percent - of the seats, based on their party vote. If none of the parties has enough to reach more than 50 percent, they must negotiate with each other about their plans until a combination of the parties has at least half the seats.

This can result in a coalition - where the bigger party and smaller party form a government together and come up with a complete policy plan - or a confidence and supply agreement, where the smaller parties agree to support the main, governing, party on specific policies.

National leader and PM Christopher Luxon. Mark Tantrum

Under confidence and supply, the smaller party does not need to support policies that fall outside the agreement.

With 50 percent of the seats in Parliament, the governing party or coalition can decide what to change about how the country works and enact these decisions in Parliament.

The governing parties have most of the power. The parties that are not governing are known as the opposition, and it is their job to criticise and poke holes in the plans the government is putting forward.

Will MMP ever change?

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has promised to hold a referendum on the system if re-elected in November - along with looking at extended the parliamentary term to four years.

But while not everyone likes MMP, last time it was checked, more people wanted to keep it than replace it.

In the 2011 election, a referendum - much like the recreational cannabis and end of life choice referendums in the 2020 election - was held to see if MMP was still the preferred way of doing things.

The referendum asked two questions: whether voters wanted to keep MMP or replace it, and what system would be preferred if it was changed. Almost 58 percent of voters wanted to keep it, an increase of 3.91 over the 1993 binding referendum.

World.title: City Rail Link opening date officially revealed - but billboards got in first
World.content:
City Rail Link - a project that has been discussed in one way or another for 100 years - is finally opening.

The CRL is New Zealand's largest transportation infrastructure project, and construction has been going on for the past 10 years.

Transport Minister Chris Bishop and Auckland mayor Wayne Brown made the formal announcement of its opening date of 13 September at one of the new stations - Karanga-a-Hape Station - on Thursday morning.

But that wasn't before billboards announcing the opening date of the $5.5 billion project were put up in error around the CBD in the early morning hours.

An AT spokesperson told RNZ they were put up in error and only supposed to be displayed after the official announcement.

"It was a mistake by the billboard provider," they said.

At the announcement, Bishop said he was "thrilled" to announce the opening date, marking a turning point for Auckland.

In just five and a half weeks' time, Bishop said trains would be running all the way through the middle of the city, creating faster journeys and seeing more frequent trains.

People won't have to worry about missing the train because another would be arriving just a few minutes later.

Bishop said the project had been talked about since the 1920s and he was proud to be the minister who got to deliver it.

He said it had not been easy.

City Rail Link is opening on 13 September. RNZ / Irra Lee

Aucklanders have had to live with the project for a decade, disrupting local businesses and closing roads, meaning communities experiences hardships.

But Bishop said once people jump on the first train, they would realise it's all been worth it.

At the announcement, Brown said "finally, we did something ahead of time".

"We announced it this morning, accidentally."

Brown said the project would change the way Auckanders travel and make a better, faster and cheaper way for people to get around.

He said he had strong feelings on how much the project had cost but it was an investment that would ultimately get Auckland moving.

Supplied / Auckland Transport

Auckland Transport chief executive Stacey van der Putten said the early announcement of the opening date was disappointing.

"Things happen, it's a bummer", she said.

Van der Putten said it was a "content loading issue" with the advertising supplier and the issue had been raised.

She said mistakes happen and while it happened on the actual day of the announcement, "it's a bummer".

Bishop said, "at the end of the day, who cares?"

He joked that he hoped AT would get some "cost savings on future ".

Supplied / Auckland Transport

CRL open days

Auckland Transport, City Rail Link Limited and KiwiRail will be opening the new stations to the public through a series of 'First Look' events. These will be free, ticketed sessions, but numbers will be limited.

They will be held over consecutive Saturdays in August: 8 August - First Look at Maungawhau, 15 August - First Look at Karanga-a-Hape, 22 August - First Look at Te Waihorotiu.

The free tickets for these will be available one week ahead of each event.

World.title: FIFA pledges 'full support' for Infantino and apologises for sell-off plan
World.content:
FIFA says it has apologised to its member associations for mistakes made over its abandoned proposal to sell commercial rights linked to the World Cup, as the governing body's leadership reaffirmed its support for president Gianni Infantino after a crisis meeting in Morocco.

Following the meeting in Rabat, attended by Mr Infantino, secretary general Mattias Grafström and members of FIFA's management board, FIFA said its leadership had reaffirmed its full support for the president while acknowledging that the handling of the withdrawn FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal should have been different.

In a statement, FIFA said a separate letter had been sent to FIFA Council members and the 211 member associations apologising for the errors and promising a review.

It added that, with the proposal withdrawn, FIFA would "no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process" and would take all necessary measures to protect its reputation.

Vehicles believed to be carrying Mr Infantino and Mr Grafström were seen leaving FIFA's Africa office in Sale after the meeting, which came amid mounting criticism of Mr Infantino's leadership ahead of next year's presidential election.

The meeting followed last week's withdrawal of a proposal to sell a 20 per cent stake in a new commercial rights entity to private investors in a deal that would have raised about $4.2 billion for football development.

The proposal, which also drew scrutiny because of the involvement of a company with family links to US President Donald Trump, prompted fierce criticism from European soccer's governing body UEFA and other stakeholders, who accused FIFA of poor governance and a lack of consultation.

Gianni Infantino's closeness to US President Donald Trump has been criticised. (Getty Images: Eva Marie Uzcategui)

The apology underscored FIFA's acknowledgement that mistakes had been made in the handling of his proposal for a new commercial rights body, which has become the most serious challenge to his leadership since he became FIFA president in 2016 after triggering a torrent of criticism from UEFA, several member associations and senior FIFA officials over governance and consultation.

His backdown last Friday has done little to assuage those critics, most notably UEFA, which accused him of selling the soul of the game and has said it no longer has confidence in his leadership.

That has cast a shadow over Mr Infantino's re-election for a fourth term at the FIFA Congress in Morocco in March, which had looked like a foregone conclusion two months ago.

A handful of European federations have withdrawn their backing for the Swiss Italian, but perhaps more damaging are the messages coming from Infantino's FIFA colleagues.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also questioned Mr Infantino's leadership on Wednesday, saying he has lost confidence in the FIFA president after learning senior advisers had not been consulted on the abandoned proposal.

"I don't have confidence in Mr Infantino," Mr Carney told reporters, adding that failing to inform senior executives and fellow board members of such a significant proposal "should be fatal" for any leader.

Mr Grafström had sent an internal memo to staff lamenting the "sad and reproachable series of events" that led to the project being "permanently abandoned", two sources told Reuters.

"Individuals, unstable moments and unfortunate episodes come and go. The institution, its mission and its responsibility towards world football continue," the Swede added in the letter, which made no mention of Mr Infantino by name.

His words echoed those of FIFA's Chief Operating Officer Kevin Lamour, who said last week that staff had been "deceived" over the plan, which he described as the project of one person.

Mr Infantino's senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro resigned in protest at the plan last week. Arsene Wenger, FIFA's chief of Global Football Development, said he had not been involved in drafting the proposal, and called the decision to withdraw it "absolutely necessary".

Former Portugal great Luis Figo, who had planned to run for the FIFA presidency in 2015, said Infantino should resign over the affair, while UEFA Vice-President Laura McAllister told Reuters the controversy surrounding the abandoned proposal had brought the FIFA president's leadership to a crisis point.

Mr Infantino has spent the past week in Morocco, which will co-host the World Cup in 2030 and whose football association has announced its continued support for him.

Gianni Infantino has garnered the support of FIFA's executive, but many national governing bodies are sharpening their knives. (AP: Eduardo Verdugo, File)

The meeting was widely seen as an effort to reinforce support for Mr Infantino and ensure that he emerges from the crisis with enough backing to remain the favourite for re-election in March.

An Extraordinary Congress could be called if 43 or more FIFA member associations make a formal written request for one.

Qatar, which hosted the 2022 World Cup, Kuwait, Lebanon, Sri Lanka, Indonesia and the Philippines have declared their loyalty to Mr Infantino.

Mr Infantino has always enjoyed a lot of support away from the traditional heartlands of the game, where impoverished football associations rely on FIFA's largesse to operate.

But European Leagues, which represents more than 1,300 clubs across Europe, said FIFA must not be allowed to "continue taking unilaterally disruptive decisions" that affect clubs, players and fans.

It also criticised the "impractically short assessment timeline" of four weeks given by FIFA to study the plan to expand the World Cup from 48 to 64 teams for the 2030 edition.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Leading African football administrators have sent messages of support as Mr Infantino looks to the continent's 54 members for backing. The African confederation (CAF) has yet to take a stance.

The executive committee of the smallest and least wealthy regional confederation, Oceania, will meet next Wednesday to discuss their approach.

Under FIFA rules, the vote of San Marino, whose men's team are ranked 211th and last in the world rankings, counts as much as that of World Cup winners like Brazil, Germany, Argentina and Spain.

One clear advantage for Mr Infantino as he looks to extend his presidency until 2031 is that no clear candidate to stand against him in March's election has yet emerged.

Jordan FA President Prince Ali bin Hussein has twice stood for the post, and he made his position clear on Tuesday when he accused FIFA of "blackmail", saying it had offered to help solve problems in exchange for endorsing Mr Infantino.

"We did not endorse him before and certainly will not now," Prince Ali wrote on social media.

A FIFA spokesperson rejected reports that Mr Infantino had made promises over the host of the 2030 World Cup final.

"It is false and misleading to claim the FIFA president has made any promise in relation to hosting the FIFA World Cup 2030 Final. A decision will be made by FIFA in due course," the spokesperson said.

Reuters

World.title: Vollering win sets up three-way Tour de France Femmes fight
World.content:
Dutch rider Demi Vollering won a sprint finish against her two main rivals to take stage five of the Tour de France Femmes, with Switzerland's Marlen Reusser coming in second to hold on to the overall lead.

Poland's Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM) looked to have stolen a march with 300 metres remaining, but Vollering (FDJ United-Suez) took off in pursuit and hit the front close to the line.

"I knew Kasia would go early, because she always does," Vollering said after Wednesday's win.

"I knew Marlen would gamble, so I let her gamble a bit to try and make her work, but she didn't. I gave it everything until the final sprint, and I needed every single metre in the last finish straight."

A gruelling up-and-down 140-km ride from Mâcon to Belleville-en-Beaujolais with eight categorised climbs brought the expected shake-up in the general classification, but the top two remained the same.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Reusser, who won Tuesday's individual time trial to move into yellow, holds a 12-second lead over 2023 winner Vollering, with Niewiadoma-Phinney moving up to third overall, one minute 17 seconds behind the leader.

Last year's winner Pauline Ferrand-Prévot struggled on the final climbs, and the French rider is now five minutes behind Reusser.

Mountains classification leader Puck Pieterse took maximum points on the first six climbs, and was part of a 19-rider breakaway with over 75 km remaining, but they were reeled in by the yellow-jersey group after the penultimate climb.

Niewiadoma-Phinney, the 2024 winner, appeared set to win her first Tour de France stage, but Vollering had other ideas and put in a blistering finish.

Vollering and Niewiadoma-Phinney have always finished on the final podium since the race began in 2022, and are well on course to do so again, with Reusser defending a slender lead with four stages left.

"Marlen has not won a Tour yet, and she will have to work for it as well. I'm sure it will be a hard battle, because she is not the rider who you can beat easily, because she is very strong," Vollering said.

Thursday's stage six is a 153.4-km hilly ride from Montbrison to Tournon-sur-Rhône.

Reuters

World.title: LIV Golf secures lifeline 'lead investor' for player-driven future
World.content:
LIV Golf has secured a "lead investor" to keep the lights on, and the league will move forward with players becoming majority equity holders, chief executive Scott O'Neil has announced.

A signed agreement is in place with the unnamed investor and has been approved by the LIV Golf board, O'Neil said.

The transaction is expected to close in September. No details on the amount of capital infusion were announced.

Multiple reports said LIV Golf will return next season with 10 events: five international and five in the United States.

Dark clouds have been looming over the PGA Tour and DP World Tour rival since Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) announced this spring that it will stop funding the league at the end of 2026.

The PIF reportedly invested $US5 billion ($7 billion) in the project since it launched in 2022.

LIV Golf cancelled its New Orleans event in June and reportedly has nixed its season-ending team championship, scheduled for later this month in Michigan. At least one report said that the league was considering filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection.

On Wednesday, local time, O'Neil said the new agreement will "play a key role in supporting the path forward for the League's next era, driven by and for the players".

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"We're also seeing strong interest from more than a dozen additional parties to potentially serve as minority investors, creating a multi-partner model built for long-term stability and growth," he said.

"Notably, our next chapter will make our players the majority equity holders in LIV Golf, a first for a major global sports league, and gives the League the foundation to keep growing the game worldwide. We anticipate finalising terms in the coming weeks, with the goal of entering a transaction in September.

"In the meantime, our focus is on delivering a great week for fans and players at Bedminster and finishing the 2026 season strong."

No details on the framework for the players' proposed equity stakes were provided.

Ever since the PIF pulled the financial plug, LIV Golf had been in the market for investments between $250 and $350 million, according to Sportico.

Speaking to 891 ABC Adelaide, Australian Golf Digest Magazine managing editor Steve Keipert said the announcement is promising for the tour's Adelaide pit stop in March, which had been threatened by the Saudi funding withdrawal.

"If this investor is signed on … at least for 2027 you would imagine the league would be going ahead in some capacity, and you would think that Adelaide would be top of the list," Mr Kepiert.

"There might not be many LIV events, in fact they're talking it could be more like 10 rather than the 14 we've been seeing.

"But you would imagine that Adelaide, given what's been built there and the success of it on its own, would be top of the list to stay on, at least next year."

The SA government has a significant stake in the league's survival, having cleared swathes of parkland to expand the North Adelaide Golf Course in the face of community pushback.

LIV Golf returns to action with its New York tournament this weekend, beginning Thursday at Trump National Golf Club in Bedminster, New Jersey.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: 'Gone down like a lead balloon': Ex-FA boss on FIFA's World Cup backflip
World.content:
"It's gone down like a lead balloon."

This is David Gallop's view of FIFA president Gianni Infantino's now-infamous World Cup privatisation proposal.

"It's so far off passing the pub test that I think it's like he let off a stink bomb in the middle of the pub and people ran screaming, leaving half a schooner behind," Mr Gallop told 7.30.

"That's how poorly it's been received."

Mr Gallop has been one of Australia's foremost sport's administrators. He was CEO of the NRL from 2002-2012 before jumping ship to become the boss of Football Federation Australia for seven years until his tenure ended in 2019.

He has watched on this past week as Mr Infantino's failed sell-off plan has evolved into a full-blown crisis over his leadership.

"He's definitely under pressure now … to throw out an idea like this that's gone down so badly," he said.

Mr Infantino's proposal, dubbed the FIFA Forward Enterprise, would have seen the commercial rights of FIFA's most popular tournaments, including the World Cup, transferred to a private company, and a 20 per cent stake sold to investors, valued at $20 billion.

It's been reported Joshua Kushner, the brother of Jared Kushner, Donald Trump's son-in-law, was one of the private equity figures behind the plan.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino's relationship with US President Donald Trump was under scrutiny at the World Cup. (Reuters: Dylan Martinez)

"Anytime you sell anything, you need to have good, compelling reasons, but particularly so when it comes to something like the World Cup and ... sport in general," Mr Gallop told 7.30.

"You've got to know that you really need to do it. You really need the money. What are you getting for the slice of the asset and what are you giving up?

"Clearly people have not liked the idea that private investment, and therefore, a profit motive that comes away from the game to those private investors would be something that FIFA would contemplate."

'One-off sugar hit'

Mr Gallop said privatisation was not inherently wrong but required an overwhelming strategic and financial case to be valid.

"It will be a mistake to burn the furniture to heat the house," he said.

"You need to be setting up your sport and the business of your sport for sustainability, not for a one-off sugar hit of capital.

"These are the questions that have to be answered when one is looking at private sale of these effectively community assets that people feel strongly about."

FIFA President Gianni Infantino's plan to privatise has been met with derision by many football bodies. (AP: Eduardo Verdugo, File)

The proposal offered FIFA's 211 member federations one-off payments of $20 million each, but Mr Gallop said FIFA's financial position only heightened questions about why such a proposal had been pursued.

"FIFA has $5 billion in cash now after the World Cup," he said.

" I think that's one of the reasons why a proposal to sell an equity stake has fallen so flat. They're not desperate for money. "

Within three days of the proposal, Mr Infantino and FIFA scrapped the plans.

Europe's UEFA, North America's CONCACAF and Asia's AFC, which Australia is member of, all opposed the plan.

UEFA, CONCACAF, as well as a growing number of national federations have taken it further by withdrawing their support of Mr Infantino's leadership.

Football Australia's chair Anter Isaac and CEO Martin Kugeler both declined an interview with 7.30.

The organisation has welcomed the decision by FIFA to scrap the privatisation proposal but is yet to weigh-in on Mr Infantino's, now under siege, leadership.

Mr Gallop said Australia's influence on the world game came less through political power than integrity.

Infantino's 'blotted copybook'

The integrity of Mr Infantino, like that of his predecessor Sepp Blatter has now been called into question.

Former FIFA President Sepp Blatter's tenure ended due to corruption. (Reuters: Stefan Wermuth)

Mr Infantino was elected in 2016 promising to restore confidence in FIFA, following a number of corruption scandals that occurred under Mr Blatter's 17-year reign as president.

Mr Gallop's time at FA straddled the terms of both men. He was also CEO in 2010, when Australia's bid to host the 2022 World Cup was beaten by Qatar, a decision that was mired in controversy and allegations of corruption.

"There was a bit of a stench around FIFA and Gianni came in with a pitch of transparency, accountability, consultation and putting football first," Mr Gallop said.

" I think it's fair to say this proposal, albeit backflipped on, has blotted his copybook in respect to what people expected from him and from his presidency. "

"[Especially} coming hot off the heels of a number of other contentious decisions, including the lifting of the red card on the USA player during the tournament."

United States' Folarin Balogun's red card was rescinded during the World Cup after a call from Trump to Infantino. (AP: Jeff Chiu)

Despite calls for Mr Infantino's resignation growing louder, Mr Gallop said his tenure at the top of world football might not be over just yet.

"I don't think it's necessarily so that he won't get re-elected. He has some big confederations against him at the moment, but he has others where FIFA has carefully funded development in a lot of smaller nations," he said.

Mr Gallop remembers representing Australia at FIFA congresses, sitting next to the small Caribbean nation of Aruba — "a population of a hundred thousand people."

"Behind us would be Brazil … millions of people, an absolute icon of world football … but everyone gets one vote; that's where your confederation structure comes into play," he said.

Mr Gallop believes the president's political future will depend on whether member associations believe the successes achieved under his leadership outweigh the damage caused by the failed privatisation proposal.

" Whether there's enough credit in the bank for all the good things that FIFA have produced … or whether this has blown them up will remain to be seen. "

Fan outrage

Patrick Clancy, head of the Football Supporters Association in Australia, told 7.30 many fans felt betrayed by the proposal.

Football's governing body has long been at the centre of controversy and corruption allegations. (REUTERS: Arnd Wiegmann )

"He's tried to privatise football at the expense of the game of football," he said.

"It's something that came out of nowhere and is not in line with what anyone has thought of before. And so I think that's the concern; where's it all going?"

His organisation is now very keen to understand where Football Australia stands on Mr Infantino and his leadership.

"These are very troubling times in world football and Football Australia needs to make its position very clear," he said.

Mr Clancy says football supporters want to see the game run properly.

"They want to feel that there is a degree of integrity and they don't want a money-hungry organisation that seems to be interfering with that organic nature of the game," he said.

"Within 24 hours, Infantino and FIFA completely changed the shape of world football.

" They blindsided almost everyone in the game, so goodness knows what's going to happen in the next seven days. "

World.title: Australia's coach says no tour match ahead of India Test series
World.content:
Australia will again opt for a training camp ahead of the five-Test tour of India rather than play ​a traditional warm-up match before attempting to end a 22-year wait for a Test series victory on the subcontinent.

Australia also chose not to play a tour match before ​the 2023 series, ‌instead training on specially prepared, spin-friendly pitches in Bengaluru before the opening Test.

The decision drew scrutiny after India won the Nagpur opener by an innings ‌and 132 runs, setting the tone for a 2-1 series ⁠victory that allowed the hosts to retain the Border-Gavaskar ‌Trophy.

Ifs, buts and maybes for Australia in India The record books will show that Australia left India without the Border-Gavaskar Trophy, but the series defeat offers plenty of opportunity for introspection ahead of the Ashes.

Head coach Andrew McDonald ​said Australia would scout ‌a location to immerse themselves in conditions similar to India before the series opener in Nagpur starting on January 21.

"We've got a couple of options there," he told Cricket Australia website Cricket.com.au ​on ‌Wednesday.

"We have gone to the UAE previously and we have also gone into India last time into Bengaluru, so we're ⁠just working through what that ‌would look like in terms ‌of how we then manage the individuals."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Australia has not won a Test ‌series in India since 2004 when Adam Gilchrist's side triumphed 2-1.

Australia have a gruelling schedule before they ‌arrive in ​India, with a ⁠two-Test home series starting against Bangladesh in Darwin next week followed by a three-Test tour of South Africa in October and another four-Test home series against New Zealand from December ⁠9.

Fast bowler Michael Neser has been ruled out of the Bengaluru series with a ‌calf strain suffered ‌at training in Brisbane but McDonald said wicketkeeper-batter ​Josh Inglis was expected to be available after recovering from a back spasm.

Reuters

World.title: Tony Modra medical record probe expands to extra staffer
World.content:
Another staff member is being investigated for allegedly inappropriately accessing the private medical records of AFL legend Tony Modra, SA Health has confirmed.

Modra was seriously injured in a truck crash at Back Valley, near Victor Harbor on South Australia's Fleurieu Peninsula, in June, and later underwent facial surgery.

Last month, SA Health said three staff were being investigated for allegedly inappropriately accessing the private medical records of the former Crow, while a further five employees were also being "assessed" to determine whether their access was "always appropriate".

In a statement, SA Health today said the investigation was ongoing.

Police were called to the scene of the truck crash, near Victor Harbor. (Supplied: SA Police)

"One additional SA Health staff member is under investigation for potential inappropriate access of a patient record, following an audit that identified eight staff members who remain under investigation," the statement said.

"In total, nine staff members are part of the current investigation, which is ongoing."

The alleged breaches are not the first time that concerns have been raised about SA Health staff inappropriately accessing patient records in cases involving high-profile individuals.

In 2016, 13 hospital staff were sanctioned after being caught snooping on the medical records of Cy Walsh, who was charged with the stabbing murder of his father — Crows coach Phil Walsh — before being found not guilty by reason of mental incompetence.

In 2024, ABC News revealed an SA Health investigation had found 18 staff engaged in misconduct or inappropriately accessed the medical records of a patient understood to be Charlie Stevens, the late son of SA Police Commissioner Grant Stevens.

Tony Modra was injured while driving a truck at Back Valley in June. (Supplied: 9News Adelaide)

SA Health has previously apologised to Modra's family.

The department has also previously said it regularly conducted audits "to ensure that staff are accessing appropriate information".

"Any staff member who has accessed information inappropriately may be subject to disciplinary processes, which may include termination of their employment," SA Health said previously.

Last month, Modra posted an update on his progress on social media, saying he was "getting out and about" and praising the medical staff involved in his recovery.

World.title: Hawks' Wizard looking to pull off Coleman medal shock
World.content:
Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell has sung the praises of Nick Watson as the 170cm "Wizard" attempts to snare what would be one of the most unlikely and magical Coleman medals in VFL/AFL history.

Watson's five-goal haul in last week's 16-point win over North Melbourne lifted his season tally to 52 goals.

It means Watson became the first player since Syd Dyer and Lou Richards in 1946 to kick 50-plus goals in a season despite being 170cm or shorter.

Sydney's 194cm forward Charlie Curnow leads this year's Coleman medal count with 57 goals, with Gold Coast's 202cm spearhead Ben King (53 goals) in second and Watson lurking in third.

AFL round 21 Saturday live updates Josh Fraser's bid to become Carlton's next full-time coach receives a massive boost as the Blues record a thumping win over the Brisbane Lions.

Hawthorn face Brisbane at the Gabba on Friday night before rounding out their home-and-away campaign against Collingwood and West Coast.

A big finish from Watson could be enough to snare him the Coleman, and although Mitchell says the Hawks won't go out of their way to target him in the next three weeks, they would celebrate his achievement if he gets there.

"It'd be great if it happened," Mitchell said.

"But he's young and he's got plenty of opportunities in front of him.

"I certainly hope that's not the focus of the lads going into a game like this. But I won't be shying away from it if he gets that opportunity, of course."

Watson, fondly dubbed "The Wizard", is already a superstar of the competition despite being just 21 years old and 61 games into his AFL career.

"The level of consistency is probably the best thing that we've got from Wizard this year," Mitchell said.

"And it's probably one season earlier than most. He's certainly maturing. Like, he's 21 years old and he's quite popular, and how he handles that is really impressive."

Third-placed Hawthorn (14-5-1) haven't won at the Gabba since 2016, but they have only played three games at the venue since then.

Mitchell wants his team to use Friday's blockbuster against two-time defending premiers Brisbane (13-7) as an interstate finals rehearsal.

"I think if you look at the ladder most Victorian teams are going to have to win interstate at some point, and this is a start for us," said Mitchell, who earlier this week re-signed with Hawthorn until the end of 2030.

The Hawks have a number of selection queries heading into the crunch clash with Ned Reeves (knee), Karl Amon (knee), Mitch Lewis (concussion) and Henry Hustwaite (face) all under injury clouds.

Meanwhile, an American court has formally dismissed charges against Hawthorn player Connor Macdonald for his off-season misadventure.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Macdonald and teammate Dylan Moore spent a night in a US jail after being charged with trespassing for climbing onto a cherry picker.

Moore's case was wrapped up last month, while Macdonald's case has also now been concluded with the pair having previously agreed to complete a substance abuse counselling program.

"It's probably nice for them to have it off their back," Mitchell said.

"They're both having really good seasons and really pleased with their performances. Sometimes dealing with adversity can make you grow, and I think they've both done that this year."

AAP

World.title: Pay war on ice as Australia's netball stars sign truce
World.content:
A pay war has been averted — for now — after Australia's Super Netball players agreed to an updated collective player agreement for 2027.

Under the new collective player agreement (CPA), Super Netball players will receive improved pay and conditions, more time off and greater ability to sign individual sponsorship deals.

The 12-month bridging agreement to the CPA has been agreed between Netball Australia, the Super Netball clubs and the Australian Netball Players' Association (ANPA).

It means Super Netball clubs can start contracting players and preparing for the 2027 campaign.

Before this week's agreement went through, players had been in contract limbo.

Netball agents frustrated as pay talks roll into Glasgow 2026 Messy and drawn-out pay negotiations are once again overshadowing a major tournament for the Aussie Diamonds.

The protracted pay dispute also meant plans to expand Super Netball had been placed on hold until at least 2028, despite a new five-year broadcast deal with the Nine Network starting in 2027.

With the CPA now locked in for 2027, attention will turn to a longer-term deal for 2028 and beyond in coming months, with Netball Australia hoping to avoid a repeat of a drawn-out pay dispute.

The ANPA want a revenue-share model, as well as better pregnancy and parental leave policies as part of a longer-term deal.

Netball Australia interim chief executive Mark Falvo said the 12-month bridging agreement struck the right balance between delivering immediate benefits for players, while also positioning the sport for future growth.

"We are at a pivotal moment for our sport," Falvo said in a statement.

"This agreement gives our players, clubs and the league certainty while we enter a period of significant commercial opportunity for netball.

"There is more work to do on meeting some of the asks for the athletes and the clubs, but this agreement delivers meaningful outcomes for players today while demonstrating our responsibility to balance the long-term sustainability of the league."

The news of the fresh CPA comes on the back of Sports Entertainment Group (SEG), headed by Craig Hutchison, putting the final touches on their takeover of the licence of the Giants Super Netball club.

SEG already owns the Melbourne Mavericks as well as multiple basketball clubs, with the Giants set to become the latest franchise to go under their SEN Teams banner.

The flurry of netball news comes just days after the Australian Diamonds suffered a shock 46-45 semi-final loss to Jamaica at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

The Diamonds were hot favourites to snare gold, but had to settle for bronze with a 80-65 win over England in the third-versus-fourth play-off match.

Although New Zealand walked away with the gold medal, their domestic competition faces an uncertain future after losing around $3.7 million in 2026.

With no broadcast deal in place, rumours are bubbling the Premiership in New Zealand could be placed on hold for 2027, or downgraded to amateur status.

It means a flurry of Kiwi players could seek out Super Netball deals for next year as they seek financial security.

New CPA deal:

Increase to the total player payment pool (minimum and maximum amounts) by greater than the Consumer Price Index (CPI)

Players to receive a one-off payment upon the signing of a commercial partner for the Super Netball league

Additional time off through condensing hours for club commitments that will free up an additional two weeks of time off per year

Option for athletes to enter into multi-year contracts

Greater ability for athletes to secure their own individual sponsorship deals

Increased health insurance and meal allowances

AAP

Tech.title: X product chief Nikita Bier is leaving after one year
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

X head of product Nikita Bier is stepping down and says he will move into a role as an advisor, writing that “it’s time to pass the torch and demote myself to my natural state: a poster.” He shared the update just over a month after celebrating his one-year anniversary on the job, and just weeks after Elon Musk’s combined SpaceX / X / xAI companies went public.

He says that “almost every aspect of X” has been rebuilt while he was head of product, including its timeline, Android app, chat, and notifications. Going forward, the “next leaders” mentioned are Benji Taylor leading design with iOS lead Jonah Katz and Mridul Singhai leading the product team.

Bier also called out the long-delayed and recently-launched X Money, which Elon Musk at one point expected to launch by the end of 2024. During his tenure, X has continued to focus on incentivizing native posts and login requirements for access to features, and last month Bier said that missing data from the X algorithm had made the platform feel like a “battleground.”

Bier previously co-founded the startups tbh (acquired by Meta) and Gas (acquired by Discord). He was appointed to lead product just days before former X CEO Linda Yaccarino stepped down, and has been a public face of the company ever since.

Tech.title: Two of Ring’s latest video doorbells are a lot cheaper than usual
Tech.content:
Ring’s Wired Doorbell Pro and Battery Doorbell Plus are two of the brand’s most well-rounded video doorbells, whether you’re looking for a hardwired model or one that runs on a battery. Right now, its Wired Doorbell Pro is down to $199 ($50 off) at Amazon and Best Buy, while the Battery Doorbell Plus is on sale for $119.99 ($60 off) at Amazon and Best Buy. Both deals are the second-best prices we’ve seen, just $20 shy of their Prime Day lows.

Aside from how they’re powered, the main difference between the two comes down to video quality. The Wired Doorbell Pro records sharper 4K video, and it can automatically respond to visitors with prerecorded messages. The Battery Doorbell Plus has fewer features and can capture video in slightly less sharp 2K resolution. Beyond that, the two doorbells share many of the same core features.

Both can provide a head-to-toe view of your doorstep and support motion detection, two-way talk, and support for color night vision. If you’re willing to pay $4.99 for a monthly subscription, you also get more specific alerts for people, packages, and vehicles. Upgrading to the $19.99 Ring Pro plan, meanwhile, grants access to extra AI features like facial recognition and text-based activity summaries, all of which are free for the first month. Both also work well with Amazon Alexa, allowing you to view a live feed on a compatible Echo Show smart display and receive audible announcements when someone rings your doorbell.

Tech.title: Uber CEO brushes off reports of a Waymo break-up
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After Uber and Waymo ended their partnership in Phoenix earlier this year, experts and robotaxi watchers wondered whether the companies’ improbable bromance was fraying. Not so, Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said today. The two companies are committed to continue working together in Atlanta and Austin, and the partnership remains “very strong.”

“Waymo is a very important partner of ours, and we continue to operate in Austin and Atlanta,” Khosrowshahi said in an earnings call today. “We believe we’ll continue to operate next year in those marketplaces. It’s a terrific product, and the on-the-ground partnership continues to be very strong.”

There’s been plenty of evidence that points to a weaker relationship than Khosrowshahi would like to admit, like Uber’s CTO tweeting about a “scary Waymo moment” and an Uber white paper that emphasizes a hybrid model of human- and robot-powered rides over an AV-only model. Last month, the two companies found each other on opposite sides of a bill in Washington, DC, that would legalize robotaxi services, with Waymo supportive and Uber pushing for a hybrid model.

Khosrowshahi didn’t address any of those incidents, but did note that Waymo isn’t Uber’s only robotaxi partner.

“We want to make sure that we’re not dependent on one partner,” he said on the call. “We’re absolutely seeing a plethora of newer players in the AV ecosystem, just like you see in the foundation model space. While we continue to provide a great service with Waymo in Austin and Atlanta, we’ll continue to build our services with our other players as well.”

Indeed, Uber has made a big to-do about linking up with a variety of AV partners, including Zoox, Wayve, Avride, Nuro, Motional, and Waabi. Basically, if you’re a startup with some autonomous driving experience and a few vehicles in the field, chances are you’ve received a call from Uber. The company has said it plans on spending upwards of $10 billion to build out its robotaxi business over time.

But Waymo is really the only one doing it at scale. And since the company has shown it can work in markets both with and without Uber’s imprimatur, it really seems like Uber needs Waymo more than vice versa.

But while Khosrowshahi doesn’t sound ready to break up with Waymo any time soon, he also wasn’t willing to concede that robot-driven cars would quickly become the norm. In fact, Khosrowshahi’s next move was to downplay the significance of robotaxi rides on the company’s platform, noting that they only account for “less than 0.5 percent of our overall trip volume.” Physical AI — which is industry lingo for real-world AI like robots and driverless cars — is moving at a slower pace than large-language models like ChatGPT. And in time, a Waymo competitor may emerge to challenge the Alphabet-owned company’s dominance.

“We have time to develop the partnerships with our other set of partners to create a competitive playing field with attractive commercials,” Khosrowshahi added.

Khosrowshahi’s reticence is understandable. Uber and Waymo may be partners in a couple of markets, but the companies are mostly competitors. And early data suggests that Waymo is taking away market share from traditional rideshare players like Uber and Lyft. The two companies may still need each other now, while robotaxis are in their infancy, but the future is more of an open question.
